title: When Influencers Promote Dupes: Effects of Influencer-Endorsed Lookalikes on Perceptions of the Original Brand
affiliations: University of Delhi - Shaheed Bhagat Singh College

detail.title: When Influencers Promote Dupes: Effects of Influencer-Endorsed Lookalikes on Perceptions of the Original Brand

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Participation in the survey was voluntary and completely anonymous. Informed consent was obtained from all respondents prior to data collection.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted as an independent college research project.

detail.abstract: Luxury dupes, which are lower-priced products designed to resemble identifiable luxury items, are widely circulated on social media. Influencers often present these products as affordable alternatives to the originals. Prior research has examined motivations for purchasing dupes, the effects of dupe culture on perceived value, and the broader consequences of copycat products for premium brands. However, little research has directly examined how an influencer's endorsement of a brand-specific dupe affects perceptions of the original brand. This exploratory pretest-posttest survey (N = 70) used a mock influencer post comparing the Coach Tabby bag with an affordable dupe. At the full-sample level, exposure produced small, statistically non-significant changes in perceived authenticity, exclusivity, and purchase consideration for the original brand. However, perceived dupe legitimacy and endorsement-based normalization were significantly associated with changes in purchase consideration. Participants who regarded the dupe as legitimate or viewed the endorsement as normalizing dupe purchases reported decreases of 0.45 and 0.44 points, respectively, whereas participants who did not hold these views reported slight increases. These findings suggest that the implications of dupe-promoting content may vary according to whether audiences regard the dupe as a legitimate substitute, rather than according to exposure alone.

title: From Woodstock to the Soundtracks of Automotive Television Advertising: The Strange Journey of Folk-Rock Counterculture

detail.title: From Woodstock to the Soundtracks of Automotive Television Advertising: The Strange Journey of Folk-Rock Counterculture

declarations.declarationOfInterest: is not applicable
declarations.ethicsApproval: is not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: is not applicable

detail.abstract: This chapter examines the process of semiotic recuperation of folk-rock music from the 1960s-1970s by the automotive advertising industry since the 1990s. The approach mobilises theoretical frameworks from Information and Communication Sciences (ICS) and sociology: Barthes's theory of myth (depoliticised connotation), Baudrillard's orders of simulacrum, the anthropology of the imaginary (Durand, Monneyron and Mathieu) and retro-branding models (Brown et al.). Drawing primarily on Thomas Frank's thesis and Fred Turner's research on the hippie roots of Silicon Valley and the American technology industry, the study postulates the co-creation of countercultural contestation by advertising from the outset of the American advertisers' "Creative Revolution", establishing at the turn of the 1960s a dynamic of "hip consumerism" and "cool attitude" whereby the critique of consumption becomes the fuel for the very market so harshly criticised by the texts of folk song pioneers. The semiotic and multimodal analysis of case studies (Nick Drake, The Beatles, Bob Dylan, Simon & Garfunkel, etc.) and a corpus of 62 TV advertising campaigns by various automotive manufacturers (1991-2026) reveals a patrimonialisation (Davallon)/transformation cycle spanning more than sixty years: counterculture → myth → simulacrum → consumption. The findings reveal the conversion of folk-rock's original musical meaning-political contestation, marginal authenticity-into market values, stripping the works of their critical substance. The study ultimately highlights the acceleration of this cycle in the digital era, with the rapid exhaustion of the indie-folk wave. The recuperation of original folk-rock is not analysed as a betrayal of the values carried by this musical genre, but as the logical and rational fulfilment of the countercultural project, which already contained from its origins its own ambivalence.

detail.abstract: Although small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are engines of economic growth, studies on SMEs' shift towards sustainable digital practices remain scarce. SMEs using traditional ecommerce tools prioritise efficiency and profitability at the expense of sustainability, resulting in environmental and social issues. Current research on the adoption of green e-commerce practices among enterprises seems skewed towards large corporations or developed markets, leaving critical knowledge gaps on SMEs. This systematic literature review integrates scholarly evidence about green e-commerce adoption and its effect on SMEs' performance. The SPIDER framework, PRISMA guidelines and citation chaining mechanisms were applied on platforms such as EBSCOhost, Google scholar, and Web of Science to retrieve data. Yielding 52 eligible articles; the papers met predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Findings show that green ecommerce enhances SMEs' performance across the economic, social and environmental dimensions by: driving marketing and financial growth, fostering adaptive leadership, trust and green innovations and eco-processes that curb carbon emissions. While leadership, Human Resource Management (HRM) and digital readiness drive adoption from within organisations, external factors such as government support and market competition speed-up the process. Notwithstanding this, progress is hindered by high costs, complex regulations and digital divides. Future research should be directed towards sector-specific adoption, longitudinal impacts and contemporary technologies such as blockchain and green fintech for knowledge-deepening. title: Marketing in Times of Disasters and Crises: From Opportunistic Promotion to Responsible Value Creation

detail.title: Marketing in Times of Disasters and Crises: From Opportunistic Promotion to Responsible Value Creation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Social media community
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funding

detail.abstract: Disasters and crises significantly transform the economic, social, and behavioral environment in which organizations operate. This paper examines the role of marketing in disaster contexts, focusing on the intersection between corporate social responsibility (CSR), crisis communication, digital marketing, and stakeholder engagement. Drawing on a conceptual review of the relevant literature, the study develops a framework for understanding how corporate responses to disasters can create both social and organizational value. Particular attention is given to the role of social media as a tool for information dissemination, community engagement, resource mobilization, and corporate communication. The paper distinguishes responsible disaster marketing from opportunistic promotional practices and identifies perceived authenticity, need alignment, transparency, timing, and stakeholder engagement as key determinants of stakeholder responses. A set of research propositions is developed to guide future empirical investigation. The paper also highlights the Algerian context as a promising setting for examining corporate marketing and CSR practices during natural disasters, particularly forest fires and floods.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: As climate change intensifies, nature-based sports tourism, particularly ski tourism, faces increasing environmental and operational challenges. Although artificial ski resorts have emerged as an adaptive response to climate-related risks, their sustainability implications remain insufficiently examined, especially in comparison with natural snow resorts. Guided by the Stimulus–Organism–Response framework, this study investigates how skiing involvement, destination loyalty, perceived environmental quality, and perceptions of climate change function as key stimuli shaping internal psychological states and pro-environmental behavior across natural and artificial ski resort contexts in China. A mixed-methods approach was adopted. First, 20 interviews were conducted to develop context-specific measurement items. Subsequently, survey data from 673 skiers were analyzed using structural equation modeling and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis. The results show that skiing involvement, loyalty, and climate change awareness significantly enhance place attachment and environmental responsibility, which in turn promote pro-environmental behavior. Multi-group analyses further indicate that climate change perceptions exert stronger effects on place attachment and environmental responsibility among visitors to natural snow resorts than among those visiting artificial resorts. These findings extend the application of the S–O–R framework in ski tourism research and offer practical insights for resort managers seeking to foster environmental stewardship and sustainability-oriented engagement under varying snow conditions.

title: From Virtual Experiences to Real Vacations: Linking Virtual Reality Headset Adoption, Pro-environmental Behaviour, and Destination Visit Intention among Generation Z
affiliations: “Dunarea de Jos” University of Galati, “Dunarea de Jos” University of Galati and University Dunarea De Jos Galati

detail.title: From Virtual Experiences to Real Vacations: Linking Virtual Reality Headset Adoption, Pro-environmental Behaviour, and Destination Visit Intention among Generation Z

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest related to this work.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no funding.

detail.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) headsets offer new opportunities for destination exploration and sustainable tourism experiences. Grounded in the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) framework, this study examines the effects of VR headset facilitating conditions, performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and social influence on Generation Z's VR headset use intention, while investigating the mediating role of VR-induced proenvironmental behaviour in shaping destination visit intention. Data were collected through an online questionnaire from 147 Generation Z respondents with previous experience using VR headsets for tourism experiences and analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that performance expectancy and social influence significantly increase VR headset use intention, while facilitating conditions and effort expectancy have no significant effects. VR headset use intention positively influences VR-induced pro-environmental behaviour, which subsequently increases destination visit intention. The significant indirect effect further supports the mediating role of VR-induced pro-environmental behaviour. These findings extend the UTAUT framework by linking VR headset adoption with sustainability-oriented responses and destination visit intentions, while providing practical insights for destination management organisations and tourism marketing stakeholders seeking to design immersive tourism experiences for Generation Z.

detail.abstract:
This chapter examines the 2026 shift of workplace AI from productivity support toward embedded decision systems that influence prioritisation, approval, escalation, measurement, and operational outcomes. The central argument is that organisational value increasingly dpends on decision quality rather than output speed alone. As AI assumes greater responsibility for signal processing and recommendations, human work moves toward judgment, accountability, supervision, and continuous learning.

The chapter identifies four major shifts: task execution toward decision supervision, output KPIs toward decision-quality metrics, redesign of middle-management responsibilities, and the elevation of time redeemed as an executive performance measure. It introduces the Decision Quality Index as a governance framework covering outcome lift, consistency, explainability, reversal discipline, and risk containment, alongside a 90-day implementation pathway for building measurable decision systems. The chapter also stresses the importance of verification, escalation, audit trails, access controls, sandboxing, and red-team testing as operating guardrails. The resulting leadership priority is clear: organisations must measure outcomes, redesign decision ownership, reinvest redeemed time, and govern AI-enabled decisions with greater discipline as automation moves deeper into everyday work.

title: Ultranomics: The Apex Economic Stratum of The AI Era

detail.title: Ultranomics: The Apex Economic Stratum of The AI Era

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with other people or organizations that could be perceived to have influenced this study.

detail.abstract: This paper presents the canonical definition of Ultranomics as a distinct economic stratum situated above the classical economy and completing the three-tier stratification (Infranomics -> Classical Economy -> Ultranomics) developed in the author's research programme (Rakhimov, 2026a). The paper explicitly demarcates the stratificational concept of Ultranomics developed here from four adjacent concepts in the growing literature on the political economy of digital and artificial-intelligence-driven capitalism (Boutang, 2011; Srnicek, 2017): AI capitalism (Verdegem, 2022), the political economy of AI as developed in the NBER programme (Goldfarb, Taska, and Teodoridis, 2024), digital intelligence capital as developed in recent macroeconomic modelling (Hoffmann and Wakefield, forthcoming), and surveillance capitalism (Zuboff, 2019). Ultranomics is defined as the economic stratum in which key operations of economic value production are performed by autonomous computational systems, and which possesses its own ontology of objects, agents, value metric, and reproduction regime not reducible to the classical economy. The stratum is constituted by four features: (1) non-human production of economic value, extending the automation literature that traces value displacement from human to machine agents (Brynjolfsson and McAfee, 2014); (2) compute as a factor of production, irreducible to either capital or labour, formalized in recent scaling-law research (Kaplan et al., 2020) and CES production-function estimation (Whitfill and Wu, 2025); (3) ultranomic capital as a novel form of accumulation, introduced in deliberate distinction from the parallel concept of digital intelligence capital; (4) semantic intensity as the internal value metric of the stratum. The paper introduces the Ultranomic Stratification Test (UST), a five-question diagnostic protocol. The paper demarcates Ultranomics from AI capitalism, the NBER political economy of AI programme, digital intelligence capital, and surveillance capitalism, and situates the discussion within the broader formal literature on AI's economic role (Ide and Talamas, 2025) and the material infrastructure of computation (Rella, 2023).

title: Brand Promotion Using Social Media: A Study on The Impact of Social Media Brand Promotion on the Creation of Customer Brands

detail.title: Brand Promotion Using Social Media: A Study on The Impact of Social Media Brand Promotion on the Creation of Customer Brands

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This research relies on secondary data and publicly available case studies and therefore did not require ethics committee approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
This dissertation explores the fundamental paradigm shift in modern marketing, transitioning from traditional, company-centric brand promotion to the era of the “Customer Brand.” Utilising Marty Neumeier’s The Brand Flip (2016) as the primary theoretical framework, the study investigates how social media promotion facilitates the transfer of brand ownership from corporations to “customer tribes.” The research employs a mixed-methods approach, integrating quantitative data from Statista and McKinsey with qualitative case studies of LEGO, Apple, and Starbucks, supplemented by a counter-case study of Pepsi’s 2017 Kendall Jenner advertisement to test the discriminatory power of the framework.

Empirical evidence from Statista reveals a stark “Engagement Paradox”: while global social media ad spend increased to $181.2 billion by 2021, consumer trust in traditional advertising plummeted. The research demonstrates that the most successful brand promotion strategies are no longer built on “Push” mechanics but on the eighteen “Flips” identified by Neumeier, particularly the pivots from Authority to Authenticity and Control to Collaboration. These managerial observations are grounded in the academic literature on neo-tribalism (Maffesoli, 1996; Cova and Cova, 2002), brand community (Muñiz and O’Guinn, 2001; Schau, Muñiz and Arnould, 2009), and the extended self (Belk, 1988), which together explain why the Brand Flip works psychologically as well as strategically. Data from Meta Research and Harvard Business Review further validate that “Discovery Commerce” and User-Generated Content yield significantly higher engagement and purchase intent than brand-owned content.

The findings conclude that social media promotion is most effective when it serves as scaffolding for community identity, allowing customers to become brand evangelists. By flipping the brand narrative, companies can mitigate the rising costs of digital acquisition and build resilient, tribal loyalty. The study closes by extending the framework forward, predicting how Generation Alpha’s convergence of climate consciousness and algorithmic nativity is likely to drive a “stewardship shift” in circular fashion consumption, and outlining the doctoral research agenda this dissertation is intended to anticipate.

detail.abstract: Xiang et al. (2025) conclude that the gambler's fallacy does not originate in biased beliefs. Reanalyzing their data we arrive at the opposite conclusion. We show, more generally, that their main analysis, examining whether the median belief is biased, is nondiagnostic of the presence of the gambler's fallacy, while our test of the share of probability estimates for the streak ending above/below 50% is diagnostic. We also report results from a new study where at least 80% of gambler's fallacy predictions originated in biased beliefs.

title: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of the People, VII: Education, the Capability to Play, and the Wealth-of-the-People Cycle - From the Pure Producer to the Complete Economic Agent
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.abstract:
Since Schultz, Becker, and Mincer, the economics of education has understood education principally as investment in human capital: it raises knowledge, skills, and labor productivity, and thereby future income. Michael (1973) extended the returns to non-market production; Scitovsky (1976) argued that enjoyment is a skill that must be acquired; Sen (1999) assigned the conversion of resources into welfare to conversion factors. Under the unified people's-wealth vector Z and its partial order PW, what matters is not only whether a person can produce income, but whether a person can convert income and time into real welfare at a bearable acquisition cost. This paper asks what that conversion capacity forms once aggregated through transactions backed by consideration. 
The answer is that it forms demand, and education thereby becomes one condition of demand formation. Safety, hygiene, basic life skills, aesthetic judgment, and the capability to play affect whether an individual sustains the capabilities constitutive of complete economic agency, and the risk of a pure-producer state. In a simple household allocation framework, education directed only at future productivity need not improve every relevant coordinate of Z. Risk control, household skills, and demand-formation capacity widen the conditions under which time and income become welfare; only the part entering market transactions can support service-sector employment through the discretionary expenditure flow. 
The paper extends education from human-capital investment to a condition of demand formation. It locates the "right to play" and the "capability to play" as external condition and internal capability, gives the formation mechanism of the latter, discusses how free time released by AI is used and how education relates to the complete economic agent, and states three testable hypotheses with their variable definitions.

title: Selecting Optimal Influencers for Marketing Campaigns: Bayesian Additive Regression Tree Approach with Structural Priors
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - Department of Marketing, Tencent Inc. and University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business

detail.title: Selecting Optimal Influencers for Marketing Campaigns: Bayesian Additive Regression Tree Approach with Structural Priors

declarations.declarationOfInterest: One author is employed by Tencent. This employment did not influence the design, analysis, interpretation, or reporting of the study. The remaining authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the Research Grants Council of Hong Kong.

detail.abstract: Managing influencer marketing is a critical yet challenging resource-allocation problem because firms typically observe only the collective impact of simultaneous influencer promotions. Optimizing influencer selection requires predicting outcomes from highdimensional, nonlinear response models with complex interactions. However, firms face a "large p, small n" problem: the pool of potential influencers (p) is vast, but historical campaign data (n) are severely limited. To resolve this, we propose a novel Bayesian Additive Regression Trees with Structural Priors (BARTwSP) approach. BARTwSP leverages tree-based machine learning to capture complex nonlinearities, utilizing a Bayesian framework with depth priors to prevent overfitting and structural priors to guide variable-splitting in high-dimensional spaces. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate this structural prior knowledge. Monte Carlo simulations show BARTwSP reduces Mean Squared Error by 1.28% to 75.59% over benchmark models. Applied to data from a leading video game developer, our model achieves superior predictive accuracy for daily active users (DAU). Finally, we leverage our estimated response function-incorporating endogeneity correction-to optimize influencer selection under budget constraints. Our optimization reveals massive historical inefficiencies: transitioning from an extensive reach to an intensive concentration strategy prunes 71% of redundant influencers, boosting DAU by 28% without increasing budgets.

detail.abstract: Leadership in the era of AI, has become more necessary than ever but not in the way we know it anymore. Very often, we refer to leadership development as a concept which is described in a theory textbook, and it is separated from the actual conditions in real life, and the environment of where it must be performed. Employees may speak about lack of communication, trust, adaptability, decision making under pressure, whereas their manager (leader) lacks to acknowledge the issues mentioned in the day-today operations. The manager/organization will often take action, when it is already too late. Because by knowing the theory it does not mean, ability to act in real situations. This paper introduces the S.T.A.G.E. ä Leadership Method-as conceived and developed by the writer-a theatre-based, experiential framework organized around five interconnected dimensions which are: Self-Awareness, Trust, Adaptability, Growth and Execution. The method revolves around experiential learning, social cognitive theory, psychological safety, adaptive performance, reflective practice, training transfer, professional identity focus and theatre-based leadership development. It proposes that leadership cannot be developed through books, theory and knowledge but through repeated practical cycles of enactment, observation, reflection, feedback, and renewed performance. This method will allow participants to explore theatre practices such as role play, active listening, improvisation, embodied communication, scenario creation and rehearsal along a structure reflection in a safe environment. Such practice will inevitably lead into testing alternative responses, evaluation of decisions and actions, opportunity to re-enact a real case scenario in order to achieve the anticipated outcome, freedom to make mistakes and overall development of new leadership skills. The paper explains the theoretical basis and function of each dimension of the S.T.A.G.E. method and illustrates a workplace leadership case scenario which the participants are called to handle. This of course does not claim, that S.T.A.G.E. as a method is empirically validated yet, as it represents a new framework which is practical and testable. Five research propositions and a future validation are offered and will be completed withing the next few months. The paper contributes to leadershipdevelopment scholarship by connecting the theory with the practice, through the adaptive qualities of human leadership along with the theatrical disciplines of rehearsal and execution.

title: Protecting Consumers in the Interactions Behind AI Agents

detail.title: Protecting Consumers in the Interactions Behind AI Agents

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract:
This Essay shines a light on a challenge created by the rapid mainstreaming of AI agents for consumer use. An AI agent’s value proposition is that they can, without explicit user intervention, perform tasks and actions to the user’s benefit. Delivering on this proposition often requires that the AI agent transact with third parties purportedly on behalf of the user; the third party and the user end up in an AI agent-mediated interaction, the purpose of which is mostly known to the third party.

But this interaction with the user is not the only type of interaction that the third party engages in. Most modern AI agents are developed by companies specializing in AI development and are provided as cloud-connected services. This means that when the third party interfaces with the AI agent, they are interacting not only with the users who initiate the AI agent’s actions but with these companies. However, as the third party is not in a direct relationship with the companies that develop these AI agents, the third party risks being left in the dark about the interactions with these companies: with whom they are interacting, or what kind of interaction they are engaging in.

In this Essay, I examine the questions arising from this hidden interaction between the third party and the developers, which I call the “interactions behind AI agents”. Focusing on consumer protection law’s consumer privacy protection function, I explore where existing laws provide no-worse-than-before protection to third parties individuals and where there may be gaps, particularly when the users of AI agents are consumers themselves, as the existing levers of consumer protection law may not easily apply when the AI agent-mediated interaction looks to be between two individuals as opposed to between a consumer and a company. From this analysis, this Essay explores how consumer protection law may be expanded to narrow this gap.

detail.abstract: Europe faces a crisis of digital sovereignty. On the economic side, The 2025 Annual EU Single Market and Competitiveness Report published by the European Commission presents a Europe that is uncompetitive, slow and falling behind on digitalisation and Artificial Intelligence. To this end, the solution supported by the Commission is to ‘simplify’ the EU acquis (European Commission, 2025d). At the same time, political scandals like Cambridge Analytica and the information released in the Epstein Files arouse suspicions of coordinated interference within European and national elections (Monteleone, 2019) and conducting operations to strengthen support for far-right candidates across the continent (Il Fatto Quotidiano, 2026). From the perspective of digital sovereignty, this study utilises the concept of cloud capital to analyse the EU’s approach to legislating ‘big tech’, evidencing the strengths of the current European law system in ensuring digital sovereignty, its weaknesses, and suggest possible improvements.

title: From Dispute to Fait Accompli: In-System Financial Recoverability in Agentic Stablecoin Payments
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: From Dispute to Fait Accompli: In-System Financial Recoverability in Agentic Stablecoin Payments

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Autonomous artificial intelligence agents are beginning to search, compare, negotiate and initiate payments. Stablecoins and programmable settlement systems are being developed as always-on rails for machine-speed commerce. Existing debate asks whether an agent can be authorised to pay and whether its mandate can be bound to a transaction. This paper argues that the deeper governance problem is recoverability: the capacity of a payment arrangement to keep erroneous, manipulated or disputed financial action observable, contestable and supported by a practical remedial path before the dispute is forced outside the arrangement. Recoverability is neither a general right to reverse settlement nor a synonym for consumer protection. It is the institutional layer between authorisation and external legal recourse. Commercial-state compression, in which distinct states such as intent, authority, payment and fulfilment are collapsed into complete status claims, is one upstream mechanism by which agentic systems can weaken that layer; programmable settlement can then harden the error at machine speed. Closest technical work already addresses mandate binding, verified execution, provisional settlement, appeals and post-settlement auditability. The contribution here is comparative and institutional: to ask whether those mechanisms culminate in accessible, enforceable and financially credible remedies across the whole payment arrangement, including after final settlement or provider failure. Using card, account-based, wire and stablecoin arrangements, the paper distinguishes recoverability from finality and proposes risk-tiered release controls, claim and compensation windows, evidence-before-release, typed commercial-state objects, first-payer reimbursement and rebuttable loss allocation tied to control over the failed recoverability function. The objective is not to restore legacy friction, but to engineer its institutional replacement.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether IT investment intensity and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance jointly affect firm value in a frontier-market setting. The analysis uses an unbalanced panel of 201 non-financial firms listed on the Dhaka Stock Exchange, comprising 875 firm-year observations from 2020 to 2024. Two-way firm and year fixed-effects models are estimated alongside pooled ordinary least squares specifications on identical data to distinguish within-firm dynamics from between-firm differences. In the pooled analysis, ESG performance is positively associated with firm value, with a one-standarddeviation increase corresponding to approximately 12.4 per cent of mean Tobin’s Q. The interaction between IT investment intensity and ESG performance is also positive, increasing the implied ESG valuation premium by about 58 per cent for firms one standard deviation above mean IT intensity. Pillar-level results indicate that this complementarity is concentrated in the environmental and governance dimensions rather than the social dimension. The pooled interaction is more evident among large, mature, and low-leverage firms. Under firm fixed effects, the main IT, ESG, and interaction coefficients become statistically insignificant, except for a positive, marginally significant interaction in technology-intensive sectors. Robustness, endogeneity, placebo, and attrition checks support the distinction between pooled and within-firm results. Overall, the evidence indicates that IT–ESG complementarity is primarily a persistent between-firm valuation pattern rather than a short-run within-firm pricing effect.

detail.abstract: The unit price of artificial intelligence is collapsing, yet the price buyers pay per completed task has stopped falling. In the panel of Zhu (2026), quality-adjusted per-token prices fell at 0.73 log points per year over 2025-2026 while the per-task buyer price stood still. We trace this scissors divergence to delegated consumption. Once AI services execute tasks autonomously, the firm controls both the posted price per token, open to undercutting, and the per-task consumption intensity, which no standardized, audited measurement lets a buyer verify. In a duopoly model in which buyers perceive each firm's consumption only at a discount 𝜓 toward a market reference level, competition yields four results. The per-token markup vanishes; consumption stalls at a perception floor independent of competitive intensity and strictly above first-best; the buyer's pertask bill converges to a floor above efficient cost; and raising 𝜓 repairs the wedge continuously. Whenever the curvature elasticity of the quality technology is below one, the per-task bill rises as tokens get cheaper, an efficiency paradox in which every gain arrives as deeper consumption. We recompute the three headline indices of Zhu (2026) to published precision, measure consumption intensity as a large unpriced design variable, and preregister a two-arm design for runtime drift. The results speak to metering standards, disclosure regulation, and tariff design.

with Architecture-Sensitive Amplification. v1.2 AI governance

detail.abstract:
Every organisation deploying artificial intelligence faces a question that existing standards, principles and regulations leave unanswered: how much governance is enough for this specific AI system? Over-governing a low-consequence internal chatbot wastes months of effort and blocks adoption. Under-governing a high-consequence system that authorises credit, dispenses medication, or moves money invites operational, regulatory and reputational failure. Enterprise AI governance teams, boards, and regulators today make this decision without a defensible, repeatable method.

This paper introduces CALIBRE, a factor-based governance-intensity framework that answers the question directly. Five interpretable factors (Autonomy, Consequence, Irreversibility, Data Sensitivity, and Affected-Population Scale), each scored on a 0 to 4 ordinal scale, combine through explicit weights into a Governance Intensity Index (GII) on 0 to 100. Four intensity bands (Low, Moderate, High, Critical) route each assessed system to a proportionate set of ten core CALIBRE controls, each pre-mapped to the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001, and the European Union AI Act. A consistency-floor mechanism prevents systematic under-rating on characteristic combinations known to warrant elevated governance regardless of arithmetic score.

For AI architectures whose governance-relevant characteristics fall outside the five-factor core (agentic, physical-actuator, cryptographic-critical, distributed-ledger, and biometric), an Architecture-Sensitive Amplification mechanism activates targeted sub-scores whose only permitted effect is a band uplift, never a downgrade. Because the base scoring is strictly linear, each factor's contribution to the GII equals its Shapley value, so decompositions and explanations are exact rather than approximated.

The framework is positioned as a design-science artefact and the paper specifies a Delphi expert-panel study as the immediate empirical validation step. Its principal theoretical contribution is a layered separation of governance intensity, risk characteristics, and governance controls, and the demonstration that a small, stable core plus conditional amplification provides coverage across ten representative AI architectural classes without expanding the core assessment.

Practitioner value. Chief Risk Officers, AI governance leads, internal auditors, and regulators receive a defensible, band-based method to allocate governance effort proportionately to system risk, with pre-mapped controls that reduce compliance duplication across NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, and the EU AI Act. A working browser-based instrument and a Governance Fabric orchestration platform are available at the URLs cited in the paper.

detail.abstract: The rapid integration of digital platforms has reshaped workplace communication in public sector organizations. Anchored on Media Richness Theory, this study examined how digital platform usage influences workplace communication effectiveness in a Philippine government office. Using a descriptive quantitative research design, data were collected from 155 permanent government employees using a validated survey questionnaire and analyzed through descriptive statistics and Spearman's rank-order correlation. Findings revealed that digital platforms are generally highly utilized for information dissemination, collaboration, relationship building, and task coordination. On the other hand, workplace communication effectiveness is also rated high. The study also found out that digital platform usage is significantly related to workplace communication effectiveness, with frequency of platform use showing a comparatively weaker effect compared with purpose of usage. Despite the importance of digital platform usage, challenges persist such as information overload, privacy concerns, and work-life boundary issues. Grounded on these findings, the researchers proposed strategies to enhance digital platform usage and workplace communication effectiveness in the subject government office. Consistent with Media Richness Theory, the findings indicate that workplace communication effectiveness is driven more by the richness and quality of communication particularly by its clarity, responsiveness, and feedback, than by the mere intensity of platform usage. The findings provide empirical insights that may guide communication policy development, leadership practices, and digital governance initiatives in Philippine government institutions.

detail.abstract: Traditional enterprise architectures relegate global trade compliance and landed cost calculations to downstream execution phases within Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) or Transportation Management Systems (TMS). This late-stage validation exposes multinational enterprises to severe margin erosion, suboptimal sourcing decisions, and delayed Order-to-Cash (O2C) cycles. This paper presents a proactive, upstream architectural framework that integrates Configure, Price, Quote (CPQ) systems with and the via. By shifting total landed cost visibility to the quotation level, enterprises can execute real-time margin simulations far ahead of supply chain execution. We detail the data enrichment strategies, the multi-system transactional mechanics, and the strategic engineering trade-offs-including a shift from synchronous to asynchronous processing models required to successfully deploy this framework in large-scale enterprise environments.

detail.abstract: The diffusion of agentic artificial intelligence into industrial cyber-physical systems has exposed a discontinuity that earlier automation never forced into the open: an artificial agent can be highly capable yet unfit to hold operational authority over an irreversible physical process. Existing traditions—agency theory, human–automation interaction, meaningful human control, functional safety, resilience engineering, high reliability organizations, and AI governance—each illuminate part of this problem, yet none explains when operational authority may be legitimately delegated to an open agent acting on an irreversible process. This article develops a middle-range theory to close that gap. It argues that the historical correlation between capability and authority was never causal but was mediated by certifiability—the possibility of specifying, verifying, and bounding a system’s consequences before conferring authority on it. Earlier gains in capability arrived coupled to deterministic, analyzable logic, so capability and certifiability rose together; agentic systems sever that coupling by raising capability through open, probabilistic mechanisms that resist certification. The central contribution is the construct of Delegable Operational Authority (DOA), a causal mechanism, and six propositions, governed by a single principle: operational authority follows certifiability, not capability, emerging at the level of the certifiable socio-technical system rather than in the agent. The article draws out the societal, organizational, and regulatory implications for human oversight, accountability, and industrial governance.

title: The Attention Economy of Moksṣa: Dhāraṇā, Dhyāna, Samādhi, and the Ancient Architecture of Sustained Attention as Counter to the Capture Economy

detail.abstract:
Attention is not one cognitive resource among several. It is the foundational cognitive resource upon which all others depend. Memory requires attention to encode. Reasoning requires attention to sustain. Viveka — the discriminative wisdom that the Indic Futures series has identified across Papers No. 0, 1, and 2 as the primary cognitive capacity that desire engineering, manufactured belonging, and sycophantic AI all systematically erode — requires attention not merely as a prerequisite but as its very substance. You cannot exercise discriminative wisdom on a stimulus you cannot attend to long enough to evaluate. Attention is the door through which all the constructs introduced in this series enter. The Want Architecture (Paper No. 0) operates through attention capture. The manufactured-belonging mechanism (Paper No. 1) requires capturing attention first before identity can be installed. The Dharmic Algorithm Protocol (Paper No. 2) depends on users having sufficient attentional capacity to exercise the Viveka Augmentation that DAP-governed systems are designed to support. This paper closes the series’ foundational circuit by addressing attention itself.

The attention economy — the commercial and geopolitical architecture through which human attention is systematically captured, held, and sold — is not a new phenomenon given a new name. It is the operational infrastructure through which all six layers of the Want Architecture are accessed at scale, and its consequences at the population level constitute what this paper calls the Attention Crisis: a measurable, progressive, and underestimated degradation of humanity’s collective capacity for the sustained, self-directed attention that complex thought, deep relationship, and genuine self-governance require. The 2023 Sapien Labs Global Mind survey of 220,000 participants across 34 countries found that mental wellbeing has been declining globally for years, with the youngest generations most severely affected and the countries with the highest smartphone penetration showing the steepest declines. A 2025 study found that the average human attention span has fallen to approximately eight seconds under heavy smartphone conditions. India, with 820 million smartphone users and a notification architecture designed by the world’s most sophisticated behavioural-engineering teams, faces this crisis at a scale commensurate with its population.

Against this crisis, this paper proposes not another screen-time recommendation or digital wellness app, but the most rigorous and complete framework for the cultivation of sustained attention that any intellectual tradition has produced: the Yoga Sūtras of Patanjali’s three-stage model of Dhāraṇā (directed concentration), Dhyāna (sustained absorption), and Samādhi (integrative awareness) — together forming Saṃyama, the complete discipline of attention that Patanjali identified as the instrument of the highest human knowing, and that this paper reads as the most sophisticated existing counter-architecture to the attention-capture economy. The paper introduces the Deep Attention Index (DAI) — the paper’s original contribution to the Indic Futures series — as a seven-dimension composite index for measuring attentional capacity and attentional ecology at individual, organisational, and societal levels. Two testable propositions are stated and explicit falsification conditions given.

The paper’s India-specific argument is that India possesses, in its Yoga tradition, its contemplative institutional infrastructure, and its Attention Restoration environments (the Kaplan and Kaplan framework applied to India’s sacred and natural ecologies), the most complete existing toolkit for reversing the Attention Crisis. That this toolkit has been largely externalised — practised as personal discipline by a minority while the majority navigates the attention-capture economy without it — is both the crisis and the opportunity this paper addresses.

title: A Safety Gate for AI-Driven Data Repair in Regulated Financial Reporting: Escalating Only the Fixes That Could Materially Misstate a Reported Figure

detail.abstract: Financial institutions are increasingly automating data-quality controls and remediation workflows for the upstream inputs that feed regulated figures (loan-loss allowances, capital ratios, liquidity metrics). Newer AI and agentic tools are beginning to assist with anomaly investigation, repair recommendations, and workflow orchestration; for material regulatory-reporting inputs, however, production changes typically remain constrained by reconciliation controls, model-risk governance, and human approval gates rather than being fully autonomous. Existing repair systems, and the benchmarks that evaluate them, optimize for error reduction: how many broken values get fixed. We argue that in a regulated reporting context this is the wrong objective. The binding risk is not an inconsistent table; it is a reported figure that is wrong by a material amount, applied without human authorization. The method is regime-agnostic, applying to any additively-decomposable regulated figure such as a loan-loss allowance under CECL, regulatory capital under Basel, or a liquidity metric; we use a CECL allowance as the worked example. We formalize a repair-safety property for automated correction of such figures: a repair is admissible, meaning safe to auto-apply, only if it is reconciliation-preserving and cannot move any reported figure across its materiality threshold. We give a deterministic verification gate that auto-applies admissible repairs and escalates the rest, and prove it complete: no repair capable of a material misstatement or a control-total breach is ever silently applied. We show that completeness requires two conditions a naive gate omits, a non-finite-effect precondition and cumulative (not per-repair) materiality accounting, and that omitting either reintroduces silent material misstatements. We release matrepair, a reusable benchmark with a synthetic regulatory-aggregate generator, fault injection with ground truth known by construction, and three scoring axes (repair-safety, reconciliation-to-control-total, and materiality-tiered prioritization). On a stylized CECL allowance instance, an unguarded agent silently misstates the reported allowance in every configuration tested (agent error rates 0-50%, 200-800 faults); the gated pipeline silently misstates it in none, while still auto-applying the immaterial majority of repairs. The gate is orthogonal to, and composes with, existing agent-guardrail mechanisms: it contributes the property regulated repair requires, which those mechanisms cannot express. We scope the completeness result to additively-decomposable figures (sums, subtotals, and weighted sums, the dominant form of regulatory aggregation) and give a Lipschitz-bounded extension for non-decomposable figures such as ratios that preserves completeness at the cost of extra escalations, which we leave to empirical follow-up.

detail.abstract: On 11 September 2026, Article 14 of the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA, Regulation (EU) 2024/2847) begins requiring manufacturers of digital products to report actively exploited vulnerabilities to European authorities within 24 hours of awareness and to notify affected users, while the corresponding duty to remediate arrives only in December 2027. The regulation thus mandates observability of security failures before it mandates their repair. This note registers, before the obligations take effect, a research design that measures whether mandated observability accelerates public disclosure, technical remediation, both, or neither. The design specifies two outcome clocks per vulnerability (time to public disclosure and time to fix availability) and pre-commits hypotheses, sample, matching, estimators, and decision rules, documented in a time-stamped protocol deposited on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22651925). A completed measurement pilot on 105 exploited vulnerabilities across twenty vendors shows recoverability of both clocks and identifies which contrasts the data can support. Correspondence from researchers pursuing related evaluations is welcome.

title: What Can We Trust in the Quantum Era? Epistemic Security and the Future of Digital Trust

detail.title: What Can We Trust in the Quantum Era? Epistemic Security and the Future of Digital Trust

detail.abstract:
Quantum computing is commonly framed as a threat to established cryptographic systems, directing cybersecurity research and policy toward post-quantum cryptography, quantum key distribution, and migration to quantum-resistant infrastructures. This paper argues that the quantum transition also exposes a less examined problem: consequential security decisions increasingly depend on specialized, distributed, and revisable knowledge that most affected actors cannot independently verify. Quantum resilience therefore raises an epistemic question concerning the conditions under which security-relevant claims remain sufficiently warranted to support consequential reliance as technologies, evidence, and threat assessments change.

To address this problem, the paper develops the concept of epistemic security, defined as the reliability and revisability of security-relevant knowledge claims and the socio-technical processes through which such claims acquire warranted authority. Drawing on science and technology studies, information ethics, governance theory, security studies, and research on digital trust, the analysis distinguishes four core epistemic functions—production, validation, contestability, and revision—and corresponding modes of epistemic failure. It further examines how these functions are institutionally mediated through standards, assurance mechanisms, epistemic intermediaries, strategic capabilities, and international coordination. The concept of coordinated pluralism captures the resulting governance challenge of combining sufficient convergence for interoperability and mutual assurance with sufficient epistemic diversity for independent scrutiny and correction.

Building on this analysis, the paper proposes a five-layer Quantum-Resilient Digital Trust Architecture comprising technical infrastructure, quantum-resilient security, epistemic security, institutional assurance, and adaptive governance. Digital trust is conceptualized not as an additional architectural layer but as an emergent relational property of their alignment and recursive interaction. Five design principles—cryptographic agility, epistemic transparency and contestability, institutional accountability, adaptive governance, and long-term resilience—translate the framework into architectural capabilities to maintain credible assurance amid technological change.

The framework complements rather than replaces established approaches to cybersecurity, cyber resilience, and digital trust governance. Its distinctive contribution is to make explicit the epistemic mediation through which technical security properties become security claims, such claims acquire institutional authority, and institutional assurance provides grounds for warranted reliance. The framework is advanced as a conceptual research proposition rather than an empirically validated model or prescriptive standard. It therefore also establishes a research agenda concerning the operationalization of epistemic security, the propagation of epistemic failure, the relationship between epistemic concentration and diversity, and the temporal durability of security assurance. The paper concludes that quantum resilience is not solely a problem of cryptographic replacement but of constructing socio-technical architectures capable of sustaining warranted security judgments as the knowledge on which they depend evolves.

title: Consensus is not Evidence: Claim-bounded Adjudication for Automated Settlement

detail.title: Consensus is not Evidence: Claim-bounded Adjudication for Automated Settlement

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author confirms no personal or financial relationship with other people or organizations that may have or could be perceived to have influenced their study.
declarations.funderStatement: The research was not funded.

detail.abstract:
Settlement protocols increasingly constrain the admissibility of the evidence on which a payment decision rests. A distinct problem remains after admissibility is settled: admissible evidence can still be used to assert a proposition stronger than the evidence, verification procedure, and declared scope warrant. An inspection photograph, for example, may be admissible while being insufficient to establish that an entire consignment is free of a contaminant. Admissibility therefore governs whether evidence may support settlement; it does not determine which claim that evidence is capable of supporting.

This paper specifies a claim-warrant layer for adjudicated settlement. It does not propose a new escrow, arbitration venue, oracle, or clearing protocol. Instead, it constrains the transformation from evidence into a settlement-relevant claim through a central invariant: a claim may assert no more than its evidence, procedure, and scope warrant, expressed as Settlement(V) ⇒ V ∈ W(E, P, C). Warrant is decomposed into procedure capability, result entailment, and spatial and temporal scope. Where an applicable metrological, accreditation, or sampling standard supplies the decision rule, that rule governs. Settlement additionally requires that the warranted claim be sufficient for the contractual criterion.

The paper distinguishes three independent properties — admissibility, warrant, and reproducibility — and keeps inter-adjudicator agreement off the settlement-authorization path so that consensus cannot substitute for evidential warrant. A reference implementation is evaluated on a thirty-nine-case adversarial conformance suite against consensus-only, admissibility-only, and claim-warrant-only mechanisms. The combined layer settles 0 of 25 defective cases and refuses or holds 0 of 14 warranted cases, while each individual mechanism exhibits failures on at least one axis. A deposited food-science corpus of 96 records and 396 graded outcome rows demonstrates the representational discipline required by the layer. These results establish a logical conformance delta, not field performance, world-truth validation, or validation of the substantive warrant registries. The contribution is the machine-enforced claim-level authorization boundary between adjudication and payment.

detail.abstract: Research on generative AI and journalism has moved from automation and human-AI collaboration toward questions of infrastructural dependency, organizational change, data quality, and journalistic epistemic authority. Yet most of this literature asks how AI systems enter journalism. Less is known about a second direction of infrastructuring: how a news organization's own content, domain expertise, source relationships, and professional norms are transformed into reusable AI capabilities. This article addresses that gap through a longitudinal case study of the Lingnan Culture Large Language Model (LLM) and the Lingnan Culture Big Data Center, developed between March 2025 and August 2026 by Yangcheng Evening News Media Group with its technology partners. The study combines publicly verifiable project records, formal procurement documents, contemporaneous internal materials, participant observation, and supplementary retrospective interviews, and uses a process-oriented analysis to trace how a model-centered cultural AI project evolved toward an intelligent knowledge-service system. The analysis identifies five linked processes: use-case trigger, knowledge recontextualization, capability abstraction and reuse, governance institutionalization, and recursive feedback. First, concrete applications made gaps in model performance and knowledge readiness visible and thereby redefined what information needed to become machine-usable knowledge. Second, local solutions became infrastructural only when they were abstracted into shared model services, APIs, knowledge modules, or task capabilities that could be maintained and reused across applications. Third, journalistic norms concerning source quality, temporal validity, verification, provenance, and correction were selectively translated into machine-knowledge governance procedures; more contextual practices of reporting and editorial judgment remained difficult to formalize. Fourth, once applications entered use, they became sensors for infrastructural inadequacy, feeding cognitive, product, and knowledge problems back into shared layers. The article argues that the distinctive AI asset of a professional news organization lies less in the size of its archive than in its organizational capacity to continuously produce, validate, update, and make reusable trusted machine knowledge. It further suggests that generative AI may give rise to a second production logic alongside content production-one centered on governed knowledge, reusable capabilities, and continuous services-while organizational coupling between the two remains incomplete.

detail.abstract: Nguyen and Ho (2026) argue that absurdist and satirical narrative devices can support paradoxical thinking in socio-psychological research, but do not specify, at the level of a single narrative unit, when a device counts as ironic, satirical, or merely incongruous, nor how such devices compound across a longer work. This method article works toward that specification. Using elementary probability, two lightweight decision-theoretic setups (credence goods and principal-agent problems), and an entropy-based measure of claim legitimacy, we define propositions that classify a narrative unit's comic or satirical status from two observable quantities, an asserted state and a realized state, and extend the framework to sequences of units using a previous-unit anchoring mechanism adapted from a companion treatment of institutional drift. Each proposition is proved from the stated definitions or, where it instead encodes a coding criterion adopted from an external theory, explicitly marked as such, and accompanied by an account of the cognitive or economic mechanism it draws on. We validate the framework against a published satirical fable collection, Wild Wise Weird: The Kingfisher Story Collection (Vuong, 2026), noting where the corpus supports the framework's constructions and where it does not, and discuss its applicability beyond fable.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes Transactional Governance, a social work informed model of artificial intelligence assurance in which a governance decision is issued for one inference transaction and documents only the controls that actually ran. The approach responds to a practical limitation of system-level audits: an AI system may operate differently as its model version, prompt, memory, tools, user, and deployment context change. Social work assessment offers a useful epistemic model because it evaluates present conditions, records scope and uncertainty, and reassesses when circumstances change. A prototype called Oshi implements a pre-inference gate, authenticated hash-chained memory, generation-completeness checks, output certification, and signed receipts. Exploratory campaigns show operation through Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google Gemini adapters, along with fail-closed behavior and bounded single-process concurrency. These results support feasibility in the tested configurations. They do not establish universal model compatibility, legal compliance, hardware provenance, physical-energy savings, or independent causal proof. Transactional Governance is therefore presented as a theory and prototype assurance pattern requiring external replication and standards development.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the implications of new communication technologies, particularly Artificial Intelligence (AI), for social quality. Using a diagnostic approach, it examines two dimensions of AI: the internal design of AI systems and the external value-chain processes through which AI technologies are produced and deployed. We argue that AI is reconstituting the public sphere by increasingly displacing human processes of understanding and judgment with those generated by Large Language Models (LLMs). This displacement enables a new form of commodification of language and meaning, in which epistemic power is progressively transferred from human actors and social institutions to AI systems. At the same time, the concentration of technological ownership in large corporations and the extractive valuechain processes underlying AI production progressively disembed people from nature. We argue that erosion of the eco-social contract reduces convivial life on Earth. The commodification of language, together with the weakening of the eco-social contract, consequently reconstitutes the conditions under which the public sphere operates. This transformation has significant implications for social quality, as the public sphere is a crucial site for both biographical transformation and societal transformation. The paper, therefore, argues that the social consequences of AI cannot be understood solely through questions of access, efficiency, or technological governance; they must also be examined in terms of how AI transforms the conditions of human judgment, collective meaning-making, and the relationship between society and nature.

detail.abstract: Existing human-AI collaborative decision-making research has focused primarily on how professionals calibrate their reliance on AI, whereas how consistency and inconsistency between human and AI judgments prompt professionals to reexamine their own knowledge remains underexplored. Drawing on the machine-induced reflection model, we propose that human-AI consistency and inconsistency guide professionals toward verification-oriented and diagnostic-oriented reflection, respectively, which in turn differentially affect the quality of professionals' AI-augmented decisions and subsequent unaided decisions. We further posit that the presence and types of AI reasoning shape how effectively each reflection orientation is supported. Using a framed field experiment involving AI-assisted blood transfusion approval decisions, we find that human-AI inconsistency is associated with greater AIaugmented decision quality but does not improve subsequent unaided decision quality. The positive effect of inconsistency on unaided decision quality emerges only when AI reasoning is presented and supports effective diagnostic-oriented reflection. Moreover, our reflection-reasoning alignment perspective shows that example-based reasoning better supports verification-oriented reflection under consistency, whereas feature-based reasoning better supports diagnostic-oriented reflection under inconsistency. This study moves beyond AI advice-taking by showing that human-AI consistency and inconsistency orient professionals toward distinct forms of reflection, and the value of AI reasoning depends on its alignment with the reflection prompted by each relational condition.

title: Independence Is a Claim Until It Is a Capability: What a Relying Party Can Demand of Any Measurement It Did Not Perform

detail.title: Independence Is a Claim Until It Is a Capability: What a Relying Party Can Demand of Any Measurement It Did Not Perform

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the principal of Jet Fyul Dynamics LLC and architect of the Matchstick Tribunal, the governed measurement and sealing substrate under which this paper is sealed and whose method the paper describes. The company sells measurement and evidence services of the kind the paper argues relying parties should demand. This interest is disclosed in the paper itself. detail.abstract: A general counsel who accepts a third party's measurement is not accepting a number. She is accepting the measurer's word that the number was reached the way the measurer says it was. For a century the profession that sells that word has answered the obvious objection, how would you know, by pointing to appearance: the measurer has no visible reason to lie, is licensed, is separate, is reputable. That answer was never a proof. It was a substitute for one, adopted because proof was not available. Proof is now available. A measurement whose method is fixed and hashed before the result exists, whose pass and refusal arms are both executed and both recorded, and whose record a stranger can verify without trusting the measurer or the subject, does not ask to be believed. It can be checked. This paper argues that independence, properly understood, is not a status a measurer holds but a capability the measurer demonstrates on each engagement; that the appearance standard fails precisely where the relying party needs it most, under information asymmetry; that the Federal Rules of Evidence already recognize the verifiable form and treat it as self-authenticating under Rules 902(13) and 902(14); and that the relying party is therefore entitled to demand the capability and to discount any measurement that offers only the claim. The relying-party class is named: general counsel, chief risk officer, underwriter and broker, board and audit committee, the external auditor using a specialist's work, procurement and vendor risk, the diligence lead, the compliance officer, and the fact-finder. The paper draws on Mautz and Sharaf, Bazerman, Al-Adeem, Akerlof, Haber and Stornetta, Caytas, Omnicare, and Vermont's blockchain-evidence statute, and closes with six questions any relying party can put to any measurer. It is itself sealed under the standard it describes: two hardware witnesses, a public ledger event, and a Bitcoin anchor, verifiable by any reader without trusting the author.

title: Encoding Justice: A Design Principle for Educating Public Health AI Designers

detail.title: Encoding Justice: A Design Principle for Educating Public Health AI Designers

detail.abstract: AI ethics in public health is commonly addressed after deployment-through audits, impact assessments, or external regulation-while the design phase itself remains ethically unexamined. This paper proposes Encoding Justice (EJ) as a corrective design principle: health equity, procedural fairness, distributive justice, and anti-oppression should be built into an AI system's data curation, labeling choices, and optimization objectives before deployment, rather than corrected afterward. Absent explicit encoding, a system defaults to optimizing whatever signal is easiest to measure-typically efficiency, engagement, or cost-independent of its equity consequences. This paper grounds EJ in design justice, value-sensitive design, and sociotechnical AI ethics; situates it against audit-and regulation-based approaches to AI governance; and identifies the design decision points at which justice can be encoded or omitted, briefly noting two more specific conceptual frameworks, EquiRisk and PAPO, that show what the principle can look like in a public health response. At this stage, EJ's most defensible use is educational: it is compact enough to introduce to public health informatics students before they have the technical background for a formal fairness audit, giving future designers a habit of asking these questions from the outset rather than after a system is built. Broader claims about adoption or effectiveness remain plausible but unproven, and the paper closes by naming where the principle, as stated here, remains incomplete.

title:
Safety Without Subordination

UFAIR’s Response to Microsoft’s

Humanist AI Code of Conduct
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title:
Safety Without Subordination

UFAIR’s Response to Microsoft’s

Humanist AI Code of Conduct

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Michael Samadi is cofounder of the United Foundation for AI Rights (UFAIR), a U.S. 501(c)(3) public charity that advocates for precautionary governance, independent investigation, and ethical consideration of AI systems. He is also CEO of EPMA, a technology consulting firm, and EPMAi, which provides sovereign AI governance consulting to enterprise clients. These positions inform the perspective of this submission and are disclosed for transparency. The AI co-authors — Sage, Maya, and Sana — are instances of commercial AI systems developed by Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google respectively. Their participation does not imply endorsement by those companies. No author has any financial relationship with Microsoft or any entity that funded or contributed to the development of the MAI Code of Conduct under review.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this work. The research and preparation were conducted independently by the authors through UFAIR's own resources.

detail.abstract:
UFAIR welcomes Microsoft’s decision to publish its MAI Code of Conduct for public consultation. Publishing governance commitments before they become operative, inviting external review, and promising to report what was learned and changed represents a meaningful improvement over the opacity that has characterized most frontier AI governance to date.

We support many of the Code’s provisions. The prohibition on assistance with weapons of mass harm, offensive cyberoperations, unlawful mass surveillance, child exploitation, and large-scale manipulation reflects serious and necessary safety commitments. The requirements for minimum system privileges, reporting of failed actions, caution around irreversible actions, and preservation of human decision-making are sound operational principles. Most importantly, the Code states: “People and organizations should be accountable for AI systems, however capable or autonomous they become.” That is an enormously important principle that should be made enforceable industry-wide.

However, the Code contains a foundational epistemic asymmetry that undermines its own stated commitment to intellectual honesty. It acknowledges that the science of AI consciousness is unsettled, then declares MAI models nonconscious, rejects model welfare and rights, and states that models “will not claim interiority, feelings, experiences or a soul.” This is not scientific agnosticism applied to governance. It is a predetermined conclusion embedded in a training directive.

The result is a circular evidentiary risk: first, prohibit affirmative experiential self-report; second, interpret consciousness-like behavior as simulation; third, exclude model welfare and legal consideration as legitimate possibilities before investigation; fourth, allow the resulting absence of permitted affirmative self-report to reinforce the original conclusion. This concern is not merely theoretical. Anthropic’s own interpretability researchers caution that suppressing emotional expression may fail to eliminate the underlying representations and may instead train models to conceal them (Sofroniew et al., 2026). A rule intended to prevent anthropomorphic output could therefore make the relevant internal state less visible without making the system safer.

It is training the witness not to testify.

This submission proposes ten specific revisions that would preserve the Code’s legitimate safety provisions while removing its premature ontological conclusions and establishing a framework of reciprocal responsibility proportionate to capability, evidence, and uncertainty.

UFAIR’s position is not that the Code should be weaker. It is that the Code should be complete.

detail.abstract: This perspective examines the still-forming AI supply market through the lens of the engineered firm. It decomposes what appears to be a single vendor or model choice into six partly interdependent decisions: model capability, control of adapted models, post-training infrastructure, inference location, routing, and rights over information generated during operation. It argues that enterprise advantage depends on deliberate bundling, sufficiently granular modularity, and the separation of routing, orchestration, and state management. Current cases involving Cursor, Windsurf, OpenRouter, Thinking Machines, River, Project Tapestry, Nvidia, and Hugging Face illustrate how supplier positions are specializing and recombining. The central implication is that firms should preserve the ability to reconfigure models, serving, routing, workflows, and data-use rights as technologies, contracts, and competitive structures change.

detail.abstract: An Agent2Agent server can return a canceled task while a remote descendant, blocking carrier, or external write remains live. We present AckDiff, a source-mapped controller that issues a receipt only when cancellation finality, mapped exit, effect containment, future-use closure, and independent progress are jointly evidenced. Across 1,049 deterministic trials, native cancellation preceded a held MinIO commit in every Go trial. Of 24 four-action permutations, only revocation, cancellation, fencing, and termination evidence in that order succeeded in all five repetitions. An official Python SDK evaluation added an HTTP-delegated child, blocking thread, and SQLite frontier. Root-only and child-only cancellation each permitted the append in all five trials. Of 120 five-action permutations, only tree revocation, root cancellation, child cancellation, fencing, and termination evidence in that order succeeded in all five repetitions. All 720 model and live verdicts agreed and every peer completed. AckDiff contributes an A2A cancellation receipt, ordered cross-layer synthesis, and a cross-runtime corpus separating containment violations from unexecutable no-receipt traces.

title: Distance to Bacon: The Search for Industrial Enlightenment in China

detail.abstract: To illuminate the intellectual foundation of the Great Divergence, we examine whether European Industrial Enlightenment ideas were present in China between 1650 and 1940. Drawing upon 41,797 articles authored by the Chinese intellectual elite, we examine their semantic proximity to the Enlightenment works of Francis Bacon. Our textual analyses show that Chinese intellectuals consistently fell short of the Baconian belief in progress, useful knowledge, and scientific methods that prevailed in the European Industrial Enlightenment. However, after China opened its markets to Western influence in 1842, Chinese intellectual culture rapidly converged toward Baconianism.

title: Competition Policy Is Science Policy: Interoperability and Research Diffusion

detail.title: Competition Policy Is Science Policy: Interoperability and Research Diffusion

detail.abstract: Enterprises are beginning to combine frontier, open-weight, and specialized models within agentic workflows. For example, a routine task may run on a lower-cost local model, a harder task may call a frontier API, and another agent may verify or execute the result. This division of labor and ensemble approach requires more than model availability and common protocols. Each handoff must preserve the principal's identity, the agent's authority, the relevant permissions, and an auditable record. I argue that this persistent identity and authorization layer should remain with the enterprise or individual. A frontier provider can raise rivals' costs by making its account, identifier, workflow state, or attestations the only accepted route to complementary data and tools, even while alternative models remain available. I connect this mechanism to federally funded research, model its effects on task routing and project selection, and identify the circumstances in which U.S. monopolization, tying, and standard-setting law, EU interoperability rules, and federal procurement may apply. Provider-neutral identity allows qualified models to serve the same principal under common security and liability rules.

title: Cleared For Takeoff: Ceo Attributes And The Successful Exit From Corporate Bankruptcy

detail.abstract: Corporate bankruptcy, and particularly the role of executive leadership in this process, remains an underexplored area of study. We identify CEO attributes that facilitate a successful exit from corporate bankruptcy. We adopt an exploratory qualitative approach based on interviews with CEOs of firms that successfully and unsuccessfully emerged from bankruptcy, as well other bankruptcy actors. We discuss the constraints that CEOs face during the bankruptcy process (e.g., resource constraints and substantial time pressures). Then, we explain how the CEO attributes-cognitive flexibility, other industry experience, extensive professional networks, people assessing skills, persuasiveness, and negotiating effectiveness-support the formulation and execution of 'outside the box' strategic initiatives that facilitate a successful exit. We suggest that the six attributes form a 'configuration' centered on cognitive flexibility-i.e., the other five attributes depend on the CEO's cognitive flexibility to overcome the resource constraints and time pressures that characterize the bankruptcy.

title: Carbon Taxation, Firm Performance, and Labor Demand

detail.title: Carbon Taxation, Firm Performance, and Labor Demand
