I also gratefully acknowledge financial support from Jan Wallander och Tom Hedelius stiftelse (P23-0186).

detail.abstract: Carbon taxation is one of the main policy instruments for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, yet there is still limited evidence on its effects on firms and workers. This paper studies the environmental and economic effects of carbon taxation, with a particular focus on heterogeneity in labor demand across worker groups. I exploit a reform that increased the effective carbon tax for a subset of Swedish manufacturing firms between 2011 and 2018, and combine administrative firm data with matched employer-employee records in a difference-indifferences design. The reform reduced emissions by about 30%, primarily through substitution away from fossil fuels toward biofuels and district heating. It also reduced revenue and employment, with the strongest negative effects concentrated among emission-intensive firms. The employment effects are driven mainly by older workers without a high school degree, although older highly educated workers are also negatively affected in the most exposed firms. Additional evidence suggests that firms adjusted labor demand primarily through lower hiring rather than higher separations. Scaled by the average increase in effective tax rates (measured in euro per ton CO 2), the estimates imply semi-elasticities of-0.58% for emissions and-0.20% for employment among low-educated workers. These results suggest that carbon taxation can substantially reduce industrial emissions, but with concentrated labor-market costs.

detail.abstract: Despite decades of methodological refinement, project failure rates remain stubbornly high, and much of the explanation lies not with technique but with leadership. This paper argues that the project sponsor, not the project manager, is the most under-theorised and undervalued factor in project success. Drawing on the sponsorship, governance, and agency-theory literatures, it traces how sponsorship has been reduced to a passive, transactional role-signing off on budgets and charters-even though the evidence points to an active, strategic, and behaviourally complex function. The paper deconstructs the sponsor's role across the project lifecycle, distinguishes it from adjacent roles such as the project manager and the steering committee, and sets out a typology of ineffective sponsorship (absentee, micromanaging, conflicted, unempowered) alongside its costs. It closes with practical strategies for project managers to "manage up" and organisational imperatives-role definition, training, governance structures, and recognition-to cultivate sponsorship as a professional discipline rather than an incidental duty. Aimed at practitioners, PMO leaders, and researchers alike, the paper's central claim is that the sponsor is not a peripheral figurehead but the indispensable anchor of project success.

detail.abstract: How should a review team be recruited when individually accurate AI agents can overlook the same inadequate explanation? This prospective protocol tests whether evidence validated failure maps improve recruitment beyond individual detection scores measured on the same task. It distinguishes formalizable joint inconsistency (Level I) from probabilistic explanatory misfit (Level II): in the latter, routine checks pass and the proposed explanation remains possible, but the combined evidence favors a different disposition under a public model contract. Typed evidence certificates make response scoring reproducible without treating a hidden simulator label or persuasive prose as ground truth. Deterministic baseline solve rates, witness attainability, and stratum-specific outcomes are reported explicitly. Twelve model-policy configurations support fixed-composition and unrestricted three seat recruitment experiments. The decisive comparison uses the same admissible teams and development evidence, but contrasts additive individual performance with joint validated coverage. A separate held-out test examines reproducible bench-dependent value against a difficulty-aware null. Practical success requires better grounded containment together with noninferior clean-case review demand and harmful intervention. Adjudicator-only performance and content ablations separate signal availability from effective use. Fictional manufacturing is the first domain; service incidents supply a distinct mechanism, and outbreaks are an optional surface-transfer domain. The contribution is a bounded measurement and recruitment design, not a new claim that diversity always helps. A companion reference implementation checks deterministic mechanics; no AI-agent effect or statistical power is asserted. Engineering validation and a locked run-specific registration precede confirmation.

detail.abstract: This paper seeks to interrogate the legal architecture produced by Africa's overlapping membership in regional economic communities as the African Continental Free Trade Area attempts to harmonize rules of origin across the continent. It argues that the spaghetti bowl of concurrent commitments to the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa, the Southern African Development Community, the East African Community, the Economic Community of West African States and other communities is not an incidental design flaw. It is a structural consequence of the AfCFTA's own building-block doctrine, codified in its variable-geometry clauses. Drawing on treaty text, trade-law commentary and African-authored scholarship, the paper traces how divergent regime-wide and product-specific rules generate conflicting preferential trade claims, erode the credibility of certificates of origin, and multiply forums for dispute settlement. It critiques prevailing harmonisation proposals as technocratic exercises that neglect the jurisdictional pluralism underlying African trade law, and reconceives rulesof-origin harmonisation as a constitutional question about hierarchy among African economic communities, proposing a sequenced and justiciable framework for resolving REC-AfCFTA norm conflicts.

title: The S.T.A.G.E. Leadership Method: A Theatre-Based Experiential Framework

detail.title: The S.T.A.G.E. Leadership Method: A Theatre-Based Experiential Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Columbia Univrsity and The Open University of Cyprus
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Leadership in the era of AI, has become more necessary than ever but not in the way we know it anymore. Very often, we refer to leadership development as a concept which is described in a theory textbook, and it is separated from the actual conditions in real life, and the environment of where it must be performed. Employees may speak about lack of communication, trust, adaptability, decision making under pressure, whereas their manager (leader) lacks to acknowledge the issues mentioned in the day-today operations. The manager/organization will often take action, when it is already too late. Because by knowing the theory it does not mean, ability to act in real situations. This paper introduces the S.T.A.G.E. ™ Leadership Method-as conceived and developed by the writer-a theatre-based, experiential framework organized around five interconnected dimensions which are: Self-Awareness, Trust, Adaptability, Growth and Execution. The method revolves around experiential learning, social cognitive theory, psychological safety, adaptive performance, reflective practice, training transfer, professional identity focus and theatre-based leadership development. It proposes that leadership cannot be developed through books, theory and knowledge but through repeated practical cycles of enactment, observation, reflection, feedback, and renewed performance. This method will allow participants to explore theatre practices such as role play, active listening, improvisation, embodied communication, scenario creation and rehearsal along a structure reflection in a safe environment. Such practice will inevitably lead into testing alternative responses, evaluation of decisions and actions, opportunity to re-enact a real case scenario in order to achieve the anticipated outcome, freedom to make mistakes and overall development of new leadership skills. The paper explains the theoretical basis and function of each dimension of the S.T.A.G.E. method and illustrates a workplace leadership case scenario which the participants are called to handle. This of course does not claim, that S.T.A.G.E. as a method is empirically validated yet, as it represents a new framework which is practical and testable. Five research propositions and a future validation are offered and will be completed withing the next few months. The paper contributes to leadershipdevelopment scholarship by connecting the theory with the practice, through the adaptive qualities of human leadership along with the theatrical disciplines of rehearsal and execution.

detail.abstract: We study how repeated U.S. tariff shocks interact with a slow-moving trade state-the destination allocation of existing export activity. The 2018 tariffs on Chinese products cause short-run trade destruction: U.S.-bound exports fall, non-U.S. sales do not offset the loss, and world physical export mass contracts. By 2025, China is less exposed to the U.S. market, mainly within products. Under renewed tariffs, products with greater predetermined U.S. exposure suffer larger global losses, while aggregate export growth is concentrated among products already less dependent on the United States. A 2026 courtinduced policy reset provides a partial reversal experiment. Tariff relief is persistent and triggers an immediate import rebound, but the restoration path quickly falls below the scale-matched mirror of the 2025 response. Repeated shocks therefore reveal state-dependent incidence and dynamically asymmetric policy reversal: policy moves faster than the trade state through which it is transmitted.

detail.abstract:
Gu, Kelly, and Xiu (2020) showed that machine learning can improve cross-sectional stock return prediction by capturing nonlinear relationships between firm characteristics and future returns. This study applies a simplified version of their framework to 60 US and 60 Indian large-cap stocks using 27 price and volume characteristics. Four models (Ridge regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and a neural network) are evaluated using expanding-window walk-forward validation, producing 35 out-of-sample test months in each market. 

None of the models produces statistically significant portfolio returns at the 5% level in either market. Model rankings also differ across the two markets: Ridge performs best in the US, while the neural network performs best in India. Two patterns appear consistently in both markets. Small portfolio legs (six stocks each, given the 60-stock universe) can be strongly affected by a few extreme individual stock returns, and a model's point-prediction accuracy does not always correspond to its portfolio performance. These findings show why machine learning models should be evaluated using both prediction metrics and portfolio outcomes. The results should be treated as exploratory, given the small universe size and short out-of-sample period.

title: Pan-Africanism as Symbolic Capital: The Implementation Gap in Ghana's Refugee Protection

detail.abstract: Ghana has long cultivated an international identity as a beacon of Pan-Africanism, democracy, and humanitarian hospitality. Yet, beneath this carefully maintained diplomatic image, a systematic implementation gap persists between Ghana's humanitarian rhetoric and the lived realities of refugees within its borders. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 18 participants including government officials, UNHCR staff, civil society representatives, and refugees this article examines how Ghana's normative foreign policy commitments translate into domestic protection outcomes. I argue that Pan-Africanism functions as symbolic capital deployed for reputational gain in diplomatic settings, rather than a binding operational framework that constrains domestic security and economic actors. Through three analytical lenses liberal institutionalism, constructivism, and critical political economy, this work demonstrates that Ghana's ratification of international instruments and enactment of progressive legislation have not translated into effective implementation. The article identifies three mechanisms producing the implementation gap: (1) performative Pan-Africanismnormative commitments are invoked rhetorically but not operationalised; (2) institutional fragmentationthe Ministry of Foreign Affairs sets policy while the Ghana Refugee Board implements, without systematic coordination; and (3) norm contestation humanitarian norms are contested by security and economic actors who dominate domestic resource allocation. The article challenges constructivist assumptions that norm internalisation leads to compliance, revealing instead that norms remain at the level of strategic performance. It contributes to debates on African foreign policy, humanitarian diplomacy, and the political economy of refugee protection in the Global South.

detail.abstract: The adoption of AI-powered document classification and field extraction in regulated industries is constrained by a fundamental tension: models require access to document content, but that content contains personally identifiable information (PII) that regulatory frameworks prohibit exposing to external processing systems. Existing de-identification approaches suffer from a domain-specific false-positive problem-generic Named Entity Recognition (NER) models incorrectly mask business-critical terminology that resembles personal data. In insurance, "Premium" is masked as a proper noun. In healthcare, "Cancer" is masked as a diagnosis in clinical research contexts. In banking, institution names are masked as personal names. We present a taxonomy-driven de-identification framework that resolves this tension through a four-stage pipeline-tokenize, classify, extract, re-identify-governed by a curated domain vocabulary that distinguishes PII from business terminology. The framework guarantees that no personal data reaches the AI model while preserving the domain-specific language the model requires for accurate classification and extraction. We validate the framework in a production insurance deployment processing real policyholder documents under the Swiss Federal Act on Data Protection (FADP/DSG). On a held-out evaluation corpus of 20 synthetic insurance documents, the framework achieved 91.7% partial recall and 72.1% precision, up from 63.0% and 46.6% respectively before taxonomy-guided multilingual deidentification was introduced. We further demonstrate cross-vertical applicability by constructing equivalent taxonomies for healthcare, banking, and legal document processing, and establish a repeatable methodology for taxonomy design in any regulated domain.

title: The Design of Private Property - From Fixed Coordinatesto Intelligent Matter

detail.abstract: Private property organizes who may inhabit, exclude, transform, transfer and benefit from resources. Housing gives these powers unusual force because private life depends on continuous access to a structure, a location and essential services. Five millennia of recorded arrangements show repeated changes in the distribution of those powers across households, rulers, markets, states, cooperatives and commons. This history opens a design question: if spatial resources are unusually costly because several physical and institutional constraints remain bundled, which constraints can become variables? Intelligentism is proposed as a testable programme for the joint redesign of resource capability and governing authority. A software-first bridge represents current and possible spatial states, preserves resident permissions, simulates counterfactuals and coordinates existing capacity before actuating matter. Twenty bounded applications connect homes, public space, recoverable components and territorial governance. Programmable-matter scenarios then add swarm coordination, reversible movement and qualified solidification. Four physical simulations and a synthetic 10,000-household country sensitivity experiment isolate collective motion, state transition, structural connectivity, path selection, pooling, adaptation and routing; none is treated as a price or adoption forecast. Historical cost evidence identifies mechanisms through which intelligence can reduce particular services, while complete-habitation accounting tests whether those gains survive land, infrastructure, finance, maintenance and distribution. Capitalist, communist, public, cooperative and common arrangements are treated as plural institutional families rather than binaries. The proposed adoption criteria concern capability, safety, agency, practical alternatives, lifecycle burden and ecological effects. A 99% reduction and the one-cent house remain explicit directions, not assumed results. The central proposition is that secure private life can persist while the material, computational and institutional means of habitation become more adaptive, recoverable and widely accessible.

detail.abstract: This paper develops the offer-side uncertainty architecture of Relative Rationality Theory (RRT) by extending Emotional Adjusted Value (EAV) into probability-based decisionmaking. Standard expected utility theory evaluates uncertain prospects through probabilities, payoffs, and utility, while behavioural approaches explain departures from this model through reference dependence, probability weighting, regret, ambiguity, or loss aversion. RRT proposes a different route: uncertain outcomes should first be translated into emotionally adjusted outcome consequences before utility is applied. The paper introduces Emotional Adjusted Expected Utility (EAEU) as the core uncertainty operator of RRT, in which each outcome generates a specific EAV, updates pre-decision Emotional Adjusted Wealth into Decision-EAW, and is then evaluated through utility. Probabilities remain objective or subjective likelihoods; the innovation lies in transforming the evaluated outcome rather than the probability itself. The paper also develops two counterfactual extensions: Emotional Regret Expected Value (EREV), which prices regret, relief, and rejoicing as cash-equivalent value-level adjustments before utility, and Emotional Regret Expected Utility (EREU), which evaluates emotionally weighted utility comparisons between evaluated and alternative lottery outcomes. Together, these tools connect probability, emotional valuation, counterfactual comparison, ambiguity, and utility over Emotional Adjusted Wealth within a single formal architecture. The framework is applied to Allais-type certainty effects, Ellsberg-type ambiguity, regretsensitive lottery choice, loss aversion, and fair mixed lotteries. The paper argues that relative rationality under uncertainty is not determined by monetary expectation alone, but by the full emotional-economic consequences that uncertain outcomes generate for the decision-maker's psychological wealth position.

title: Support-Size Cover Modularity and Efficient Algorithms for Generalized Network Design
affiliations: , City University of Hong Kong and University of British Columbia

detail.title: Support-Size Cover Modularity and Efficient Algorithms for Generalized Network Design

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: We study a generalized flexibility design problem in which a decision-maker selects a set of operational links and then allocates activity over the resulting network via a linear program. Each unit of activity may consume arbitrary, link-specific amounts of resource-and demand-side capacity, extending classical unit-or integer-coefficient models (DeValve et al. 2023, Soylemez and DeValve 2024). We consider cardinality, budget, and matroid constraints on the design. Even in the unit-coefficient case, the deterministic first-stage design problem is strongly NP-hard under a cardinality constraint. We show that coefficient heterogeneity does not weaken the key structural guarantee: the generalized flexibility design objective remains 2-cover modular for arbitrary nonnegative real coefficients. Our approximation algorithms are greedy: at each iteration, rather than computing the exact marginal gains of all candidate links, we use our primal-dual analysis to construct closed-form lower bounds on these gains from a single optimal operational solution. These surrogates yield constant-factor approximation guarantees with at most one operational LP solve per iteration, avoiding a separate solve for each candidate link. For matroid constraints, a direct packing-LP analysis establishes an expected 1/4-approximation for a surrogate-based residual random greedy algorithm. More generally, for set functions induced by activating variables in a nonnegative packing LP with finite full-set value, we prove max{1, s}-set cover modularity, where s is the maximum number of resource constraints involving any activatable operational variable; the same factor governs arbitrary overlapping group additions. The result holds for arbitrary nonnegative real coefficients, and the factor is invariant to positive row rescaling and worst-case tight for s ≥ 1. It thereby replaces the coefficient-sum bounds of DeValve et al. (2023), Soylemez and DeValve (2024) with a scale-invariant support parameter, without imposing coefficient integrality. We further extend return-on-investment greedy optimization from submodular to γ-cover-modular value functions with modular activation costs, obtaining a logarithmic value-cost guarantee scaled by 1/γ. Together, these results establish a tight uniform bound on set cover modularity in terms of column support and use this structure to obtain approximation guarantees for generalized network design.

detail.abstract: What happens when a representation leaves one mind and enters a group? This article names three problems the individual-level architecture does not address—reconstruction rather than copying across individuals, the stabilization of a representation into narrative the group treats as given, and the constraint that narrative then places on individual decisions. Evaluating four external frameworks (Berger and Luckmann, Clark, Sperber, and Weick) against the affect-gating result established at the individual level, it finds that Sperber and Weick independently derive the same governing variable this program isolated computationally: affective charge, not frequency of repetition. On that convergence it proposes the Group Umbra Cone, a formal extension with three falsifiable hypotheses—transmission fidelity, narrative objectification, and decisional feedback—mirroring the individual-level hypotheses already tested. No group-level data are reported; the article is a theoretical architecture and a research program, and its final section specifies what a test would require.

title: Setting CEO Pay: What Pitfalls Should We Avoid?
affiliations: Case Western Reserve University - Department of Banking & Finance and Clarkson University

detail.title: Setting CEO Pay: What Pitfalls Should We Avoid?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: For decades, boards have set CEO pay using market benchmarks, variable compensation and incentives tied to stock price performance. The increasing reliance on equity-based compensation has accompanied an enormous rise in CEO pay, with the CEO-to-median worker pay ratio at 632-to-1 for the top hundred S&P 500 firms in 2024. Yet in far too many cases, CEO pay has not corresponded closely with the performance of the companies they lead. We argue that outsized equity-based CEO pay packages raise not only concerns about inequity but, more importantly, can distort incentives, encourage risk-seeking decision making and weaken the CEO’s true “skin in the game”. Board oversight has been ineffective in fixing these problems. We recommend four remedies – 1) improve board governance by building meaningful director ownership, 2) shift away from large equity grants, 3) resist the peer-pay “ratchet-up” created by routinely targeting median-or-higher CEO pay, and 4) vest rewards based on predetermined, measurable and size-adjusted improvements in operating performance rather than stock price. Getting all stakeholders to adopt these shifts will not be an easy task, but the journey is worth it.

title: Quantified Midterm Theory (QMT): A Structural Field Model of U.S. Midterm Dynamics (1966-2022)

detail.abstract: Midterm elections in the United States are widely described as referenda on presidential performance, yet this explanation has remained largely qualitative. Quantified Midterm Theory (QMT) introduces a structural, falsifiable mathematical model demonstrating that midterm outcomes behave like a stable national mood field driven by six measurable indicators: presidential approval, independent approval, unemployment, inflation, real GDP growth, and consumer sentiment. Using centering, normalization, correlation weighting, and variance matching-without regression or narrative assumptions-QMT produces a single scalar field value for each chamber. When applied to the stable midterm window (1966-2022), QMT achieves 100% directional accuracy and low magnitude error (≈4.6 seats House, ≈1.4 seats Senate). The model is fully falsifiable: plugging today's indicators into the field equation yields a testable composite representing current national mood pressure. QMT demonstrates that midterms are not chaotic political events but a reproducible physical-like system governed by measurable forces.

detail.abstract: This chapter examines how developing countries should regulate abuses of market power in their digital economy. In doing so, it explores fundamental questions such as: (1) what makes the digital economy distinct from conventional markets?; (2) why do developing countries require a distinct approach to competition law in digital markets?; and (3) how should developing countries adapt their competition policies and enforcement approaches to address abuse of market power in the digital economy? title: A Newer Fleet, a Riskier Cooperative? A Logistic Model of Insolvency in Paraná's Cargo Transport Cooperatives
affiliations: Pontifical Catholic University of Parana (PUCPR)

detail.title: A Newer Fleet, a Riskier Cooperative? A Logistic Model of Insolvency in Paraná's Cargo Transport Cooperatives
detail.abstract: Cargo transport cooperatives allow independent truckers to compete with large carriers, but intense, sometimes predatory price competition has pushed a number of them toward insolvency. This study develops a binary logistic regression model to identify the financial indicators that best predict insolvency among cargo transport cooperatives in Paraná, Brazil, using 2,494 monthly financial statements collected between 2005 and 2016. Starting from 32 candidate indicators and removing highly collinear variables, a ten-variable final model was obtained through iterative elimination. Eight variables show the expected negative relationship with insolvency risk (liquidity, collection period, cash cycle, fixed-asset turnover, revenue growth, leverage, net debt to EBITDA, and net financial debt to results): lower values mean higher insolvency probability. Two variables show the opposite sign: asset turnover and, unexpectedly, average fleet age, where younger fleets show higher risk, consistent with debt taken on by the cooperative to finance vehicles. Five of the ten variables are individually significant at the 5% level; the other five, including fleet age (p = .077), are only marginally significant but were retained because they improved overall model fit. The findings offer cooperative monitoring bodies a concrete, ranked set of indicators to watch.

detail.abstract:
The evaluation of corporate governance in banks mainly depends on structural indices derived from disclosure checklists. In cases where regulatory requirements make formal compliance nearly universal, these indices cease to show the cross-sectional variation needed to allow for discrimination. In the panel under consideration, a structural index based on a mandatory directive is associated with the number of items a bank disclosed, with a correlation coefficient of 0.938; nine of the twelve possible items have a single value in every bank-year for which they are disclosed.
The paper presents an alternative screening framework which is designed to derive risk-oversight signals from audited financial statements. This framework is based on the fact that the governance mechanisms most important for banks are those which limit risk-taking, a point that corresponds to where the Basel Committee has placed Principles 6 and 7 (BCBS, 2015) and also to where the empirical literature has found effects that are not picked up by conventional board variables (Aebi, Sabato, & Schmid, 2012; Ellul & Yerramilli, 2013). The structure of RAROC is kept, but both the numerator and the denominator are revised; one of the signals looks at the extent to which earnings cover the regulatory capital charge and the other at the level of reserve coverage of the non performing balance. The inputs used are operating profit, regulatory capital, risk-weighted assets, the capital adequacy ratio, non-performing loans, and general and specific provisions. Four analytical properties are described. The classification is unaffected by the benchmark rate and is thus relevant in a system without an agreed-upon risk-free rate; it is unaffected by the confidence multiplier; it is scale-free; and, by the conjunctive sound-class rule, no bank-year below the coverage median is able to enter that class through lowered provisioning.
Three empirical constraints, based on 63 bank-year observations of 11 Iranian banks in the fiscal years 1398 to 1403, build the specification. The first constraint is that no signal scaled by regulatory capital may be correlated with the capital adequacy ratio. It was possible to replicate this association using a permutation test with random inputs, and it is located in the shared term with decomposition. The second constraint states that provisions scaled by total risk-weighted assets enter coverage multiplied by deterioration. Here, the deterioration factor accounts for 68 percent of the variation, implying that the coverage signal is taken against the non-performing exposure balance. There is no correlation with the capital adequacy ratio (rho = +0.118, p = 0.415). The third constraint is that changes in specific provisions are aligned with the migration of asset quality by regulatory rule, and not by managerial discretion. 
This dictates a level rather than a flow specification. The panel's calibration results include twelve observations classified as relatively sound, nineteen as high risk, thirteen as capital collapse, and nineteen as abstentions. The framework is presented as an outcome-based diagnostic tool for prioritising both supervisory and internal audits; it is not a measure of governance quality, although it does cover one of the thirteen principles of BCBS (2015), and has not been benchmarked against an external measure.

detail.abstract: That quantitative easing was in effect a fixed-for-floating swap, and that it would cost the Eurosystem when rates rose, was shown by Belhocine et al. [2023]. This paper does not claim the mechanism. It measures the composition that produced it, for all 21 national central banks monthly from June 2016 to June 2026, and reports the outturn. Four findings follow. The share of monetary policy assets held as secured, floating-rate credit fell from 37.2 per cent in March 2021 to 0.80 per cent in June 2026, widening the repricing gap, defined as reserves less secured credit, from EUR 626 billion in 2016 to EUR 3,146 billion in 2024. Capital subsequently fell for three consecutive years, by EUR 76 billion in total, extending beyond the period in which their baseline anticipated roughly two years of losses, and leaving four national central banks in negative equity. A counterfactual bounded by demonstrated collateral capacity puts the fiscal value of the composition margin between nothing and two fifths of the realised funding cost. And matching acquisition-month sovereign yields for Germany, France, Italy and Spain against the realised deposit facility rate, on windows that have actually been realised, gives a stock-weighted carry of-16 basis points at a four-year horizon, where every vintage is complete: roughly break-even, and decomposing against a random-walk benchmark into +97 basis points of ex-ante yield compensation less a +113 basis point rate surprise. The paper revises the TARGET debate accordingly: Sinn and Wollmershäuser [2012] was right that the asset side determines what the Bundesbank's claim is worth, but what materialised was interest rate risk, not the credit risk they named, and these data cannot cleanly attribute national losses to national balance sheets. A digital euro bears on the same margin, and its income effect depends jointly on remuneration and on the source of take-up: it narrows the repricing gap when the remuneration share plus the cash-substitution share is below one, is neutral at equality, and widens it above.

title: Congested Waiting Lists and Organ Allocation
affiliations: Stanford University - Department of Management Science & Engineering, Stanford University - Department of Economics and Boston University - Questrom School of Business

detail.title: Congested Waiting Lists and Organ Allocation
detail.abstract: More than 25% of the kidneys recovered from deceased donors in the U.S. and offered to patients on the national waiting list are not utilized. This paper shows that waiting-list designs can suffer from a form of congestion that can lead to valuable organs being discarded. As organs have a limited "cold ischemia time" during which they can be offered before expiring, an organ may expire before being offered to a patient lower on the waiting list who would accept it. We develop a parsimonious framework to study equilibria of waiting lists with congestion and show that congestion creates a strong enough externality to substantively affect utilization and welfare. The delegation of organ-acceptance decisions to risk-averse transplant centers can worsen congestion and thereby increase all waiting times. We discuss how recent changes to the waiting-list design affect congestion, and policies and market designs that can mitigate congestion and thereby improve welfare.

title: Who Owns the Decision? Formal and Substantive Institutional Possession in the Age of Artificial Intelligence

detail.title: Who Owns the Decision? Formal and Substantive Institutional Possession in the Age of Artificial Intelligence

No other financial or personal relationships that could have influenced the work are declared.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is increasingly capable of producing, shaping and executing consequential institutional judgements. Most governance frameworks respond to this development by asking whether AI systems are accurate, explainable, controllable, auditable and subject to meaningful human oversight. These questions are necessary, but they do not resolve a more fundamental institutional problem.

An institution may retain full legal authority over a decision, remain clearly responsible for its consequences and preserve formal human approval, while progressively losing the reasoning capability required to understand, challenge, substitute or continue that decision without machine-mediated support.

This paper distinguishes Formal Possession from Substantive Institutional Possession. Formal Possession concerns authority and consequence. Substantive Institutional Possession concerns whether the institution that bears those consequences retains enough of the surrounding decision architecture to make the decision meaningfully its own.

The distinction reveals a Possession Gap that can arise even when responsibility is completely clear and conventional AI governance controls remain intact. The paper develops three related concepts to analyse this condition: Capability-Consequence Asymmetry, Continuation Capacity and Institutional Decision Closure.

The argument is not that institutions should preserve inferior human processes or remain computationally self-sufficient. Dependence on superior machine reasoning may be entirely rational. The institutional question is whether that dependence remains governable, substitutable and continuable.

The paper concludes that one of the most important risks created by increasingly capable AI is not the formal transfer of authority to machines. It is the possibility that institutions retain authority after losing the substantive capability required to exercise it.

title: Adopted but not internalized: why the mission statement movement disappointed — evidence from 519 organizations at the fashion's peak

detail.title: Adopted but not internalized: why the mission statement movement disappointed — evidence from 519 organizations at the fashion's peak

Data were collected through voluntary mail and fax surveys of senior executives, completed in their professional capacity and concerning their organizations' management practices. Consistent with standard practice for survey research, voluntary completion and return of the questionnaire constituted consent to participate; respondents were free to decline or to leave any item unanswered, without consequence. detail.abstract: In 1993, mission and vision statements led Bain & Company’s inaugural Management Tools & Trends survey, used by 88% of executives worldwide; by 2023, usage had fallen to 28%. No management tool of its era rose higher or fell further. This paper offers a data-based explanation for that trajectory, drawing on the Mission Audit database: 559 survey responses from 519 organizations spanning corporations, hospitals, international airlines and municipalities across three countries and one international industry, collected at the movement’s peak in the mid-to-late 1990s and spanning more than 1,000 variables on mission creation, content, communication, systems alignment and perceived outcomes. The record shows a consistent pattern. Missions were created by CEOs and senior teams, communicated effectively mainly to the top of the hierarchy, and aligned with planning documents rather than with the systems that govern behaviour — rewards, promotion, evaluation and hiring. We call this the internalization gap. It coincided with mediocre functional outcomes, while systems alignment showed the strongest association with mission achievement, commitment and guidance (r = 0.57–0.65), a pattern that replicated across sectors and countries. The findings ground a proposition for research on management tools: tools are abandoned not because their concepts are hollow, but when symbolic adoption outruns organizational internalization — a mechanism with direct implications for the contemporary corporate purpose movement.

detail.abstract: In cement, glass, abrasives, ceramics and related industries, most plants still plan material requirements from average historical consumption plus the latest sales forecast. This approach works reasonably well when demand is steady, but it consistently leaves operations exposed when construction-related surges arrive. Because a large share of volume moves through dealers and project channels, those surges often become visible only after orders have already landed. Drawing on the supply-chain resilience literature, this conceptual paper argues that continuous material availability is better achieved by designing the operating system to absorb surges than by chasing ever-more-accurate forecasts. We propose a three-layer framework that combines leading-indicatoraugmented demand sensing, multi-tier visible buffers sized for surge magnitude and duration, and pre-engineered process and recipe flexibility. When these layers operate as the default system rather than as emergency measures, plants can reduce material-related stock-outs by up to 90 percent relative to prior-year baselines while depending far less on forecast quality. The paper discusses implications for operations leaders and outlines directions for empirical testing.

(This paper is written by Andrew Wong (Hong Kong Monetary Authority), Kelvin Ho (Hong Kong Monetary Authority) and Icarus Chan (Hong Kong Monetary Authority).)

In this study, we examined how supplementary leverage ratio (SLR) requirements may reduce primary dealers’ incentives and capacity to act as intermediaries in the U.S. Treasury (UST) market during periods of market stress. Based on transaction-level data drawn from the March 2020 cash-for-dash episode, during which dealers’ balance sheets were overwhelmed by an unprecedented surge in sales of UST securities, the results provide empirical evidence that concerns about the risk of SLR noncompliance led more constrained primary dealers to sell UST securities aggressively to the Federal Reserve’s market functioning purchase program at lower prices than less constrained dealers to offload their UST securities positions. The results suggest that SLR constraints are an important factor limiting dealers’ intermediation activities during such a market stress episode, thereby amplifying market volatility. A hypothetical quantitative analysis, assuming static dealer positions and an immediate relaxation of SLR requirements at the onset of pandemic crisis, suggests that increasing SLR headroom ratios could meaningfully alleviate bond illiquidity and improve UST market functioning.

title: Institutional Rigor in Higher Education: Institutional Dependability, Cross-Functional Capability, and a Diagnostic Measurement Architecture

detail.title: Institutional Rigor in Higher Education: Institutional Dependability, Cross-Functional Capability, and a Diagnostic Measurement Architecture

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: Higher-education institutions are routinely evaluated through measures of current performance: retention rates, graduation outcomes, financial ratios, accreditation status, research productivity, and student achievement. These measures reveal what an institution is presently accomplishing. They do not necessarily reveal whether the organizational capabilities producing those accomplishments have become sufficiently institutionalized to persist beyond the particular individuals, relationships, and conditions currently sustaining them. This paper proposes Institutional Rigor as a cross-functional construct describing the institutional dependability of mission-critical capabilities—the extent to which those capabilities are formalized, reproducible, evidentially observable, accountable, transferable, continuous, and capable of adaptive reproducibility across changes in personnel, organizational context, and time. The construct is distinguished from institutional effectiveness, governance, quality assurance, organizational resilience, high-reliability organization theory, implementation capacity, program institutionalization, and capability maturity. A function/property architecture is presented in which mission-critical functions serve as loci of assessment and institutionalization properties serve as the characteristics evaluated across those loci. Capability criticality is analytically separated from capability rigor. A provisional hierarchical-formative measurement architecture is specified alongside alternative model specifications, and person dependency, observed post-transition performance, and capacity conversion are positioned as external validation criteria or downstream outcome relationships rather than constituent dimensions. The paper presents ten research propositions and a phased validation agenda. Institutional Rigor is offered as a theoretically grounded construct requiring empirical validation, not as a confirmed measurement framework.

detail.abstract: Credit unions occupy a distinctive position in the U.S. financial system because their cooperative structure combines financial intermediation with member ownership and a community-oriented purpose. Yet institutional purpose does not automatically produce continuing relevance. Relevance must be experienced through accessible products, responsive service, responsible credit, trusted relationships, digital capability, community presence, and governance decisions that translate cooperative identity into contemporary value. This article argues that the central strategic challenge for credit unions is not whether the cooperative model remains valuable, but whether individual institutions can continually convert that model into outcomes that members and communities can recognize and use. Current system data illustrate both strength and pressure. Federally insured credit unions held approximately $2.48 trillion in assets and served 145.8 million members in the first quarter of 2026, while the number of federally insured institutions declined from 4,411 to 4,250 over the preceding year (National Credit Union Administration [NCUA], 2026). The article develops an integrated framework of member, digital, economic, community, generational, and institutional relevance and considers leadership, culture, governance, artificial intelligence, responsible lending, and financial inclusion as mechanisms through which relevance can be sustained. The analysis concludes that cooperative identity becomes strategically consequential only when it is converted into measurable and repeatedly experienced value.

title: The Evolving Market for CEO Talent: The Value of Nonprofit Experience

detail.abstract: Nonprofit experience has become increasingly common among public-company CEOs. By 2023, roughly one in four CEOs of U.S.-listed firms had worked for at least one nonprofit organization during their career. We examine whether this pattern reflects changing demands on corporate leadership. We find that firms are more likely to appoint nonprofit-experienced CEOs when environmental and social concerns are salient and when ESG-oriented investors hold greater ownership stakes. Flow-induced changes in ESG-fund ownership, Russell index reconstitution, and state anti-ESG laws provide quasi-experimental evidence that appointments respond to exogenous changes in stakeholder pressure. These appointments are also associated with positive stakeholder-related outcomes that appear to motivate them. Firms led by nonprofit-experienced CEOs have higher CSR ratings and employee satisfaction, more green patents, and lower toxic emissions. Instrumental-variable estimates and evidence from plausibly exogenous CEO departures support a causal interpretation. Overall, the evidence suggests that nonprofit experience becomes more valuable as firms face greater stakeholder-oriented leadership needs.

title: Emerging Geopolitical Alliances or Issue-Specific Coalitions? A Network Analysis of UN General Assembly Voting Patterns (2016-2025)
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN, Ramjas College, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Ramjas College, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Ramjas College, University of Delhi and National Law University, Delhi

detail.title: Emerging Geopolitical Alliances or Issue-Specific Coalitions? A Network Analysis of UN General Assembly Voting Patterns (2016-2025)
detail.abstract: This study examines whether voting alignment in the United Nations General Assembly reflects fixed geopolitical alliances or issue-specific coalitions that shift depending on the resolution at hand. Using roll-call voting records from Sessions 71 to 79 (2016-2025), the analysis applies social network analysis and the Louvain community detection algorithm to four voting networks: an aggregate network covering all resolutions, and three issue-specific networks addressing Russia-Ukraine, Gaza and Palestine, and Climate and Development resolutions. Pairwise voting agreement scores were calculated for every pair of states, and links below a 0.70 threshold were removed before community detection was applied. The Aggregate network produced a recognizable but weakly separated division, below the 0.3 reference threshold. Ukraine produced by far the strongest community structure, well above threshold, while Gaza showed broad consensus and weak bloc formation, with Climate and Development falling between the two. Among the G4, Germany and Japan clustered together throughout while India and Brazil converged on Aggregate and Climate votes but split on Ukraine and Gaza. Shared institutional goals do not translate into stable voting cohesion; UNGA politics are better described through issue-specific coalitions than fixed geopolitical alliances.

title: From Attraction to Embedding: A Comparative Analysis of Human Capital Policies for R&D+I in the GCC and Singapore

detail.abstract:
Gulf Cooperation Council states have substantially expanded research investment over the past decade, establishing dedicated research authorities and increasing researcher numbers; in Saudi Arabia, researcher density more than doubled between 2020 and 2024. Innovation outputs have not followed. Every GCC state ranks materially lower on the output measures of the Global Innovation Index than on its input measures; high-technology goods account for between zero and three per cent of exports in five of the six states across the fifteen years from 2010, and academic-corporate collaboration has not exceeded five per cent of regional research output. This divergence is documented in the existing literature; the mechanism behind it is not.

This paper examines talent policy as one candidate explanation, in economies where non-nationals hold roughly four-fifths of employment and all foreign residents are classified in law as temporary regardless of length of stay. It develops a three-dimensional framework — attraction, retention and embedding — and applies it to all six GCC states individually, with Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates examined in depth and Singapore serving as comparator. Evidence is drawn from national statistical sources, international indicators, and primary legal and policy documents including the Saudi Premium Residency Permit Law, UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 29 of 2021, and Singapore's Ministry of Manpower and A*STAR scheme documentation.

The findings differ by dimension. Attraction has succeeded: the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia both recorded higher net inflows of artificial intelligence talent than Singapore in 2025. Retention cannot be assessed through outcomes, since no published study has measured how long foreign researchers remain in any of the seven cases; assessed through instrument design, both available routes are closed in the Gulf, as researchers are admitted without a pathway to membership while workforce localisation programmes exempt the positions they occupy. The cases separate most clearly on embedding, and on a measure of ownership rather than employment: between eighty and ninety per cent of GCC patent applications are filed by individuals rather than companies, the reverse of the proportion in industrialised economies, against ninety-two per cent of granted patents held by private firms in Singapore. Attraction and embedding are separable achievements, and the Gulf states have secured the first without the second.

A transferability assessment applying Dolowitz and Marsh's framework finds that the instruments easiest to adopt depend most heavily on conditions the Gulf states currently lack, while those requiring no institutional groundwork lie outside the reach of talent policy. The paper contributes a comparison at the instrument level between two settings the literature has treated separately, an account of institutional variation within the region that bloc-level analysis obscures, and the identification of a measurable evidence gap.

detail.abstract: We introduce reciprocal search, a form of interdependent search in which relational histories of prior help and harm guide searchers’ behavior. Using preregistered experiments in which human-human and human-bot pairs search a shared rugged landscape, we first test preregistered predictions that focus on the existence of reciprocal search and then conduct a series of in-depth analyses on its process by separating alternative generation and selection. These process analyses reveal a stage- and valence-asymmetric pattern of reciprocal search. During alternative generation, prior help from a partner makes an actor’s next search responsive to the partner payoff revealed through the preceding candidate option. Following prior harm, partner payoff no longer predicts the subsequent search. During alternative selection, positive relational histories increase the adoption of partner-benefiting alternatives, whereas negative histories reduce it. Partner-payoff responsiveness is not detected in the human-bot treatments. Human-human pairs display higher and more stable joint performance. By introducing reciprocal search, we extend organizational search theory beyond structural interdependence to illuminate how relational histories shape both the use of feedback and the selection of discovered alternatives.

detail.abstract: In recent years, the geopolitical situation has been greatly affected by the complex relationship between energy issues, security problems, and climate change, with the conflict between Russia and Ukraine being a key point. This conflict has not just increased political disagreements but also raised important concerns about the security of global energy supplies and the environmental effects of relying on certain energy sources. As countries try to maintain a delicate balance between energy safety and sustainability, the effects of this conflict reach well beyond its immediate area. The interruption of energy supplies in this region has caused worldwide market changes, which has led to incessant reassessment of energy policies in many nations. Also, the need to shift to renewable energy sources has become more urgent, as countries face the tough task of ensuring energy safety while also addressing climate change. This article will discuss the various impacts of the ongoing Russia-Ukraine crisis, focusing on its important effects on energy, security, and environmental sustainability.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether a controlled AI-assisted policy-review workflow can move beyond document generation toward evidence-based assurance in Finance and governance. It uses a two-case applied comparative design based on two real policy reviews undertaken at Cannons Creek Independent School NPC in South Africa: a Financial Management Policy review on 24 August 2026 and a Recruitment Policy review on 25 August 2026. Both cases used the same broad seven-step Policy Review Advisor architecture: document classification, legislative and compliance context, organisational context, an explicitly approved alignment baseline, sourcedocument review, human-approved recommended changes, and a final reviewed document that remained subject to organisational governance approval. Evidence comprised the full conversation/process records, approved alignment profiles, recommendation registers, final reviewed documents, and an OpenAI account data export containing message-level timestamps. Paper 01 recorded 3h 16m 16.409s total elapsed time, of which 5m 21.486s was timestamp-derived AI response time and 3h 7m 7.965s was human-gate latency. Paper 02 recorded 1h 37m 48.510s elapsed, 5m 34.586s AI response time and 1h 29m 38.862s human-gate latency. Paper 02 was 50.17% faster end-to-end even though AI response time was 4.07% longer; the principal difference was 52.09% lower human-gate latency. Qualitative evidence also shows the value of explicit context correction, recommendation approval and controlled escalation: in Paper 02 a remuneration-authority conflict was preserved as unresolved rather than silently decided by the AI. The study does not establish a percentage productivity saving versus manual review, legal compliance, or independent output accuracy because no defensible manual comparator or blind external quality review has yet been performed. The main contribution is an applied demonstration that workflow performance in governed AI work depends not only on model capability, but on context, human decision rights, approval gates, traceability and the operating model around the AI.

title: Prediction of Fatigue and Performance Decline Using Salivary Biomarkers in Response to Short-Term High-Intensity Exercise
affiliations: Payame Noor University, Payam-e-Noor University and Payam-e-Noor University

detail.title: Prediction of Fatigue and Performance Decline Using Salivary Biomarkers in Response to Short-Term High-Intensity Exercise
detail.abstract: Purpose: Accurate prediction of exercise-induced fatigue is essential for optimizing training loads, preventing performance deterioration, and reducing the risk of overreaching. Salivary biomarkers offer a non-invasive and practical approach for monitoring physiological responses to intense exercise. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the predictive value of salivary biomarkers for fatigue and performance decline following shortterm high-intensity exercise. Methodology: A repeated-measures experimental design was employed involving physically active adults who completed a short-term high-intensity exercise protocol. Saliva samples were collected before and immediately after exercise to assess selected biomarkers, including cortisol, alpha-amylase, and immunoglobulin A. Performance outcomes were evaluated using anaerobic power and repeated sprint tests. Data were analyzed using paired-samples t-tests, Pearson correlation coefficients, multiple linear regression, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Statistical significance was established at p < 0.05. Results: Significant post-exercise increases were observed in salivary cortisol and alpha-amylase levels, accompanied by reductions in peak power output and repeated sprint performance (p < 0.001). Salivary cortisol demonstrated the strongest association with fatigue-related performance decline (r = 0.68, p < 0.001). Regression analysis indicated that the combined biomarker model significantly predicted performance deterioration, explaining 52% of the variance (Adjusted R² = 0.52). ROC analysis revealed acceptable predictive accuracy for identifying athletes at risk of substantial performance decline (AUC = 0.84). Conclusion: Salivary biomarkers, particularly cortisol and alpha-amylase, represent sensitive indicators of acute physiological stress and can effectively predict fatigue-related performance impairment following short-term highintensity exercise. These findings support the integration of saliva-based monitoring systems into athlete load-management strategies. Novelty: This study introduces a practical biomarker-based predictive model that combines salivary physiological indicators with performance metrics to facilitate early detection of exercise-induced fatigue in high-intensity training environments.

detail.abstract: Purpose: This study develops an Integrated Construction Waste Minimisation (ICWM) framework to address the construction sector's high material demand and waste generation by integrating complementary design, digital and circular-economy strategies. Methodology: A critical systematic literature review following PRISMA synthesised 78 sources published between 2015 and 2023, including peer-reviewed studies, policy documents and selected industry evidence. We standardised quantitative waste-reduction data from 54 construction projects for comparative analysis. The framework was developed through thematic synthesis and grounded in institutional theory and the Technology-Organisation-Environment framework; we appraised study quality using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Findings: Integrated implementation can reduce material waste by 40-60%. Design for Manufacture and Assembly shows the highest direct reduction potential (60-75%); Building Information Modelling achieves 15-25%; material passports support 40-50% recovery; leasing models achieve 70-92% material reduction; and enabling technologies such as blockchain and Internet of Things systems provide approximately 15-25% indirect savings. The ICWM framework identifies three implementation pathways: Incremental (20-30% reduction; 12-24 months), Transformative (40-50%; 24-36 months), and Disruptive (60-75%; 36-60 months). Originality/value: The study integrates quantitative performance evidence with institutional and organisational adoption theory, providing a phase-based decision framework for practitioners and policymakers pursuing 2030 waste-reduction targets.

detail.abstract: The concept of supply chain viability (SCV) has recently evolved into a thriving research area within supply chain management. To date, SCV has largely been theorized from the narrow perspective of survival amid increased disruption and crisis. In this paper, we argue that while this perspective is valuable, organizations should consider the needs of primary and secondary stakeholder groups to achieve long-term viability. Based on a semi-systematic literature review and eight expert interviews, we have identified 26 overarching stakeholder requirements across the three SCV performance dimensions of efficiency, resilience, and sustainability. We identify that those requirements frequently diverge in content and priority across stakeholder groups. This divergence results in either paradoxical tensions or synergies. Building on these findings, we introduce a vector-based model to systematically analyze and compare these requirements and present two research propositions for future validation: Firstly, each identified stakeholder requirement influences efficiency, resilience, and sustainability simultaneously, albeit to varying degrees. Secondly, the aggregated direction and dispersion of all stakeholder requirements determine priorities for the strategic development of SCV. This paper contributes to existing theory by introducing a stakeholder-focused approach to the systems-theoretical conceptualization that has dominated SCV research to date. For practitioners, the model provides a method for anticipating trade-offs and identifying potential synergies to support the prioritization of SCV practices.

detail.abstract: Indonesia’s rupiah has come under renewed pressure, but the underlying risks differ from those of the 1997 Asian financial crisis. detail.abstract: This working paper is a documentary and conceptual analysis of a bounded corpus of Chinese policy texts, official statistics and press of record, closed on 13 September 2026; it collects no original data beyond a one-day reading of vendor price pages, and its comparisons reach only as far as that corpus. China reports the consumption of machine intelligence as an official figure: its National Data Administration announces daily token-call totals at State Council Information Office press conferences, and Xinhua carried the series above 140 trillion a day by March 2026. Beijing's July 2026 measures on agent-led development call, in their own text, for token factories, exploratory token vouchers and the monitoring of a token economy; the power-grid reading of that stack belongs to a business-press analysis, not to the measures. Carriers, banks and restaurants sell or give away prepaid token allowances through phone bills, cards and receipts: commercial, opt-in programs, months old. Within the review corpus defined in the paper, no equivalent official series and no equivalent household entitlement were identified elsewhere; the comparators run through subscriptions and institutional compute support. This documentary analysis records that architecture with tiered source attribution and compares four jurisdictions without ranking. It also prices the unit: a dated table of official list prices shows posted prices for the same nominal count spanning about three orders of magnitude in the United States sample and under two in the China sample, a spread of tiers within each market rather than a gap between markets, and a measure of prices, not capability. Building on prior proposals for universal basic AI access, the paper's contribution is deliberately narrow. It applies a universal service framework to verified Chinese token products, shows why a raw-token allowance alone is not an adequate entitlement, and sets out the eight-element entitlement architecture, from beneficiary to remedy, that a universal basic token would need to become enforceable, with some elements stipulated for illustration, the rest marked open, and the guaranteed quality tier as the political crux.

detail.abstract:
Virginia's State Corporation Commission spent nearly nine months deciding whether the Commonwealth needed a 944 megawatt gas plant, then suspended that decision and took another two months to reconsider it. Two intervenor experts told it that the Company's own resource plan places its gas-fired fleet in a fully subscribed pipeline corridor, and that the omitted cost of firm fuel delivery could add roughly $300 million to a project the Commission priced at $1.47 billion. The Company answered in rebuttal that CERC requires no new pipeline transportation contract at all, because its planning convention for combustion turbines is interruptible service, a capacity factor below twenty percent, and oil through the winter. The record carries at least four different capacity factors for the plant, ranging from 2.7 to 20 percent, and an intervenor told the Commission the figure kept changing between analyses. The twenty-seven page final order does not mention the exchange, names no pipeline company, and does not use the phrase “capacity factor.” Asked on reconsideration whether it had ignored evidence it did not discuss, the Commission answered that the allegation is “incorrect as a matter of both fact and law,” and that it need not write down what it weighed. Twenty days after the hearing closed, an indirect subsidiary of the applicant signed a twenty-year contract for 200,000 dekatherms a day of new interstate transportation capacity, filed for certification with a federal agency that has said, in a neighbouring Virginia certificate, that it “does not weigh end uses differently for the purpose of determining need.” This paper traces what each forum wrote down and finds that no Virginia forum states what the capacity costs.

detail.abstract: Supply chain resilience has become a central theme in the face of global disruptions, from pandemics, natural disasters, climate change, and geopolitical instability. This review explores data-driven approaches that enhance resilience by integrating predictive analytics, optimization, and risk modeling. Predictive analytics enables organizations to anticipate demand fluctuations, supplier risks, and external shocks through statistical, machine learning, and hybrid methods. Optimization techniques strengthen supply chain continuity by balancing cost efficiency, flexibility, sustainability, and redundancy. Risk modeling frameworks, including stochastic simulations, network-based approaches, and AI-driven systems, provide structured tools for quantifying vulnerabilities and stress-testing supply chain networks. Applications across sectors such as healthcare, retail, energy, and transportation demonstrate how these methods support adaptability and continuity in uncertain environments. Building on this synthesis, the paper proposes an integrated framework that connects predictive analytics, optimization, and risk modeling, offering a pathway toward robust, adaptive, and sustainable supply chains. This revised version adds a fully quantified applied case study, using an exact mixed-integer optimization model to measure the cost of facility redundancy in a location-routing setting, illustrating the optimization layer in concrete rather than purely conceptual terms. The review concludes with a discussion of limitations, emerging trends, and future research opportunities to guide both academics and practitioners in advancing supply chain resilience.

detail.abstract: All-electric vehicles, especially battery electric vehicles, have been the focus of public attention for emission-free mobility worldwide, but market demand for them is still lagging behind political and industry expectations in many countries. The discussion about (pollutant) emission-free driving is now also expanding to include hydrogen-based drive systems with combustion engines. Up to now, the central assessment criterion has been “energy efficiency,” which, however, has a purely technology- and supply-oriented character. Given the (current) global buying restraint toward battery electric vehicles, the author therefore proposes a market- and demand-oriented perspective on emission-free vehicles. He defines the criteria of “ecological effectiveness” and “economic efficiency” instead of “energy efficiency” as assessment standards. In the context of portfolio and product life cycle analyses, this results in new insights and perspectives that particularly concern the emission-free “combustion engine”. title: Network Freshness Score (NFS): A Sensor-Free Metric for Quantifying Upstream Shelf-Life Consumption in Perishable Food Supply Chains

detail.title: Network Freshness Score (NFS): A Sensor-Free Metric for Quantifying Upstream Shelf-Life Consumption in Perishable Food Supply Chains

declarations.declarationOfInterest: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: n/a

detail.abstract: Food loss and waste in U.S. perishable supply chains is a documented national priority, with USDA and EPA targeting a 50% reduction by 2030. A substantial share of produce loss is determined upstream — by sourcing decisions, network architecture, and cold-chain compliance — before product ever reaches the point-of-sale systems that existing measurement approaches address. We propose the Network Freshness Score (NFS), a sensor-free metric quantifying the fraction of a commodity's post-harvest shelf life consumed by upstream network operations, computable from data retailers already hold: supplier dwell time, transit duration, and node temperatures from standard operating procedures. Building on Q₁₀ degradation kinetics and calibrated to published postharvest science, the NFS model connects network design decisions to store-arrival shelf life, which we then link to waste outcomes using validated store-level waste estimators (van Donselaar and Broekmeulen, 2025). We introduce Maximum Allowable DC Dwell (MADD) — the maximum holding time a distribution centre can impose given upstream consumption — as an actionable design constraint. Simulation across five network configurations and three commodity archetypes shows that: (1) NFS and MADD are highly commodity-sensitive; (2) cold-chain compliance investment has sharply diminishing returns for long-shelf-life commodities; and (3) consolidation nodes add measurable upstream shelf-life consumption that must be offset by tighter dwell discipline. The binary two-state NFS approximation is validated against continuous time-temperature telemetry with 0.14% variance (Abdella et al., 2021), confirming its accuracy as a representation of continuous degradation dynamics. The framework is designed for adoption without sensor infrastructure, enabling comparison of alternative sourcing and network designs before capital is committed.

detail.abstract: Organizations may experience productivity improvements from artificial intelligence without corresponding increases in enterprise value, as AI-driven productivity does not inherently lead to additional economic value. The Margin-Cap Trap occurs when AI enhances productive capacity without a strategic decision regarding its allocation. This article examines three strategies for utilizing released capacity: Labor Cost Optimization, Operational Workforce Augmentation, and Strategic Capacity Investment through Value-Based AI Arbitrage. An Enterprise AI Value Simulation assesses these strategies by modeling variations in workforce, workload demand, operating costs, operating profit, and enterprise value under different business scenarios. Under the modeled conditions, Strategic Capacity Investment through Value-Based AI Arbitrage yields the highest enterprise value by converting released capacity into additional value-generating demand in areas such as innovation, market expansion, and customer value. This framework offers a systematic approach for assessing AI-enabled capacity-allocation decisions and their financial implications.

detail.abstract: The rapid advancement of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has increased the creation and circulation of realistic Synthetically Generated Information (SGI), creating new challenges for intermediary liability. The Information Technology (Intermediary Guideline and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026 introduce a statutory framework for SGI and reduce the timeline under Rule 3(1)(d) for intermediaries to act upon qualifying government or court notification from thirty-six hours to three-hours. This article examines the interacts between the compressed timeline, the conditional safeguard under Section 79 of Information Technology Act, 2000 (IT Act 2000) and the protection of freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) of Indian Constitution. It argues that the concern is not the requirement of rapid action itself, but the difficulty of assessing the legal status of flagged content within a compressed period where the consequences of non-compliance may affect the availability of the Section 79 Safeguard. This may encourage precautionary removal, including where synthetically generated content constitutes protected expression. The framework adequately distinguishes synthetic content from unlawful content and argues for calibrated procedural safeguard, including differentiated timeline, authorized notifications, rapid review of wrongful removal and greater transparency, consistent with Article 19(2) and doctrine of proportionality.

title: Blockchain-based Dispute Resolution as Sanctuary Justice? Exit, Voice and the State
affiliations: CERSA/CNRS

detail.title: Blockchain-based Dispute Resolution as Sanctuary Justice? Exit, Voice and the State

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author served as Chief Legal Officer of Gnosis until June 2022 and remains a member of GNOciety, the channel of GNO token-holders, on which parts of the paper's account of Gnosis draw. The author is a co-author of the Backstop Layer 2 whitepaper, which Section 7 discusses as a candidate design. The author holds GNO, ETH, UMA, and PNK tokens.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this research.

publicationDetails.detailsText: A short version is in preparation as a chapter for Primavera De Filippi and Morshed Mannan (eds), A Research Agenda for Blockchain and the Law (Edward Elgar).

detail.abstract:
In March 2026 Vitalik Buterin called on the Ethereum community to reorient its purpose: not to remake the world in blockchain's image, but to prevent any single power from gaining total control over people's digital lives. The means he proposed are "sanctuary technologies": open infrastructures without an owner, designed so that dependence on them cannot be weaponised. This paper examines a component his call leaves out, the resolution of disputes, and asks whether blockchain-based dispute resolution as it now operates can become “Sanctuary Justice”. 

The paper provides a framework for mapping blockchain-based and blockchain-supported dispute resolution processes along three axes, drawn from Hirschman: exit, voice, and reliance on the state's monopoly on violence. It distils from Buterin's framing a single test of sanctuary compatibility: whether the bond a dispute system creates can be worked against those it binds, through control of the mechanism or through the exposure participation creates. It applies the test to empirical case studies from deployed systems using on-chain records, governance votes and public deliberation: on the exit axis, the Nouns DAO ragequit and the raider campaigns at Rook and Aragon, all in 2023, and the 2026 GnosisDAO redemption vote, together with the 2025 Gnosis Chain fork and the 2020 Steem/Hive split; on the voice axis, a set of Kleros and UMA/Polymarket disputes; on the state-based axis, Immunefi's arbitration framework and the 2026 KelpDAO litigation.

The findings are not encouraging. In the cases examined, none of the mechanisms meets the test. Exit is priced and permissioned, and the chain-level fork examined operated as voice exercised by a small interested circle through exit's machinery. Within the existing protocols, voice is capped by an economic security bound and is worked from within, by insiders who hold the stake and platforms that frame the questions. The examined systems survive below the bound because it is masked, not escaped. Recourse to the state borrows its authority to decide and pays in exposure that design can narrow but not remove. The field's stall, the paper argues, reflects demand as much as design: every dispute these systems handled could be returned to the state, so they never had to solve their hardest problems. Autonomous AI agents, for whom the state route is (currently) not open, are the first demand that cannot be sent back. The paper identifies the bound as the central technical obstacle, and insider conflict and platform discretion as failures that occur below the bound and that it does not measure. Because the two axes fail in complementary ways, the paper proposes a candidate route beyond the bound: combining voice, which can decide, with exit, since a user's own choice of which fork to adopt is the one element money cannot buy. It illustrates the combination with a forkable-ledger design and sets out the unresolved problems the design inherits from exit. It concludes by setting out a research agenda to bring blockchain-based dispute resolution closer to becoming Sanctuary Justice.

title: Swarm Intelligence Risk - When Intelligence Becomes Distributed Infrastructure

detail.title: Swarm Intelligence Risk - When Intelligence Becomes Distributed Infrastructure
