detail.abstract: Financial institutions increasingly route analysts, portfolio teams, and risk processes to a few shared artificial intelligence (AI) models. We show that which model serves which user is a design margin distinct from vendor concentration. An institution can hold each user's probability of receiving each model, and expected accuracy, fixed and still change the common error in its aggregate forecast, because they leave the joint assignment across users free. Aggregate loss depends on model-error covariance through assigned exposures, and coordinated assignment reduces it whenever model errors differ, at no cost to any user's forecast quality. We characterize when a policy comparison holds for every covariance matrix, give a routing algorithm with an approximation guarantee, and derive a personalized dependence charge under which every optimal assignment is a Nash equilibrium. In a competitive rational-expectations market with two exchangeable models, balancing risk-bearing capacity locally improves price discovery when crossmodel covariance is at most three times idiosyncratic error variance; with stronger covariance, a closed-form supply-noise threshold separates gains from reversals. When investors choose models, an accuracy improvement can induce migration toward the model with more common error and worsen price discovery. Assignment and adoption are distinct margins through which shared AI errors reach prices.

title: Does Platform-Enabled Personal Servicisation Raise Living Standards in Indonesia Four Years After the COVID-19 Pandemic? Instrumental Variable Double-LASSO Estimator
affiliations: , BPS-Statistics Indonesia, BPS-Statistics Indonesia and Institut Teknologi Sepuluh Nopember

detail.title: Does Platform-Enabled Personal Servicisation Raise Living Standards in Indonesia Four Years After the COVID-19 Pandemic? Instrumental Variable Double-LASSO Estimator

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare no competing interests in conducting and publishing this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The participants gave their consent for the administrative collection of the data to the Badan Pusat Statistik - Statistics Indonesia.
declarations.funderStatement: We received no funding for this work.

detail.abstract: Digital platforms increasingly coordinate fragmented service activities across markets and households, yet evidence remains limited on whether personal participation in digital platforms improves living standards. We investigated the welfare effects of platform-enabled personal servicisation in Indonesia and whether effects differed by channel and gender. Crosssectional data for 602,906 adults aged 15-55 years were drawn from the 2024 Indonesian National Socioeconomic Survey and linked by district to the 2024 Village Potential Census. Platform-enabled servicisation was defined as internet use for service information, buying, selling, working from home, online banking or digital-content creation. The outcome was log personal consumption expenditure. Two advanced, complementary estimators were applied. Double/debiased machine learning with lasso-based nuisance estimation flexibly adjusted for high-dimensional observed confounding while limiting model-selection and regularisation bias. Instrumental-variable double-lasso then addressed residual endogeneity, reverse causality and measurement error using local base transceiver station coverage as instrument. Supporting analyses comprised a placebo test, channel-specific models, gender-stratified estimation and an instrumental-variable interaction model to estimate heterogenous welfare effects across gender. Platform participation was reported by 34.5% of respondents. The double-lasso estimate was positive and precisely estimated (β=0.130, SE=0.005; p<0.01), equivalent to approximately 13.9% higher expenditure. All six channels were positively associated with expenditure, with the largest adjusted associations for online banking (β=0.278) and working from home (β=0.210). The complementary instrumental-variable estimate was considerably larger and remained strongly positive (β=1.099, SE=0.293; p<0.01), identifying the local effect among adults whose participation responded to telecommunications infrastructure. The placebo estimate for pleasure travel in the preceding year was null (β=-0.140, SE=0.208). Gender-stratified double-lasso estimates were nearly identical for women and men, while stratified instrumental-variable estimates were positive in both groups. Crucially, the interaction model identified a significant additional benefit for women. In conclusion, platform-enabled 1 servicisation is strongly and affirmatively associated with higher living standards in Indonesia across complementary identification strategies and a large, diverse national population. Benefits extend across several forms of participation and are larger for women in the formal interaction analysis. Digital infrastructure can therefore expand welfare-enhancing economic opportunities, but equitable gains require complementary access to devices, skills, finance, logistics and effective platform protections.

title: Beyond the Discrete Micro-Price. A Continuous Spectral Resolvent Approach to High-frequency Asset Valuation with Order Flow Velocity
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Beyond the Discrete Micro-Price. A Continuous Spectral Resolvent Approach to High-frequency Asset Valuation with Order Flow Velocity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human participants, clinical trials, animal subjects, or sensitive personal data. All empirical analyses are based entirely on publicly available or anonymized historical financial market data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Stoikov's classical micro-price (Stoikov, 2018) models future mid-price expectations through a finite-state, discrete-time absorbing Markov chain constructed on a discretized grid of order book imbalances and spreads. While mathematically tractable, Stoikov's framework suffers from three severe structural drawbacks: (i) an intractable O((nm) 3) computational bottleneck induced by large matrix inversions, (ii) substantial discretization bias that discards intra-tick continuous dynamics, and (iii) strict blindness to continuous order flow momentum and depth replenishment velocities. 

      In this paper, we propose an alternative, strictly superior framework: the Spectral Resolvent Flow-Price (SRFP). By formulating the joint dynamics of the limit order book as a continuous-state Jacobi-type diffusion coupled to a marked point process of order cancellations and aggressive market orders, we model the microstructure price as the continuous resolvent operator of the infinitesimal generator of the order book state. We obtain an explicit, closed-form expansion for the fair price via Sturm-Liouville spectral decomposition without requiring discrete state binning or artificial empirical symmetrization. 

      We prove that the SRFP is a strict local martingale, possesses uniformly bounded variance, and converges asymptotically to the continuous-time efficient price. Using submillisecond NASDAQ Level-3 (ITCH-5.0) and CME futures tick data, we demonstrate that the SRFP outperforms the Stoikov micro-price by reducing out-of-sample root-mean-square error (RMSE) by up to 34.8%, eliminating residual autocorrelation artifacts, and speeding up online numerical evaluation from O((nm) 3) to O(K) operations, enabling sub-microsecond execution in production ultra-high-frequency algorithmic environments.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Mechanistic Misspecification Correction for Sparse Longitudinal CT-Derived Lung Nodule Trajectory Prediction
affiliations: Vanderbilt University and Harvard University

detail.title: Uncertainty-Aware Mechanistic Misspecification Correction for Sparse Longitudinal CT-Derived Lung Nodule Trajectory Prediction

publicationDetails.detailsText:
Submitted to Biomedical Signal Processing and Control (Elsevier)
Manuscript ID: BSPC-D-26-11232

detail.abstract: Predicting lung nodule volume trajectories from sparse longitudinal computed tomography (CT) follow-up remains difficult because available scans per lesion are few and CT-derived measurements are affected by registration, segmentation, and annotation variability. A further obstacle is systematic misspecification of mechanistic growth models across heterogeneous patient populations. We propose a three-stage framework that combines a Bayesian Gompertz mechanistic backbone with a population-level deviation correction module and a conformal calibration layer for distribution-free uncertainty adjustment. Evaluated on 300 NLSTt-derived three-scan trajectories under grouped subject-level cross-validation, the correction module reduces log-volume RMSE from 0.5662 to 0.5279 and volume-space MAE from 0.8551 to 0.7636 cm^3. Conformal calibration raises empirical 95% coverage from 0.600 to 0.950 and reduces interval score from 12.1614 to 8.4727. These results show that explicitly correcting mechanistic misspecification, rather than replacing the Gompertz backbone, yields more reliable predictions under sparse CT follow-up.

title: Quantum-inspired Simplicial Learning for Multiclass Cancer Classification with Synchronization and No-phase-locking Analysis
affiliations: Macquarie University

detail.title: Quantum-inspired Simplicial Learning for Multiclass Cancer Classification with Synchronization and No-phase-locking Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: We present a quantum-inspired simplicial topological framework for multiclass cancer classification from RNA-Seq gene expression data. Building on the quantum algorithms of Leditto et al. [1] for the Simplicial Kuramoto Model (SKM), we map RNA-Seq profiles of 801 tumour samples across five cancer types (BRCA, KIRC, COAD, LUAD, PRAD) onto a gene co-expression simplicial complex. Each sample is encoded as phase-like and frequency-like oscillator states on nodes, edges, and triangles of the complex. Two classes of features are extracted: (i) Task-1 simplicial order parameters measuring higher-order synchronization, and (ii) Task-2 no-phase-locking (NPL) critical values certifying the absence of phase-locked states. A Random Forest classifier achieves 92.5% accuracy using only these 29 topological features. We further implement quantum circuit analogues: a Hadamard-test circuit (Task 1) and a Variational Quantum Linear Solver (Task 2) in PennyLane, demonstrating mean absolute errors of 0.0080 and 100% NPL agreement across 10 test samples respectively. Quantum advantage analysis shows a super-polynomial cost ratio 𝑇_𝐶/𝑇_𝑄 exceeding unity in the regime 𝑘 = 𝛩 (𝑙𝑜𝑔 𝑛). All source code and results are made publicly available.

title: Governing AI and Shaping the Future of Education: Toward a Context-Sensitive Governance Framework for Small-State and Developing Education Systems

detail.title: Governing AI and Shaping the Future of Education: Toward a Context-Sensitive Governance Framework for Small-State and Developing Education Systems

detail.abstract: A curriculum officer in a small-island ministry of education opens an international AI governance guidance document and, on its first substantive page, finds a checklist for auditing algorithmic bias in adaptive learning platforms. Her ministry has never procured the kind of platform the checklist assumes. This paper argues that the mismatch is not incidental but structural: the AI-in-education governance literature has converged on a fairly stable set of variables, namely equity, data privacy, algorithmic bias, teacher capacity, and academic integrity, derived almost entirely from research conducted in, or generalising from, infrastructure-rich contexts. Drawing on a verified literature corpus alongside comparative policy evidence from UNESCO, the International Telecommunication Union, and a 2026 systematic review of AI-in-education adoption across developed and developing states, the paper shows that small-state and developing education systems face a substantially different set of binding constraints, organised around infrastructure and connectivity, data sovereignty, workforce capacity, and regional institutional cooperation. This divergence has not been tested empirically, nor has it been synthesised into a peer-reviewed governance framework fit for small-state application. The paper formulates this as a specific, examinable research problem, namely whether the dominant governance variable set is adequate for small-state contexts or whether governance priorities must be re-derived from the binding constraints those contexts actually face, and proposes a research agenda to address it, anchored in the Caribbean Small Island Developing State context.

title: Where Imported Physical Climate Risk Stops: Supply Chains, Overseas Plants, and the Manufacturing Balance Sheet

detail.title: Where Imported Physical Climate Risk Stops: Supply Chains, Overseas Plants, and the Manufacturing Balance Sheet

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest
declarations.funderStatement: The research was conducted as a component of the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment (MCEE)-funded Graduate School Specialized in Climate Change.

detail.abstract: Physical climate risk realised abroad reaches a manufacturing economy through two channels: the inputs its firms buy and the plants they own. We measure both for Korean manufacturing and ask how far a shock travels. For the ownership channel we geocode 1,399 overseas plants and 1,844 sales offices of 474 listed manufacturers and evaluate daily ERA5 temperature, precipitation and wind at each site; for the trade channel we weight supplier-country hazards by embodied value added from international input-output tables. National-aggregate exposure measures overstate the heat that plants actually face by a factor of three to four in the hottest supplier economies and understate their flood exposure, because they average over territory with no production. Tracing the shock step by step, we find that severe floods and droughts at a firm's principal plant leave a trace on consolidated asset growth of about two percent, consistent with write-downs; they do not move profitability, capital expenditure, or plant survival, and each null is bounded. Through the trade channel a severe drought in the largest supplier reaches the input bill as 0.2 percent, trade with the stressed partner falls symmetrically in both directions, and the dispersion of marginal revenue products of capital across domestic establishments is unmoved, with effects above two to five percent ruled out. An earthquake placebo, the contrast between consolidated and separate statements, and the contrast between plants and sales offices separate a climate effect from disaster exposure in general, an overseas effect from parent-side shocks, and a production effect from mere presence abroad. Extreme heat is the one hazard on which the evidence divides, and plant-level tests do not resolve it.

title: Focus or Spread? Attention Allocation under High-Dimensional Uncertainty

detail.abstract: This paper brings the rotate-then-quantize (RTQ) strategy of Zandieh et al. (2025) to economics and finance as a general tool for high-dimensional decision problems. RTQ converts a d-dimensional problem into d one-dimensional quantization problems, addressing the curse of dimensionality. We illustrate with rational inattention. Conventional wisdom says to focus on a few variables and ignore the rest; RTQ accommodates non-Gaussian priors with discrete signals as Sims (2006) conjectured and gives a computable criterion for focus vs broad coverage. Portfolio-choice tests on CRSP merged with the LSEG 13F panel over five decades are consistent with these predictions.

title: Interest-Parity Condition Around the Opening of the Telegraph Between London and Paris in 1851
affiliations: Swiss National Bank - Study Center Gerzensee

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the interest-parity condition around the opening of the international telegraph between London and Paris on November 13, 1851. Connecting these financial hubs by the first means of modern information technology changed the financial environment. Before, a London speculator comparing the short-term return between British pounds and French francs had to form an expectation about the current exchange rate in Paris. Thereafter, this expectation became obsolete. Biweekly data around 1851 suggest that the deviations from the interest-parity condition between London and Paris were relatively small. Apparently, speculators had on average already quite accurate exchange rate expectations before the introduction of the telegraph.

title: Revisiting deterministic spatial interpolation methods: A review and benchmarking for surface reconstruction
affiliations: Curtin University, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) - Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), University of Southampton, University of Twente and University of Twente

detail.title: Revisiting deterministic spatial interpolation methods: A review and benchmarking for surface reconstruction

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no relevant financial or non-financial interests to disclose.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received to assist with the preparation of this manuscript.

detail.abstract: Spatial interpolation methods (SIMs) have been intensively applied in geography applications for generating spatial surfaces and predicting values at unsampled locations. Deterministic interpolation methods, however, often remain under-recognized in the mainstream geospatial literature, despite their feasibility for spatial prediction. Some of these originate from numerical analysis, and primarily focus on numerical stability and computational efficiency. They are non-stochastic in nature and follow general principles of spatial continuity and dependence. This study aims to highlight these methods to spatial data science by (1) reviewing their characteristics, applications, and implementations; (2) classifying them based upon their features and identifying their mathematical associations; and (3) benchmarking their performance using both Monte Carlo simulations and a realworld scenario. Given their benchmarked performance, methods with relatively clear performance characteristics can be grouped into two categories. The first group, including Kriging, RBF, linear, and cubic methods, have higher prediction accuracy, but at the cost of more computational time. The second group consists of Chebyshev, Bezier, and B-spline methods, which show similar RMSE levels within the group but slightly lower accuracy than the first group, while offering lower computational cost. Overall, the results demonstrate that deterministic interpolation methods can provide stable and reliable predictive performance with favourable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs.

title: The $3 Trillion Question: A Macroeconomic Analysis of the AI Debt Market in 2029

detail.abstract: This paper examines the macroeconomic implications of the projected $3 trillion to $7 trillion AI-related debt market by 2029, analysing the structural transformation of corporate financing, financial stability risks, and broader economic consequences. Drawing on recent analyses from the Bank for International Settlements, industry research firms, financial institutions, and academic research, this study argues that the AI debt wave represents a paradigm shift in technology sector financing comparable to historical infrastructure buildouts. The analysis identifies four key macroeconomic channels: the transition from equity to debt financing, the creation of new asset classes, the concentration of credit risk, and the potential for a destabilising investment correction. The paper concludes that while the AI debt market could become a significant component of global credit markets, its sustainability depends critically on the commercial viability of AI applications and the resolution of structural bottlenecks in energy and semiconductor supply chains. Particular attention is paid to the opacity of private credit markets and the reflexive nature of AI infrastructure financing, where commitments sustain valuations that in turn enable further borrowing. A specific parallel is drawn between the current AI debt complex and the subprime securitisation crisis of 2007-2008.

detail.abstract: We study estimation of a linear functional in random-design linear models when γ = p/n ∈ (1, ∞) under the dense regime where the design covariance is unknown, and neither the regression vector nor the precision matrix is assumed sparse. Suppose the spectrum of the design covariance belongs to [ℓ, L] and κ = L/ℓ, we establish the minimax mean squared rate for the linear functional has the order n^{-α(κ,γ)} , where the exponent α(κ, γ) has an explicit elliptic-integral representation and α(κ, γ) < 1 when both κ > 1 and γ > 1. We propose the Bocca estimator, which combines empirically calibrated resolvents through a complex contour integral to attain the optimal rate.

title: The Corcyra Dilemma: A Theory of Dynamic Strategic Commitments
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Corcyra Dilemma: A Theory of Dynamic Strategic Commitments

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract: This paper develops the Corcyra Dilemma as a theory of dynamic strategic commitments. Existing scholarship explains why states design conditional or probabilistic commitments, how alliance relationships create risks of abandonment and entrapment, and why credibility varies across contexts. The argument here addresses a narrower temporal problem: what happens when an adversary tests a deliberately limited commitment and the test itself changes the guarantor's incentives. The Corcyra Dilemma occurs when a limited commitment leaves enough uncertainty to permit a coercive test, but the test raises the political, strategic, military, or alliance costs of abandonment sufficiently to strengthen the effective commitment after deterrence has failed. The theory specifies a triadic structure, identifies the test-induced change in abandonment costs as the central causal variable, derives a non-linear 'Corcyra interval' in which intermediate commitments are especially vulnerable to test-plus-intervention sequences, and states demanding process-tracing criteria for falsification. Historical evidence from Corcyra, Korea, and the 1958 Taiwan Strait crisis provides positive and negative probes, while Saguntum and Munich are treated as shadow and boundary cases. The final section applies the framework to Taiwan. The central implication is that deterrence analysis should examine not only whether a commitment is credible before a crisis, but whether the first coercive move can change the commitment being tested.

title: A semiparametric approach to marginal likelihood computation for multimodal posterior distributions
affiliations: University College London - Department of Economics

detail.title: A semiparametric approach to marginal likelihood computation for multimodal posterior distributions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: Nothing to declare.

detail.abstract: I propose a semiparametric modified harmonic mean estimator of the marginal likelihood that flexibly captures multimodal posterior distributions while remaining computationally feasible. Building on the approach introduced by Sims, Waggoner and Zha (2008), this estimator uses a multidimensional elliptical distribution as the weighting density but nonparametrically approximates a one-dimensional distribution within the ellipsoid. It calculates the normalizing constant of the weighting density by combining rejection sampling from this nonparametric distribution with direct sampling from the ellipsoid. Monte Carlo simulations confirm that the new semiparametric estimator approximates complex distributions more accurately than its parametric counterpart. Furthermore, I show that estimators based on Sims et al. (2008) outperform both sequential Monte Carlo and Geweke (1999) estimators. I also demonstrate that the simplified, simulation-free variants occasionally used in the literature suffer from upward bias.

title: (Mis)measuring Uncertainty: Bunching in Probabilistic Expectations
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin, Banco de España, Banco de España, Universidad de Barcelona and Banco de España - Research Department

detail.title: (Mis)measuring Uncertainty: Bunching in Probabilistic Expectations
detail.abstract:
Probabilistic expectation questions are often used to measure subjective uncertainty, but respondents frequently assign all probability to one outcome. We show that this bunching is partly a survey artifact rather than genuine certainty. In the (online) ECB Consumer Expectations Survey and the (in person) Spanish Survey of Household Finances, bunching is higher among less financially literate respondents and increases with panel tenure. Two survey-design changes provide stronger evidence: enforcing neutral interviewer protocols reduces bunching by about 15 percentage points, and a later questionnaire redesign reduces it by a further 18 percentage points. Interviewer-level variation also falls after standardization. These findings imply that degenerate responses in probabilistic expectations can reflect task burden and survey administration, causing standard measures to overstate certainty and understate uncertainty.

title: Strategic Sovereignty: U.S.–Israeli Strikes and the Reversal of Anti-Regime Protest in Iran
affiliations: New Economic School (NES), ESSEC Business School and Princeton University

detail.title: Strategic Sovereignty: U.S.–Israeli Strikes and the Reversal of Anti-Regime Protest in Iran
detail.abstract:
Can foreign intervention redirect domestic mobilization toward the regime it seeks to weaken? We study the 2026 U.S.–Israeli strikes on Iran, which occurred amid a nationwide anti-government uprising. Combining high-frequency geocoded data on protests with geocoded records of U.S.–Israeli strikes, we document a sharp reversal in political mobilization. Anti-government protest was widespread before the strikes and receded sharply through February amid domestic repression and an intensifying “foreign-agent” narrative. Following the strikes, pro-government rallies and protests against the United States and Israel spread across the country. Exploiting the precise location and staggered timing of counties’ first exposure to a U.S.–Israeli strike, we find little change in total protest activity but a sharp shift from anti-government to pro-government protest. Public statements by U.S. and Israeli leaders increasingly aligned themselves with the protest movement, while Iranian officials portrayed the unrest as foreign-backed. These patterns are consistent with strategic sovereignty: overt foreign intervention can make domestic opposition easier to portray as aligned with an external adversary, weakening its legitimacy and redirecting collective action toward defense of the state.

title: Flowers of Invention: The Economic Impacts of Patent Rights
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

detail.title: Flowers of Invention: The Economic Impacts of Patent Rights
detail.abstract:
How do patent rights affect innovation and downstream production? Patent protection was introduced for plant biotechnology in the United States in 1985, and it affected crops differentially depending on their reproductive structures. Exploiting this unique feature of plant flower structure and a new dataset of crop-specific technology development, I find that the introduction of patent rights increased the development of novel plant varieties. Technology development was driven by a rapid increase in private sector research investment, was accompanied by positive spillover effects on innovation in certain non-biological agricultural technologies, and led to an increase in crop yields. Patent rights, however, may come with potentially significant costs to the consumers of technology and distortions to downstream production. Nevertheless, despite higher spending on seeds, US counties that were more exposed to the change in patent law because of their crop composition experienced an increase in agricultural land values and profits. Taken together, the results suggest that the prospect of patent protection spurred innovation and increased downstream productivity and profits.

title: The Welfare Impacts of Urban Renewal and Forced Relocation: Evidence from Chicago’s HOPE VI Demolitions
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, University of Texas at Austin and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia

detail.title: The Welfare Impacts of Urban Renewal and Forced Relocation: Evidence from Chicago’s HOPE VI Demolitions
detail.abstract:
This paper studies one of the largest spatial redevelopment efforts in the United States: HOPE VI public housing demolitions. Focusing on Chicago, we estimate a neighborhood choice model combining administrative records tracking displaced public-housing residents with Census Bureau data capturing citywide sorting and prices. Demolitions generate large welfare losses driven by displacement costs, partially offset by housing vouchers. Demolitions also raise housing prices and reshape neighborhood composition, with gains concentrated among higher-income homeowners. Counterfactuals show that more generous vouchers and counseling programs mitigate but do not eliminate displaced residents' losses, while expanded redevelopment yields larger citywide gains through general-equilibrium effects.

title: Food Labeling Policies: Aggregate Impacts and Heterogeneity Across Categories
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Department of Economics, Columbia University, Columbia University and Facebook Inc

detail.title: Food Labeling Policies: Aggregate Impacts and Heterogeneity Across Categories
detail.abstract:
We study the aggregate and heterogeneous effects of a front-of-package labeling policy implemented in Chile. We find that consumers reduced their sugar and caloric intake by 9% and 6%, respectively. On the demand side, labels prompt consumers to substitute within categories rather than switching between categories. Within-category responses are more pronounced when labels provide new information. On the supply side, we observe bunching at regulatory thresholds, with substantial heterogeneity across categories, consistent with differing costs of product reformulation. We conclude that considering policy-response heterogeneity is key for effective policy design.

title: From UPI to ULI: Is India Building The Next Revolution in Credit?

detail.abstract: In nine years, UPI has made Indian payments almost unrecognisable. From approximately 3,873 crore transactions in 2021 to 22,828 crore in 2025. Transaction value rising from ₹72 lakh crore to around ₹300 lakh crore over the same period. It demonstrated what open, interoperable infrastructure can accomplish when it meets a genuine unmet need. India is now attempting something considerably harder. Applying the same architectural logic not to move the money, but to move the information on which money is lent.

title: The City Through Her Eyes: Gender-Based Harassment in Public Spaces in Urban India
affiliations: Northwestern University - Department of Economics, Princeton University and Ashoka University

detail.title: The City Through Her Eyes: Gender-Based Harassment in Public Spaces in Urban India
detail.abstract:
Gender-based harassment in public spaces affects women directly through victimization and indirectly through fear. We measure these dual effects in urban India, where harassment is widely regarded as pervasive. Surveying over 4,000 women recruited in public spaces in New Delhi and Bengaluru, we document that 65% of women in New Delhi and 29% in Bengaluru experienced harassment in public spaces in the past year. Past-year prevalence of groping, stalking, or sexual assault is 41% in New Delhi and 14% in Bengaluru. Both frequent, less severe forms of harassment and rarer, more severe forms generate anxiety among women; for example, 46% of women in New Delhi and 25% in Bengaluru report feeling extremely anxious about sexual assault when in public spaces. Not all of the indirect effects track the across-city variation in experienced harassment: in both cities, roughly 70\% of women report that fear of harassment affects whether they work. Finally, on measurement, we show that measured prevalence is more sensitive to questionnaire design where harassment is less common and victims have fewer and less recent incidents to recall.

title: Recommendation Quality and the Concentration of Consumption: Experimental Evidence from Netflix
affiliations: , , Netflix, Netflix, Netflix and

detail.title: Recommendation Quality and the Concentration of Consumption: Experimental Evidence from Netflix
detail.abstract: We study an experiment with 8.5 million users on Netflix's recommender system to measure how improvements in recommendation technology affect the set of products that get consumed. Improvements increase total consumption and users' reliance on recommendations while diffusing recommendations and consumption away from the most popular products ("superstars") toward a larger number of moderately popular products ("middle-tail"), with minimal effects on the most niche products ("long-tail"). Our results challenge the notion that recommender systems polarize consumption — raising the consumption shares of the head and tail at the expense of the middle — and suggest that the returns to investing in middle-tail products grow as algorithms improve and platforms scale.

title: Comparative Statics of Information Acquisition and Risk Aversion
affiliations: University College London - Department of Economics, ,  and

detail.title: Comparative Statics of Information Acquisition and Risk Aversion
detail.abstract: We study how willingness to pay for information depends on risk aversion when a decision maker faces background risk and can acquire information before choosing from a menu of assets. We distinguish investment menus, whose payoffs are procyclical with background wealth, from insurance menus, whose payoffs are countercyclical. Our main results show that the interaction between asset cyclicality and the tail geometry of background risk determines the direction of the comparative statics. When the density of background risk is log-concave, willingness to pay for information decreases with risk aversion for investment menus, whereas with downward-log-convex background risk it increases with risk aversion for insurance menus. The proofs compare the distributions of terminal wealth with and without information and develop new aggregation arguments for state-dependent single-crossing comparisons. We also construct reversals under strictly log-convex tails for investment menus and super-exponential left tails for insurance menus.

title: The Fed Put and Bank Risk-Taking: Evidence from the Loan Book
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, , University of Münster, University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business and University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business

detail.title: The Fed Put and Bank Risk-Taking: Evidence from the Loan Book
detail.abstract: This paper shows that monetary policy changes the risk composition of bank lending by altering the perceived tail risk of bank equity: when FOMC announcements compress the likelihood of costly low-equity states, banks originate riskier commercial and industrial loans. We measure bank-specific tail-risk shocks using equity put option returns and link them to originations in supervisory loan data. The shift toward riskier lending emerges after announcements and extends to lending within existing bank-borrower relationships. Stress-test capital and banks' own reports tying lending standards to risk tolerance corroborate the mechanism. Short-term compensation, earnings pressure, and competition amplify this risk-taking channel.

title: The Convergence Effect: AI and the Political Economy of State Capacities
affiliations: ,  and George Mason University

detail.abstract: What is the effect of the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) on government operations and constitutional rules? The purpose of this paper is to explore the answer to this question through the lens of public choice and constitutional political economy. We explore the spread of generalpurpose technologies (GPTs) across government and how this spread enhances the state's coercive capabilities. To do so, we develop a theory of the "convergence effect" of GPTs. We apply this framework to Artificial Intelligence (AI) as an illustration. In doing so, we show how expansions in the scale and scope of government and the erosion of constraints on government may occur endogenously, without crises or other exogenous changes.

title: A Sin Ban, Not a Sin Tax? Consumption and Incidence of SNAP Soda Restrictions
affiliations: , Yale School of Management and University of Florida

detail.title: A Sin Ban, Not a Sin Tax? Consumption and Incidence of SNAP Soda Restrictions
detail.abstract:
We study the first statewide SNAP restrictions on sweetened beverages and candy. Restricted spending falls 11 percent; calories and sugar fall 5–8 percent. Substitution is asymmetric: eligible fruit drinks partly offset soda declines, while candy restrictions reduce purchases of eligible snacks. Retailers barely change shelf prices. Losing SNAP’s sales-tax exemption raises tax-inclusive prices only 1.9 percent. Spending declines are larger at retailers with greater SNAP use and remain large online, where checkout stigma is less salient. Nationwide adoption would impose 13 percent of the out-of-pocket burden of an equivalent excise tax, while welfare gains reach roughly $1.1 billion annually.

title: The Sovereign-Bank Nexus in Venezuela: GDP Collapse, Financial Repression, and Fiscal Contingency, 1997-2026

detail.title: The Sovereign-Bank Nexus in Venezuela: GDP Collapse, Financial Repression, and Fiscal Contingency, 1997-2026

The quarterly GDP series, the calibrated default model and the debt-perimeter reconciliation were developed as part of the company's analytical work on the Venezuelan restructuring. No external funding was received for this research. The author has no financial position in Venezuelan sovereign or PDVSA bonds.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses publicly available macroeconomic data and regulatory filings; it does not involve human participants, patients, or personal data.

detail.abstract: Debt-sustainability analysis asks how much a sovereign can pay. This paper asks a different question: what happens to the banking system when the sovereign cannot pay. We quantify the sovereign-bank nexus in Venezuela across three structural regimes: the pre-crisis period (2017), hyperinflationary collapse (2020), and the ongoing stabilization attempt (2023-2026). Using a newly assembled dataset drawn from SUDEBAN regulatory filings, BCV monetary statistics, and high-frequency secondary sources, we construct four metrics that the existing literature on Venezuela has not measured: (i) the share of banking-system assets constituting claims on the sovereign or its central bank; (ii) the real (INPC-deflated) capital position of the banking system; (iii) the shortfall that would emerge under stylized inflation-and-haircut scenarios; and (iv) the fiscal contingency-expressed as a share of GDP-that recapitalization would impose on the consolidated public sector. The sovereign exposure ratio peaked at 72.4 percent of total assets in December 2020, driven by a 93-percent reserve requirement (encaje legal) that channeled virtually all deposit growth to the BCV. Even after the encaje eased to 73 percent, exposure remained at 44.2 percent in December 2023-still above the 30-percent threshold that the IMF's June 2026 EMDE study associates with systemic vulnerability. Real bank capital, deflated by the INPC (base December 2007), shows a cumulative erosion of over 99.9 percent from its 2007 level, leaving the system technically insolvent in real terms since at least 2020. A Denton-benchmarked quarterly GDP series (118 quarters, 1997-2026) provides the macroeconomic context: output fell 79.7 percent peak-to-trough (2013-Q4 to 2020-Q3), the deepest peacetime contraction in modern Latin American history, and has recovered only 42.2 percent of the loss by mid-2026. The paper contributes to the IMF's sovereign-bank nexus framework by documenting an extreme case-one where financial repression, not voluntary portfolio choice, is the transmission mechanism-and derives policy implications for any future debt restructuring or IMF-supported program for Venezuela.

title: (How) Do We Teach Emotions?
affiliations: University of Chicago, , University of Wisconsin-Madison, , The University of Chicago and

detail.title: (How) Do We Teach Emotions?
detail.abstract: Emotional intelligence constitutes a key component of human capital, shaped partially by educational materials. Using machine learning and generative AI tools, we examine emotional content in public-school textbooks and children’s literature. A stark mismatch emerges: text exposes children to a broad emotional range, but images overwhelmingly depict happiness and calm, regardless of emotions described in text on the same page. Nearly half of pages show zero overlap between the emotions described in text and those shown in images. This pattern persists across time, contexts, and identities. Household purchases and library inventories suggest content may be endogenously shaped by consumer demand favoring "positive" cover imagery, implying market forces narrow the emotional landscape children encounter.

title: Is It a Lie If I Don’t Know? Mechanisms and Mitigation of Dishonesty Under Ignorance
affiliations: Max Planck Institute for Tax Law and Public Finance

detail.title: Is It a Lie If I Don’t Know? Mechanisms and Mitigation of Dishonesty Under Ignorance
detail.abstract: Ignorance of facts and laws may provide an excuse for self-serving reporting behavior, even at the risk of telling the untruth. This paper examines what decision-makers report when they do not know their true entitlement to a financial gain, why they do so, and how the resulting dilemma under ignorance can be mitigated. In a theory-guided online experiment, I show that ignorance substantially increases self-serving but potentially untruthful reporting behavior relative to a full-information benchmark. Three mechanisms – two behavioral and one institutional – drive this shift: (i) decision-makers' beliefs about their true entitlement, (ii) social norms governing reporting under ignorance, and (iii) the requirement to provide a definite statement. I evaluate two interventions: allowing information acquisition and offering a fair buyout of the unknown entitlement. Both mitigate self-serving reporting under ignorance, but the fair buyout involves a trade-off: it has the unintended side effect of increasing dishonesty among informed decision-makers.

title: From Research Funding to Industry Partnerships: The Gateway and Gatekeeper Roles of University Technology Transfer Offices
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Rady School of Management and University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Rady School of Management

detail.title: From Research Funding to Industry Partnerships: The Gateway and Gatekeeper Roles of University Technology Transfer Offices

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: University Technology Transfer Offices are usually judged by patents, licenses, and revenue. This patent-centric view misses a critical part of their work: helping coordinate the broader process through which protected knowledge contributes to subsequent university-industry collaboration. We examine whether Technology Transfer Office presence changes how Japanese national universities convert publicly funded nanotechnology research into patent and publication outcomes. Using temporally ordered panel measures and university and year fixed effects, we find that Technology Transfer Office presence strengthens the association of prior research funding with subsequent patent grants and university-industry coauthored publications. University Technology Transfer Office presence is also associated with a stronger relationship between patents and later collaborative publication output. Separately, the complementarity between research funding and collaboration is stronger for junior than for senior researchers. The paper's central contribution is to move Technology Transfer Office evaluation beyond patents and licenses by treating collaborative publication as a technology-transfer outcome in its own right. The findings are consistent with Technology Transfer Offices helping universities protect potentially valuable knowledge while sustaining subsequent scientific collaboration. Theoretically, our study recasts the Technology Transfer Office as an organizational capability that may connect protection and dissemination, rather than as an office whose contribution ends with patents and licenses. Practically, it suggests that universities should evaluate Technology Transfer Offices not only by patent counts but also by whether protected knowledge is followed by scientific collaboration and lasting research ties with firms.
