detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence and robotics may change labour demand before unemployment becomes visibly high. At the same time, ageing can reduce the number of available workers even when technology is not causing layoffs. This paper develops the Early AI Economic Transition framework, or EAET, to help governments manage these two changes together. The framework asks a practical sequence of questions. How many jobs are likely to remain unfilled after expected workers are counted? How much verified automation can realistically cover that gap? Which types of skilled workers will become more important as AI and robots expand? And how should social insurance and productive investment adapt if more output is produced with fewer paid human workers? EAET distinguishes automation that fills a genuine vacancy from automation that actually reduces paid employment. It also separates planned automation capacity from work that has already been performed. New labour admissions are reduced only when usable automation is verified within the relevant planning horizon, and only through channels that governments are legally allowed to adjust. The framework also includes electricity, grids, compute, software, strategic materials and skills because large scale AI and robotics cannot expand without them. Bulgaria is used only as an illustrative example of an ageing EU economy. The paper is conceptual: it does not report an implemented EAET test, new causal estimates or calibrated policy effects. Instead, it sets out clear propositions and explains how they could be tested in future research.

title:
The Global Middle Class, Domestic Saving, and Frontier-Validated Growth 
A Long-Run Test of the Economics of Belonging

detail.title:
The Global Middle Class, Domestic Saving, and Frontier-Validated Growth 
A Long-Run Test of the Economics of Belonging

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No interest
declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract:
This article develops and tests a long-run growth proposition derived from the Economics of Belonging. Its central thesis is that domestic saving determines the scale of accumulation, but sustained access to the manufactured consumption of the global middle class determines whether that accumulation remains technologically valid. Such access can arise through a broad domestic middle class or through manufacturing value added ultimately absorbed by final demand in the United States and developed Western Europe. The theory therefore distinguishes frontier-validated growth from artificial growth based on protected demand, obsolete capital, natural resources, or post-collapse rebound.


The empirical analysis proceeds in two stages. The first uses four initial cohorts from 1995 to 2010, OECD Trade in Value Added data, World Bank distribution and macroeconomic data, and Penn World Table productivity measures. Baseline regressions confirm that domestic saving predicts ten- and fifteen-year GDP-per-capita growth, while global-middle-class access predicts subsequent manufacturing growth. The stricter test excludes economies with insufficient access and relates initial conditions to twenty-year outcomes. Among developing industrial economies with an access measure of at least 15 percent of manufacturing value added, the standardized access-saving interaction is positive for manufacturing value added per capita, total factor productivity, and capital productivity, but not for aggregate GDP per capita.


The second stage examines historical cases from 1960 onward. Soviet growth slowed sharply before political collapse despite high accumulation; independent evidence documents declining capital efficiency, a widening productivity gap, and weak world-market validation of manufactured exports. East German manufacturing productivity was far below West German levels before reunification and industrial production collapsed when protected demand disappeared. A separate low-access, low-saving cluster—Madagascar, Niger, and Burundi—records virtually no long-run growth per resident. China before and after opening, Korea, Mexico, and post-Soviet Russia provide additional contrasts. The evidence supports a qualified conclusion: access and saving behave multiplicatively for structural and technological outcomes within developing economies, whereas GDP growth alone cannot distinguish frontier-compatible development from artificial accumulation.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a framework for understanding the intrinsic motivation underlying voter turnout by decomposing it into two distinct affective components: political passion and political dislikeness. Building on the calculus of voting and the expressive voting literature, the paper incorporates these components into a spatial model of electoral participation and maps them into a two-dimensional policy space based on economic and immigration policy positions. The framework is empirically evaluated using German survey data from the 2017 and 2021 federal elections. Political passion and political dislikeness are constructed from voter–party ideological distances, and their relationship with turnout is estimated using a probit model. The results show that political passion is positively and significantly associated with voter turnout, while political dislikeness has a small and statistically insignificant effect. The finding remains robust after controlling for election-year fixed effects. These results suggest that intrinsic motivation is not necessarily a homogeneous source of utility: in the German multiparty context, positive political attachment appears to be a more important channel for electoral participation than negative evaluations of political opponents. The paper therefore provides a framework for opening the black box of intrinsic voting motivation and highlights how its components may operate differently across institutional contexts.

title: Arbitrage at the Regulatory Frontier-European Energy Market

detail.title: Arbitrage at the Regulatory Frontier-European Energy Market

declarations.declarationOfInterest: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: n/a

detail.abstract:
European energy prices are set through a repeated bargaining game between public authorities and holders of sunk, long-lived capital. This paper models that game across four arenas — wholesale spot markets, regulated network tariffs, generation support contracts, and end-user tariffs — using arbitrage in three linked mechanisms: the regulator’s trade-off between current consumers and future investors, the investor’s exploitation of differentials across jurisdictions and instruments, and third-party arbitration as an enforcement mechanism.

Seven results. (i) Hold-up risk rises with project scale and political salience, not with profitability. (ii) Commitment fails during price crises, when reneging pays most and political horizons are shortest. (iii) Zero-bid auctions are corner solutions: participation goes to zero rather than declining, once risk transfer exceeds what globally scarce developer capital will accept. (iv) States compete on risk allocation rather than subsidy level; optimal risk transfer is interior and set by fiscal capacity, so capital allocates by sovereign balance sheet rather than by resource quality — a distortion state-aid control does not measure. (v) Where assets turn over, regulatory deviation is punished immediately through secondary-market valuations rather than later through failed auctions. (vi) Immobile network capital generates no participation signal, only delivery shortfalls indistinguishable from permitting or supply-chain constraints. (vii) Regulatory variance selects for short lead times and fuel-cost passthrough, biasing against firm low-carbon capacity independently of system value.

The model is applied to the 2024–26 offshore wind auction failures, the 2022–23 infrastructure marginal revenue caps, German and Spanish network determinations, the French post-ARENH mechanism, and the UK’s substitution of contractual for fiscal commitment. Fourteen falsifiable predictions are set out. The central design implication is that contractual commitment dominates statutory commitment, and symmetric instruments dominate generous unilateral ones.

detail.abstract: Timely disaster response is hindered by the slow arrival of reliable loss information, as claims take weeks to reveal damaged properties. We develop a hazard–exposure–vulnerability framework that predicts property-level damage probabilities before claims are reported, combining property characteristics and weather information through deep learning with a generalized extreme value (GEV) link for rare events. Evaluated on National Flood Insurance Program policies, both weather information and the deep learning architecture substantially improve predictive performance. The GEV link further raises precision among top-ranked properties. The resulting probabilities enable insurers and public agencies to prioritize inspections and estimate claim volumes early.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a public-data framework for evaluating incremental bank lending when plausible climate scenarios imply different sector credit outcomes but defensible scenario probabilities are unavailable. The calibration combines 2025 Shared National Credit industry commitments, January 2026 U.S. industry leverage, interest coverage and equity volatility from Damodaran, and official 2027 sector-level probability-of-default adjustments from the NGFS CLIMACRED model. One-year Merton probabilities provide independent baseline credit-risk proxies for 16 non-financial sectors representing $5.2808 trillion of commitments. Minimax regret is compared with symmetric scenario weighting and maximin under two principal decision scores: expected loss and a credit-compensation payoff using Damodaran synthetic spreads. DAPS raises the commitment-weighted one-year PD from 0.0592% to 0.0897%. At a 12.5% sector cap, minimax regret reduces maximum expected-loss regret by 29.1% relative to symmetric scenario weighting; under the credit-compensation score the reduction is 69.1%. Sensitivity to concentration limits, crosswalk weights, Merton inputs and the climate-PD transport shows that the value of minimax regret is conditional on scenario-specific sector rankings differing near binding portfolio constraints. The contribution is an operational decision-fragility framework for financial institutions and supervisors, not evidence about realized bank behavior or universally optimal climate lending.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the joint design of central-bank balance sheets and Treasury supply. Reserves provide settlement liquidity, while Treasuries provide collateral and broader convenience services. Central-bank Treasury purchases increase reserves but reduce privately held Treasuries, while Treasury policy changes the overall supply of public liquidity. Optimal policy therefore jointly manages the scarcity of both forms of public liquidity and the real cost of balance-sheet expansion. This yields a balance-sheet Friedman rule and a Treasury-supply Friedman rule. The two Friedman conditions form a monetary–fiscal Friedman cross whose intersection identifies the coordinated optimum. The framework therefore links reserve supply, Treasury supply, and the choice between monetary and fiscal Treasury absorption in a single welfare criterion.

detail.abstract: This article subjects Charo v Republic 1 a 2016 decision of the High Court of Kenya at Malindi acquitting an adult convicted of defiling a fourteen-year-old girl on the ground that her conduct disclosed the "behaviour of an adult" to sustained doctrinal, comparative and interdisciplinary scrutiny. It argues that the judgment is not, as some later courts have implied, a defensible if unfashionable application of the statutory defence in section 8(5) of the Sexual Offences Act, but a conceptually incoherent departure from the strict-liability architecture of Kenyan defilement law, from the text of the Constitution of Kenya, 2010, and from binding international child-rights obligations. The article develops what it terms the doctrine of asymmetric agency: a framework, assembled from developmental psychology, feminist legal theory and comparative constitutional law, for distinguishing the peer sexual conduct of adolescents which courts in South Africa and elsewhere have rightly begun to decriminalize from adult-mediated sexual conduct with a child, which no degree of apparent willingness can convert into a lawful encounter. In so doing, the article takes a position within, rather than merely reporting, the vigorous post-2010 Kenyan debate about the fairness of the Sexual Offences Act, distinguishing legitimate judicial revolt against mandatory minimum sentences from illegitimate judicial revolt against the offence itself.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how Florida local governments adjusted property-tax rates during the 2015-2024 property boom. Among 66 counties and 222 municipalities with populations of at least 5,000, taxable values grew at median annual rates of 8.4% and 8.7%, while cumulative millage changed by-2.1% and 0.0%. Real implied levy per resident increased 31.4% and 45.6%, compared with 24.0% and 11.0% growth in core-service spending. Levy growth exceeded coreservice growth in 62.1% of counties and 87.7% of municipalities. Results were robust to inclusion of all comparable municipalities, to the choice of deflator, and to exclusion of jurisdictions with implausible expenditure reporting. Rate stability rather than rate increases generated the expansion in property-tax capacity; limitations that act on rates or revenues therefore target a different margin than limitations on assessed value, a distinction relevant to Florida's Amendment 3 on the November 2026 ballot.

detail.abstract: This paper develops and empirically validates a spatio-temporal framework that integrates extreme weather events and climate-related risk drivers with conventional borrower, loan and macroeconomic variables to explain and predict mortgage default risk. We use discrete-time survival models ranging from linear specifications to flexible general additive models with P-splines, time-varying coefficients and interaction surfaces. We contribute to the literature in three ways. First, unlike existing literature we investigate the predictive efficacy of models with time-varying coefficients and with coefficients dependent on other risk drivers. Second, we explore linear effects, nonlinear effects and nonlinear interactions between a wide range of weather drivers of default and between macroeconomic drivers of default, which have not been incorporated into credit risk models before. Third, we assess the relative contribution to the required economic capital of uncertainty over weather events and uncertainty of the macroeconomy. We do this by building time series models for weather and for macroeconomic variables. The omission of weather events results in significant underestimation of the capital required, especially under joint macroeconomic and weather stress. The approach is validated using mortgage defaults and wildfires in California. Recent wildfire occurrences across the world make our methodology particularly appropriate for risk modellers in banks.

title: The Epistemic Loop

detail.title: The Epistemic Loop

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with other people or organizations that could be perceived to have influenced this study.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a meta-analytical framework for the study of AI governance, motivated by an empirical observation that has been registered in decolonial AI literature (Mohamed, Png, and Isaac, 2020; Mhlambi, 2020) but not formalized: the dominant frameworks of AI governance are produced by the same corporate actors whose frontier models they are intended to regulate, and consumed by Global South regulators through the very infrastructure those frameworks are intended to analyze. This closed circuit, here conceptualized as the Epistemic Loop, is invisible to its own participants and therefore cannot be repaired by means internal to the loop itself. The paper develops four original conceptual contributions: the Epistemic Loop formalized as the structural intersection of a technological, a discursive, and an institutional sub-loop; the extension of the Infrastructure Projection of Geopolitics (IPG) framework from physical and digital infrastructure to cognitive-epistemic infrastructure; a four-test operational instrument for assessing the epistemic independence of any AI governance framework; and the Sovereign Frame, extending the Sovereignty of the Question concept (Rakhimov, 2026a). The paper anchors its argument empirically in post-Soviet Central Asia, treated as a diagnostic limit case in which the Loop operates in its purest form due to structural zero representation in the production of AI governance.

detail.abstract: I study optimal carbon taxation when capital is misallocated across firms. Using data on U.S. public firms, I document that firm-level revenue-based emissions intensity is negatively correlated with the return to capital, indicating that capital is misallocated toward dirty firms. Embedding this pattern into a misallocation framework, I demonstrate a reallocation mechanism: a carbon tax can reduce resource misallocation and boost aggregate productivity by reallocating capital from dirty to clean firms. I develop a dynamic, general-equilibrium climate-economy model with heterogeneous firms and tangibility-dependent financial frictions: dirty firms hold more tangible assets and face looser collateral constraints, attracting excess capital. Calibrated to firm-level balance sheet and emissions data, the model implies that a carbon tax raises aggregate productivity over a wide range of tax rates. The allocative efficiency gains generate welfare improvements beyond those from internalizing emissions, increasing the optimal carbon tax by 75% relative to a benchmark without pre-existing misallocation. Consistent with the same mechanism, removing financial frictions to equalize returns further reduces economy-wide emissions intensity.

detail.abstract:
Why can reality be known? The problem appears under many headings: the intelligibility of nature, the success of science, the applicability of mathematics, realism, representation, information, consciousness, and meaning. This monograph argues that these discussions intersect around a broader phenomenon that deserves explicit analysis. Reality is not merely orderly; it is repeatedly available for disciplined discovery. Human beings and other epistemic systems can encounter patterns, construct representations, expose them to correction, predict novel results, and accumulate knowledge across persons and generations. The study calls this phenomenon readability.

Readability is defined as the objective availability of reality to constrained, corrigible, and progressively integrative inquiry. The concept is distinguished from order, intelligibility, information, meaning, and signification. Naturalism, physicalism, structural realism, informational and mathematical ontologies, and classical theism are compared without assuming that scientific success deductively proves any one of them. The final movement studies the Qurʾānic concept of āyāt as a framework in which revelation, nature, history, and the human self can function as domains of indication. The conclusion is deliberately qualified: the Qurʾānic theistic framework possesses distinctive resources for unifying objective order, the possibility of knowers, epistemic normativity, and signification, though the inference remains open to philosophical criticism.

detail.abstract: Populists govern more of the world's countries than at any point in the past century, on both the right and the left. What they share is not an economic programme but a worldview that casts politics as a struggle between ordinary citizens and a self-serving establishment, a conflict that is zero-sum at its core. We show that exposure to this political environment leaves a durable imprint on citizens' beliefs. Combining data on populist leaders with surveys of more than 260,000 respondents in 53 countries, we exploit within-country-survey-year variation across birth cohorts and find that greater exposure during early adulthood is associated with stronger zerosum beliefs later in life. The result is replicated in two independent surveys and across multiple measures of zero-sum thinking and perceived economic conflict and persists into respondents' mid-forties. The associations extend to voting intentions: exposure does not predict support for populist parties overall, but it does predict support for ideologically extreme parties aligned with the populist rule experienced in early adulthood. The mechanism evidence provides little support for an economic-scarcity explanation and instead points towards a rhetorical channel, as populist rule features substantially more anti-elite rhetoric in two independent measures and more domestic zero-sum framing in United Nations speeches.

title: The Role of Stock Markets in Economic Growth: Empirical Evidence from Panel Data Analysis *

detail.title: The Role of Stock Markets in Economic Growth: Empirical Evidence from Panel Data Analysis *
detail.abstract: Stock market development is widely viewed as an important component of economic performance, influencing how economies mobilise capital, allocate resources, and support long-term growth. This study explores the link between stock market development and economic growth using a quarterly panel of 36 countries from 2003 to 2022. Employing panel cointegration tests, fully modified OLS, and a panel vector error correction framework, we analyse both the long-run and short-run dynamics of this relationship. The long-run association between stock market capitalisation and economic growth is positive and significant, and the magnitude of this effect is substantially larger in high-income economies. Short-run causality is bidirectional in high-income countries but flows only from stock market development to growth in low-and middle-income countries. A threshold panel VECM, which uses financial development level to endogenously identify regimes based on financial maturity shows that the adjustment process is non-linear and depends on countries' level of financial development. The findings suggest that financially less developed economies may benefit from strengthening market institutions, improving liquidity, and enhancing regulatory quality to better harness the growth contributions of stock markets.

detail.abstract: We study a single-agent contract-design problem in which the agent privately chooses a subset of costly actions and the principal can inspect selected action coordinates. The principal recommends an effort set, pays only after success, and withholds payment when an inspected coordinate differs from the recommendation. We first show that incentive compatibility is equivalent to a coordinate-restricted demand condition, or equivalently to hitting every strictly profitable deviation. For additive success probabilities and inspection costs, the fixed-payment problem is exactly a 0–1 Knapsack problem. It is weakly NPcomplete and admits a pseudopolynomial algorithm and an FPTAS. When the payment is chosen endogenously, individual action breakpoints no longer suffice, but the problem remains NP-complete in the weak-Knapsack regime and admits a multiplicative FPTAS. For gross-substitutes success functions, incentive compatibility for a fixed target is certified by improving additions, deletions, and swaps; minimum-cost implementation is a weighted bipartite vertex-cover problem. We then identify an internal tractability boundary: unit demand is exactly solvable, partition unit demand admits an FPTAS, whereas fixed-payment weighted matroid rank admits no FPTAS in the qualified oracle and explicit representations, even when every inspection coordinate has strictly positive cost. Finally, a three-action coverage instance shows that the gross-substitutes local certificate fails immediately for submodular success functions. These results distinguish the complexity of agent response from the complexity of designing inspections and contracts.

title: When Judicial AI Becomes Procedurally Relevant: Disclosure, Reasons and Institutional Competence in Swiss Civil Procedure

detail.abstract: Courts are beginning to use AI systems for legal research, file summarisation, risk scoring and the drafting of reasons. Swiss law has no AI-specific procedural regime for them. This paper asks when a court’s own AI contribution becomes procedurally relevant in Swiss civil procedure, and what could make a duty of oversight bind. It makes three claims. First, the exhaustive list of means of evidence in article 168(1) ZPO entails that a court-operated tool is not evidence, although no decision has yet said so of an AI tool; it does not settle what the tool is. Classification should follow the output’s function, provenance and decisional use. Article 183(3) ZPO, the right to be heard under article 29(2) BV and the case law on standardised decision aids supply partial analogies for disclosure and reasons; the exclusion of internal judicial materials from the right of access blocks a general disclosure duty. The paper proposes a three-step trigger and separates the duty to give reasons from an AI-governance record. Second, state liability offers almost no ex post leverage over a final judgment. The procedural duties have their remedy on appeal; the infrastructure that makes them performable requires an ex ante organisational duty addressed to the body that organises the court. Third, an empirical finding about which oversight design works cannot create a duty; it can fix the content of an existing guarantee only through a pre-specified evidential standard, a proportionality test and a competent institution. A preliminary comparison with Türkiye finds the reasons-based control the most portable.

title: Unsafe and Unsound: A New Analysis of the CFPB's Misuse of BISG Race Proxies for Disparate Impact Enforcement

detail.abstract: Between 2013 and 2016, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau built a landmark indirect-auto fair lending enforcement program on two technologies novel to that arena: Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding ("BISG") race proxies and a regression framework-"BISG Continuous"-that used those proxies to estimate disparate impact pricing disparities. It did so without the model-validation discipline that the federal banking agencies expect of supervised institutions' models under SR 11-7-a discipline the Bureau has itself invoked in examinations, yet did not apply to the models on which more than $160 million in settlements rested. This paper supplies that missing validation. Using a one-million-borrower synthetic laboratory built on actual U.S. Census geography, in which true race is known and the proxy is calibrated by construction, I show that under the disparate impact theory the agencies themselves pled, BISG Continuous roughly doubles the true pricing disparity for Black borrowers (82-134% across groups), and I identify the mechanism: the proxy cannot see race within neighborhoods, so the regression discards within-neighborhood racial variation and inflates the disparity by exactly 1/V, the reciprocal of the portfolio's segregation index. The bias is structural and footprint-specific, worst in integrated markets where a compliance officer would feel safest, and predictable in advance from public Census data with no outcome data at all. A simple probability-weighted average recovers the disparate impact disparity exactly, yet understates disparate treatment disparities by the same factor V: one identity viewed from two sides, with each estimator right for exactly one scenario and neither "principled" in general. The correct choice turns on where the alleged mechanism's racial correlation lies relative to the BISG geography-which a properly specified discrimination theory supplies and the Bureau's never did. I close with practical guidance for compliance officers and a proposal for an independent technical oversight function, mirroring SR 26-2, for the Bureau's own use of novel technologies.

detail.abstract:
General Human Ecosystem Theory: A Multi-Layer, Multi-Flow Mathematical Framework for Social Systems
My current research develops a mathematical theory for modeling society as a dynamical system. The framework represents society as seven interacting institutional layers — government, market, family, media, religion, academia, and digital networks — each carrying a seven-dimensional state vector of heterogeneous flows: money, information, knowledge, belief, trust, energy, and reputation.
The core contribution is a coupling structure that goes beyond existing approaches (multilayer networks, system dynamics, management cybernetics, Bourdieu's capital theory): a dynamic, nonlinear tensor that governs how each flow type propagates between layers independently, combined with sparse conversion channels between flow types (e.g., trust generating economic investment) and a memory term that allows the model to reproduce hysteresis and institutional trauma — effects that purely Markovian models cannot capture. Governance is formulated as a constrained, multi-generational optimal control problem.
The theory yields two falsifiable predictions — a causal link between power concentration and social trust decline, and early-warning signals (critical slowing down) preceding systemic transitions — both implemented and tested in a numerical simulator. It is further extended with bifurcation-based critical-point analysis and a multiplex cascade model for predicting avalanche-style systemic collapse.
I am currently working on calibrating the model against real-world panel data (World Values Survey, V-Dem, World Bank, RSF Press Freedom Index) and preparing the work for submission to arXiv (physics.soc-ph). I welcome feedback, collaboration, and critical discussion from researchers in complex systems, computational social science, and network theory.

detail.abstract: We study the fair division of indivisible goods among agents with nonnegative additive valuations. An agent's maximin share (MMS) is the value she can guarantee by partitioning the goods into as many bundles as there are agents and receiving a least-valued bundle. We prove the existence of exact MMS allocations for a valuation domain that generalizes several few-valued domains as well as weakly lexicographic valuations. For each agent, the lower-valued goods, after a positive rescaling, may take values in {0, 1, d, d + 1}, {0, 1, 2, 2e}, or {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}, where d, e ≥ 2 are integers. Above these goods, the valuation may contain arbitrarily many value classes, subject to the condition that a single good in each class is worth at least the total value of all strictly lower-valued goods. The value classes, scaling factors, and parameters may vary across agents. We give an algorithm that computes an MMS allocation in O(nm log^2 (2 + m)) time, where n is the number of agents and m is the number of goods.

title: Structural Non-Preservation in Black-Scholes Inversion: The Volatility Smile as an Operator-Induced Effect

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no interest
declarations.funderStatement: no fund to declare

detail.abstract: Implied volatility is widely used as a reduced representation of option prices and as an object for model calibration, comparison, and interpretation. In this paper, we analyze implied volatility as a transformation induced by the pointwise inversion of the Black-Scholes pricing map on the space of arbitrage-free call price functions. We show that this transformation does not, in general, preserve the structural properties of admissible price functions: monotonicity and convexity in price space do not imply corresponding properties of the implied volatility function. We express the local relation between price and implied volatility curvatures through a closed-form necessary and sufficient criterion involving the local curvature of the price function and the differential structure of the Black-Scholes pricing map. As a consequence, we construct a non-empty set of admissible price functions whose implied volatility profile is non-monotonic in strike, showing that such profiles can arise from the action of the inversion operator without specifying an underlying stochastic process. The results provide a structural qualification to the interpretation of implied volatility as a direct representation of underlying price dynamics.

detail.abstract: Democratic accountability: the capacity of citizens to evaluate and respond to the public servants who exercise power over their daily lives, has no continuous infrastructure in modern governance. This paper examines the structural causes of that gap and proposes a civic counteraction architecture: a set of institutional design principles through which civil society can build persistent, scalable accountability systems operating independently of government. Drawing on architecture, political theory, and democratic governance literature, the paper argues that the failure of accountability is not a failure of citizen will but a failure of civic infrastructure. Citizen Stance is presented as a working instantiation of these principles.

detail.abstract: This paper provides early evidence on the economic impact of the European Union (EU) Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act, the world's first comprehensive legal framework governing AI, on EU firms, focusing on innovation and firm valuation. We infer the act's impact on AI-related innovation from its effect on the total innovation input of firms more likely to engage in AI innovation (hightech firms) relative to other firms. We find that, following the enactment of the act, high-tech firms reduce their R&D expenditures compared to other firms. The effect strengthens for smaller firms and is largely concentrated among them. We further find that Tobin's q declines for high-tech firms compared to other firms following the act's enactment, with the effect also concentrated among smaller firms. The decline in firm value is not fully due to the reduction in R&D investment. High-tech firms also experience a relative decline in profitability, suggesting deterioration of firm operations as another potential channel through which the act reduces firm value. Overall, our findings suggest that the act has, in the short term, hurt firm innovation and valuation, especially for smaller firms.

detail.abstract: We examine how intraweek periodicity affects realized variance forecasts for cryptocurrencies and compare two ways of incorporating it: adjusting realized measures for estimated weekday periodicity, and allowing intraweek variation to enter directly in the forecasting model. We estimate rolling weekday periodicity profiles using a nonparametric method and evaluate one-day-ahead out-of-sample forecasts over 2023-2025 for Bitcoin and Ether, re-estimating each model daily. Weekday periodicity adjustment lowers both MSE and QLIKE for every matched specification, although not all MSE reductions are statistically significant. Models that allow the variance level and short-run persistence to vary across the trading week attain similar forecast accuracy, indicating that the forecast gains are not unique to periodicity adjustment. We also find that removing weekday periodicity improves the fit of the finite-horizon scaling relations of log realized volatility and yields higher estimates of the Hurst exponent for both assets across rolling windows.

detail.abstract:
This paper delivers a rigorous, data-driven analysis of structural drift within global capital markets, modelling how low-probability, high-impact anomalies have shifted from transient black swan events into an entrenched, perpetual baseline. Traditional asset management paradigms rely heavily on standard Gaussian distribution models, which treat extreme market shocks as statistical outliers that rapidly revert to a mean. By contrast, this work establishes an analytical framework demonstrating that modern financial plumbing, coupled geopolitical networks, and centralized institutional interventions have fundamentally fractured the bell curve, resulting in severe excess kurtosis and permanent fat-tailed risk profiles.
By charting the transmission mechanisms of systemic contagion, the text exposes the severe operational friction and capital attrition that occur when structural anomalies collide with rigid corporate strategies. The diagnostic section isolates the exact failure points where standard risk metrics—such as traditional Value-at-Risk (VaR) boundaries—fail to account for non-linear, compounding market shocks. Shifting from empirical analysis to execution-ready preservation, this book outlines concrete capital insulation protocols designed to immunize institutional balance sheets, manage systemic variance, and ensure capital survival amidst engineered market chaos and cascading network fragility.

detail.abstract: Commons Capitalism is easy to misread because it uses familiar legal and economic vocabulary while changing the relationships among the concepts that vocabulary usually joins. The Commons Capitalism Entity (CCE) is a commercially operating enterprise system consisting of a nonmember, nonshareholder, nonprofit Commons Corporation and one or more wholly owned, market-facing Subsidiaries. It earns profits, uses conventional financing, competes in markets, employs workers, accumulates productive capital, and is governed through corporation law. Yet it has no private residual owner; workers benefit without owning the productive corpus; the nonprofit parent is not organized around charity; productive capital is governed as a commons without becoming state property; surplus is governed rather than privately claimed; and fiduciary duties run to the corporation rather than to a beneficiary class. This Article identifies ten discourse conventions that can cause readers to translate the CCE into familiar categories before evaluating it on its own terms. Its central claim is methodological: Commons Capitalism disaggregates ownership, control, benefit, surplus, fiduciary obligation, management authority, capital formation, and intergenerational continuity, then recombines them through familiar legal components. The resulting architecture is novel less because every component is new than because conventional assumptions about which functions must travel together are rejected. Clarifying those assumptions is a necessary precursor to evaluating the CCE's economic claims, financing, governance, and legal formation in later research.

detail.abstract: Can an inaccurate forecast of future self-control improve the pursuit of a distant goal? The answer depends on how the task is completed. For agents who weakly overestimate their future self-control, we compare a task completed by one irreversible action with effort accumulated across dates. In the completion problem, an intermediate forecast can induce immediate completion while both sophistication and full naivete induce delay. We characterize the forecast interval, its welfare gains, and the losses from missing it. The mechanism requires at least three continuation dates: a more optimistic forecast of one future self can make an earlier future self wait longer. In the cumulative-effort problem, under strict present bias and concave reference continuation surplus, every admissible forecast leaves current effort below its efficient level at every nonterminal date. The best forecast for one action therefore remains second best. These results separate the incentive value of self-knowledge from its accuracy and identify when forecasts can substitute for immediate incentives.

detail.abstract: Quasi-Monte Carlo methods based on Sobol' sequences are widely used in derivative pricing and risk management for their improved convergence over pseudorandom methods. Their deterministic nature makes sampling uncertainty difficult to measure. This is particularly problematic for discontinuous payoffs and their respective Greeks. This paper studies the application of randomised quasi-Monte Carlo to diagnose and control numerical uncertainty across a portfolio of similar products. By applying independent Sobol' scramblings, one obtains replicated low-discrepancy estimates and can construct approximate confidence intervals while retaining the main benefits of the underlying sampling scheme. We show how randomisation can be used to estimate sampling uncertainty in prices and Greeks, compare path constructors, assess numerical treatments such as payoff smoothing and allocate additional paths adaptively. The results emphasise that optimal choices are model-and payoff-dependent, so production implementations should be tested on their own products rather than relying on universal rules.

title: The Political Cost of Fiscal Flexibility
affiliations: Virginia Tech

detail.title: The Political Cost of Fiscal Flexibility

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: When should a government limit its ability to change who receives fiscal transfers? I study a production economy in which household spending creates gains and losses for firms, giving them incentives to influence transfer targeting. Changing the recipients can concentrate firms' gains and disperse their losses without changing the program budget, aggregate output, or total operating profit. When firms face the same lobbying cost function and effort responds more than proportionally to stakes, a single beneficiary exerts more pressure than several firms sharing an equal aggregate loss. I show that full flexibility can lower expected household welfare even when it would improve welfare without lobbying. The welfare loss comes from how transfers are targeted, even before lobbying costs are deducted. By committing to a limit before firms lobby, the government can improve welfare while retaining flexibility over who receives transfers. The resources spent on lobbying justify tightening that limit further.

detail.abstract:
This book examines a systematic gap in three decades of research by Chilean economist Andrés Fernández (IMF, former Head of Research at the Central Bank of Chile) on capital controls, commodity-driven business cycles, and firms' financial vulnerability in emerging economies. While this body of work has produced rigorous measurement tools — including the widely used FKRSU capital control dataset and, more recently, the use of large language models to reconstruct historical capital-flow restrictions — it does not address the institutional capacity of regulators to execute policy using equivalent AI-enabled tools in real time.

The book proposes a four-dimension AI-Governance Readiness framework (data infrastructure, internal analytical capacity, enabling regulatory framework, and institutional response speed) specific to the macroprudential and capital-flow-management function, extending the institutional-readiness research program developed in the author's previous volumes (The Compliance Gap; The Adaptation Gap). This is a conceptual and methodological volume; empirical validation with real-world data is left to a planned companion volume.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between multi-dimensional Labour Vulnerability and Climate Shocks among regional labour market and climate-sensitive workers in an advanced European economy Poland with robust institutional protections. Using a balanced four-pillar Labour Vulnerability Index (LVI) is constructed by combining GUS BDL administrative registers Employment Security, Income Security, Under-employment and Sectoral Vulnerability with direct meteorological coverage as well as ERA5-Land (Muñoz Sabater, 2019) Climate exposure is measured through four domains: extreme cold/wind chill, extreme heat, precipitation and snowfall), and solar radiation for all 380 Polish powiats (counties) from January 2024 to December 2025 (N=9,120 powiat-months). Because the heat/solar and cold/rain shock components are highly correlated (r = 0.835 and r = 0.843 respectively), they are combined into two composite indices- HEAT_SOLAR_COMPOSITE and COLD_RAIN_COMPOSITE-to obtain stable, individually interpretable coefficients. Two-way Fixed-effects estimates a positive but only marginally significant association between combined heat/solar exposure and labour vulnerability (p= 0.081). Spatial diagnostics (Global Moran’s I≈0.43, KNN-4 weights, p=0.001 in both years, LISA with permutation-based significance testing, Getis-Ord Gi*) reveals strong statistically significant Geographic clustering of both climate shocks and Labour vulnerability. Spatial Lag (SAR), Spatial Error (SEM) and Spatial Durbin (SDM) models confirm substantial spatial dependence (ρ≈0.57-0.61; λ≈0.59-0.61). The findings support regionally coordinated, heat-focused labour-market adaptation policies.

title: Two-Sided Volatility Jumps in Short-Maturity VIX Options
affiliations: , Temple University-Fox School of Business and

detail.abstract: VIX options pose a distinctive modeling problem: accommodating downward VIX jumps while preserving a positive VIX level and capturing the inverse relation between stock returns and VIX changes. We develop a risk-neutral state-dependent marked Hawkes-type mechanism in which the pre-jump intensity and signed stock-jump mark jointly determine the intensity update. Negative stock jumps generate excitation and upward VIX jumps, whereas positive stock jumps generate de-excitation and downward VIX jumps. Multiplicative VIX jumps preserve a positive VIX level, and a local admissible stopped construction keeps the stock-jump intensity nonnegative. Thus, a single marked stock-jump process generates two-sided VIX jumps without an independent VIX jump process. Under a local linear-in-intensity squared-VIX approximation, we derive explicit short-maturity option-price expansions. With positive current intensity and fixed out-of-the-money strikes, calls and one-jump-reachable puts have strictly positive leading terms proportional to maturity; the two benchmarks allowing only upward VIX jumps instead yield put values of smaller order. The nearly flat within-expiration-cycle maturity profile of put-call ratios at symmetric absolute log-moneyness is consistent with equal-order short-end put and call pricing.

title: From Shock to Collapse: How Climate-Driven Disasters Cascade into Political Crises
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: From Shock to Collapse: How Climate-Driven Disasters Cascade into Political Crises

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no personal, financial, or organizational relationships that could be perceived as a conflicts of interest or as having influenced the conduct or outcomes of this study.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding or grants.

detail.abstract:
This dissertation examines how climate-driven disasters escalate into political crises through cascading processes, arguing that while not every disaster destabilizes political systems, those that do follow a common cascade pattern. Escalation hinges less on the scale of disruption than on mediating conditions: pre-existing vulnerabilities, narrative framing, amplification loops, parallel stressors, and institutional off-ramps.

The analysis develops a cascade model that conceptualizes escalation as probabilistic rather than deterministic. Drawing on crisis studies, disaster sociology, and cascading crisis theory, the model identifies six stages: trigger, governance pressure, response failure, contestation, legitimacy erosion, and political crisis. Case studies of Syria, Chile, Pakistan, and Australia demonstrate both the utility and limits of this framework. Disasters became political not through material disruption alone, but when responses were framed as negligence, injustice, or betrayal. Vulnerabilities rooted in inequality, repression, or polarization provided fertile ground, while feedback loops and latent stress accumulations magnified crises once underway. Conversely, Australia showed how resilient democracies with credible off-ramps can contain legitimacy erosion at the government level.

The refined model contributes theoretically by integrating discursive dynamics into disaster sociology and extending cascading crisis theory with institutional off-ramps. Empirically, it shows how climate change can catalyze instability while identifying pathways of resilience.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a longitudinal case study tracking the Predictive Convexity Score (PCS) of three stocks, Nike (NKE), NVIDIA (NVDA), and Visa (V), from Q4 2019 through the most recently reported quarter for each. These three stocks represent the full spectrum of PCS tier behavior: Tier 1 (NVDA), Tier 3 (V), and Tier 4 (NKE). This September 2026 update focuses specifically on Nike to illustrate a broader point about beta and the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM). As of this update, Nike's five-year monthly beta stands at 1.11, close to the market average, while the stock has fallen approximately 77% since its Q4 2021 peak, and S&P Dow Jones Indices removed Nike from the S&P 100 index effective September 21, 2026, ending an 18-year run in that index. A beta near 1.0 implies a stock should move roughly in line with the broader market. Nike has instead collapsed while the market rose. This is not a one-quarter anomaly. Nike's PCS has correctly flagged deteriorating fundamentals for seven consecutive periods, while its beta has remained within an unremarkable range throughout the decline. CAPM has missed Nike for years, not because of a single bad estimate, but because beta does not measure what actually predicts a stock's asymmetric price behavior: the trajectory of its revenue and earnings growth.

detail.abstract: A separable deterrence surface treats travel time and money cost as distinct marginal impedances. I show that such a surface can be collapsed to a fixed-value-of-time generalised cost only under exponential decay; any other decay function on generalised cost imposes an interaction between time and cost. Recomputed from Wardman and Toner's (2020) published rail models, the local value of time implied by their separable model varies at least twofold within every panel. A fixed-value-of-time generalised-cost model absorbs this only as share-dependent component elasticities, which their tests do not support.

title: Revisiting the Doctrine of Commercial Wisdom under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016: Need for Judicial Scrutiny, Institutional Accountability and Revival-Oriented Insolvency Resolution

detail.title: Revisiting the Doctrine of Commercial Wisdom under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016: Need for Judicial Scrutiny, Institutional Accountability and Revival-Oriented Insolvency Resolution

detail.abstract: The creditor-driven framework of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) revolves around the doctrine of commercial wisdom. Although the Committee of Creditors (CoC) should be treated as an organ which enjoys commercial autonomy, rendering its decisions to be placed beyond meaningful scrutiny would frustrate the very objectives of value maximisation, stakeholder protection and revival sought to be achieved by the Code. The paper contends that commercial wisdom ought to work in a regime of judicial restraint, rather than as a principle of judicial exclusion. Based on a review of important Supreme Court judgements, the paper examines the space for minimal judicial interference when CoC decisions are arbitrary or irrational or unlawful or not in consonance with the legislative framework. It also looks at questions of creditor accountability, Section 12A settlements, promoter participation, neutrality of resolution professionals and sector-specific challenges those relating to real estate and MSME insolvency. This paper ultimately argues for a move away from the regime of absolute creditor primacy toward one of accountable creditor primacy that preserves commercial discretion while requiring its exercise to be transparent, rational and directed toward Code-reviving ends.

title: Objective, critical and pluralistic? Relationships and Sexuality Education in Northern Ireland after JR87 [2025] UKSC 40

detail.title: Objective, critical and pluralistic? Relationships and Sexuality Education in Northern Ireland after JR87 [2025] UKSC 40

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I am a member of the Board of Govenors for a public school
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded from professional salary

detail.abstract: In November 2025 the United Kingdom Supreme Court held that Northern Ireland's core religious education syllabus breached article 2 of Protocol 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), applying the requirement, derived from the Strasbourg jurisprudence, that curriculum content be conveyed in an objective, critical and pluralistic manner. This commentary argues that the Relationships and Sexuality Education (RSE) curriculum fails the same standard, on two grounds. First, its gender content is internally incoherent. It deploys three mutually inconsistent definitions of gender, rests a central classification on a circular criterion, and, once gender is detached from biological sex, supplies no non-circular criterion at all. As such, the content cannot be conveyed objectively on any resolution of the wider dispute. Secondly, its remaining contested claims are presented as settled fact without critical treatment or plurality, in circumstances where the Cass Review and recent litigation establish live medical and legal contest. The commentary further argues that the excusal provisions invert the ECHR's logic, attaching a right of withdrawal to the curriculum's empirically grounded content while its contested group-identity-based content remains compulsory. The Department of Education may voluntarily extend the exercise it has already begun for the RE syllabus to the RSE syllabus or await the standard's application by a court.

title: Progress at the Expense of Accountability: Why the European Commission's Approach to DMA Compromise Falls Short

detail.abstract: Apple's latest revision of its app distribution terms, following on the European Commission's settlement on Meta's pay or consent subscription model, reveal a troubling pattern in the Digital Markets Act's enforcement. Substantive compromises negotiated behind closed doors with gatekeepers, with no accompanying public decision or reasoning. This paper examines both episodes to show that the Commission's informal settlements leave critical legal questions unaddressed and unreviewable. Because no formal decision is published, third parties and scholars cannot assess whether the outcomes actually satisfy the DMA's requirements, nor can affected stakeholders seek judicial redress. The paper argues that this practice undermines two pillars of legitimate enforcement, accountability and third-party participation, and that the DMA's institutional design, which lacks any formal mechanism for third-party involvement, exacerbates the problem. It concludes by calling for public consultation or transparent debate on contested provisions such as Article 6(4) DMA, arguing that the regulation's contestability goals cannot otherwise be realised.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the effects of railway expansion on China's foreign trade and agricultural commercialization during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries-a period that marked China's transition from a largely self-sufficient agrarian economy toward a marketoriented and globally integrated commercial economy. Leveraging a market-access framework and exploiting the fact that foreign trade was conducted exclusively through treaty ports, we construct an index measuring each port's access to its hinterland. We show that railway construction reduced transportation costs, lowering trade costs and expanding the market reach of treaty ports. Econometric analysis indicates that railway expansion accounted for 19.4 percent of export growth and 10.4 percent of import growth during the period. Railway expansion also triggered a transformation in the hinterland by fostering agricultural commercialization: it led to a higher commercialization rate, a proliferation of agricultural firms in inland regions, and a surge in exports of bulk agricultural commodities, such as tea, peanuts, silkworm cocoons, sesame seeds, and wool.

title: How Disability Benefits in Early Life Affect Adult Outcomes
affiliations: University of Chicago, Stanford University and Uber

detail.title: How Disability Benefits in Early Life Affect Adult Outcomes
detail.abstract:
We estimate the effect of receiving Supplemental Security Income (SSI) in childhood on adult outcomes using multiple sources of variation. Using variation across and within two quasi-experiments, we find that the program has heterogeneous effects that vary with the parental earnings response to SSI benefits: the program has positive effects on children when parents do not adjust their labor supply in response to SSI income (meaning household income increases), but zero or negative effects on children when parents offset the transfer by reducing earnings (meaning household income remains constant or falls). These results suggest that, relative to parent non-work time, income is crucial in the human capital production of low-income children with disabilities. We estimate a model of maternal labor supply and child human capital formation to quantify the relative importance of these channels. Our findings indicate that 1) the income effects of SSI on children's human capital are substantial, with a limited role for perverse incentive effects from conditioning benefits on disability status, and 2) parental work on net improves children's outcomes by increasing household resources, despite the potential decrease in parental time.

detail.abstract: In canonical New Keynesian benchmarks, the Taylor Principle (φ_π > 1) guarantees rational expectations determinacy. When firms pre-fund working capital via bank credit, monetary tightening activates an endogenous cost channel. This Note establishes that monetary determinacy is policy-contingent, deriving the closed-form interaction between working-capital credit exposure, endogenous borrowing spreads, firm heterogeneity, and financial policy capacity. We establish three main results: (i) the structural bifurcation threshold shifts dynamically with financial policy capacity, γ*(φ_m) = (1+φ_m)/(1+φ_m+σ), proving that targeted credit support expands the permissible domain of monetary tightening (∂γ*/∂φ_m > 0); (ii) when working-capital exposure exceeds 1/σ, increasing policy aggressiveness eventually destabilizes determinacy, establishing a strictly positive minimum financial policy capacity φ_m^min = max{0, σΩ_γ-1} required to restore unbounded determinacy; and (iii) by Jensen's inequality, cross-firm credit dispersion strictly amplifies aggregate cost-channel pass-through (E[γ_j/(1-γ_j)] > γ/(1-γ)), compressing the determinacy window even in economies with moderate average leverage.

title: Racial Dynamics of Federal Property Buyouts in Flood-Prone Areas
affiliations: Sociology Department, University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill, University of Kentucky, Department of Economics and University of Wisconsin-Madison

detail.title: Racial Dynamics of Federal Property Buyouts in Flood-Prone Areas
detail.abstract:
The use of managed retreats, or “buyouts,” of flood-prone properties is likely to grow as an adaptation response to increasing flood risks. This paper investigates the role of race and ethnicity in buyout bargaining outcomes and how those outcomes affect longer-run neighborhood change. We combine nationwide administrative data on federal property acquisitions, housing sales transactions, and restricted-use Census microdata to estimate whether there are systematic differences by race in buyout payments relative to a property’s fair market value. We then use a database tracking individual movement over time to examine the quality of the neighborhoods to which participants move and how neighborhood outcomes vary by race and program participation. We find that the buyout compensation received by households of color is at least 6 percent lower than that received by white households. White participants relocate to higher quality neighborhoods and are better off than white nonparticipants. Black participants, on the other hand, move to worse neighborhoods and are worse off than Black non-participants. Our work highlights how government policy, aimed to address increasing climate impacts, may exacerbate the burden of climate change on vulnerable communities.

title: Regulated Twice: How EU Mandates and National Gold-Plating Erode French Competitiveness

detail.title: Regulated Twice: How EU Mandates and National Gold-Plating Erode French Competitiveness

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is employed by Hospital Clínic de Barcelona; the institution had no involvement in, nor does it endorse, the research presented in this article.
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
EU regulatory requirements and national over-implementation are eroding France's competitiveness by raising production costs and constraining flexibility in trade-exposed sectors. This paper combines ex-post evidence with scenario analysis to quantify the macroeconomic cost to France of four EU regulatory files. A difference-indifferences design associates pesticide bans with a 2022 GDP loss of approximately EUR 5.4 billion and over 90,000 jobequivalents at risk. Under the baseline scenarios, the CO2 emission standards for cars and vans, Digital Omnibus Act and restrictive Tobacco Products Directive revision would reduce 2030 GDP by approximately EUR 1.3 billion, EUR 3.75 billion and EUR 7.3 billion respectively, putting around 9,200, 4,700 and 37,000 jobs at risk. Together, the four annual steady-state effects amount to approximately EUR 17.8 billion in GDP, around 141,000 job-equivalents at risk and roughly EUR 2.8 billion in foregone investment. The pesticide estimate is measured in 2022 and assumed to persist through 2030 absent policy change while the other effects are 2030 scenario projections.

These costs reflect instrument choice rather than policy objectives. Better-regulation scenarios, risk-proportionate, technology-open and market-based designs would raise French GDP in 2030 by more than EUR 20 billion relative to the baseline while preserving each file’s stated objective. In the tobacco case, a risk-differentiated framework would reduce smoking prevalence by nearly 15 percentage points by 2040 and raise 2030 GDP by up to EUR 12.8 billion relative to a restrictive scenario, which would increase prevalence by approximately 3.1 percentage points. The relevant choice is therefore between rigid and more effective regulatory instruments.

title: Who Matters in College? Familiarity, Ability Signals, and Student Achievement
affiliations: , University of Texas at Austin and University of California, Davis

detail.title: Who Matters in College? Familiarity, Ability Signals, and Student Achievement
detail.abstract:
This study examines how social influences on academic performance evolve during transition to university when students encounter new social environments and publicly observable signals of academic ability. Using administrative data from a large, elite, and linguistically and culturally heterogeneous public university in Uganda and exploiting random assignment of students to dormitories, we examine how exposure to coethnic peers and peers with scholarship status affects academic performance. We find that greater exposure to peers from similar linguistic and cultural backgrounds improve academic achievement early in university, but these effects fade over time. In contrast, exposure to scholarship peers generates persistent gains in academic performance that increase in magnitude over time. Our setting allows us to distinguish between peers’ underlying academic ability and publicly observable signals of ability since scholarship status is visible, while underlying academic preparation is not. We find that exposure to scholarship peers improves academic performance regardless of those peers’ underlying ability, while exposure to high-ability peers without a scholarship signal has no detectable effect. These results suggest that students respond more strongly to observable signals of academic standing than to peers’ underlying academic preparation. Taken together, our findings indicate that the sources of academic influence evolve over time.

title: Measuring Racial Disparities in Police Stops: Evidence from Telemetric Mobility Data
affiliations: University of Connecticut, Northeastern University, Northwestern University - Feinberg School of Medicine, Claremont Colleges - Claremont Graduate University and University of Connecticut - Department of Economics

detail.title: Measuring Racial Disparities in Police Stops: Evidence from Telemetric Mobility Data
detail.abstract:
We establish a reliable counterfactual for evaluating racial disparities in traffic stops using telemetric data to estimate the racial composition of motorists. We measure of motorist racial composition using telemetric mobility data and a novel two-stage correction methodology anchored by an independent measure, racial composition of motorists involved in accidents. Applying this to Massachusetts State Police stops, we find non-White motorists are stopped at rates exceeding their roadway presence by 6.7 percentage points. We demonstrate that uncalibrated telemetric data significantly understates minority presence (15.2 vs. 28 percent), and the uncalibrated telemetric data yields disparities that are over twice the size of our preferred estimates. We use this validated measure to assess the accuracy of several commonly-used disparity tests. We find that the widely used “Community Standard” test dramatically overestimates disparities, even when restricting to local roads or non-commuting hours. In contrast, the less-often used “Crash Benchmark” accurately captures disparities even when aggregated to higher temporal levels covering up to 94 percent of stops. Finally, the “Veil of Darkness” test yields smaller estimates than our telemetric measure, consistent with its focus on disparate treatment rather than the broader legal standard of motorist composition.

title: Beyond the Conventional Narrative: Economic Heterogeneity and Human Capital Among American Indians
affiliations: Harvard University and Johns Hopkins University

detail.title: Beyond the Conventional Narrative: Economic Heterogeneity and Human Capital Among American Indians
detail.abstract:
There is substantial heterogeneity in economic, educational, and health outcomes among American Indians, shaped by factors such as geographic location (urban vs. rural), resource endowments, and historical experiences with federal policies. Nonetheless, there is clear evidence that historical policies, including forced relocation, boarding schools, and assimilation efforts, have had long-lasting negative effects on human capital development and intergenerational mobility in these populations. Recent decades have seen improvements in some areas, particularly where tribes have exercised greater self-governance and implemented innovative economic development strategies. This paper emphasizes that a “one-size-fits-all” approach is inadequate for analyzing the sources and potential remediation of disparities across various outcomes between Native populations and descendants of later arrivals. A unique challenge is that the measurement and analysis of American Indian outcomes are complicated by issues of racial and tribal identification, data limitations, and changing definitions. These challenges can obscure true trends and make it difficult to evaluate the effectiveness of policies or programs, underscoring the need for more precise and disaggregated data. This essay comments on the need for caution and clarity in the use and analysis of data for this population in both historical and contemporary settings.

title: When Microenterprises Grow, Are Consumers Better Off? Evidence from Large Loans to Microenterprises in Chile
affiliations: Northwestern University, Harvard University - Business School (HBS) and Harvard University - Business School (HBS)

detail.title: When Microenterprises Grow, Are Consumers Better Off? Evidence from Large Loans to Microenterprises in Chile
detail.abstract:
Evaluations of microenterprise credit typically measure effects only on borrowing firms. But what about their customers? If microenterprises sell relatively undifferentiated goods and services, as is often hypothesized, credit may simply reallocate sales across firms and create little consumer benefit. In a randomized controlled trial in Chile, large loans increased treated firms’ profits by USD 292 per month, a 13.4% increase. Customer survey data indicate even larger benefits for customers: a gain of USD 494 per month in consumer surplus. Furthermore, using a sample of more than 125,000 non-treated firms operating in the same markets, we find little evidence of business stealing. The welfare gains from credit expansion thus extend well beyond the borrowers themselves.

title: Housing Wealth Accumulation and Electoral Representation
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD), Cornell University and University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Rady School of Management

detail.title: Housing Wealth Accumulation and Electoral Representation
detail.abstract:
Political representation is systematically aligned with economically consequential differences in individual behavior: homeowners who are most deeply incorporated into electoral institutions are systematically more effective at accumulating housing wealth. Using a nationwide voter-property dataset, we find that realized housing appreciation increases monotonically with electoral participation, robust to controls for geography, partisanship, demographics, wealth proxies, and income. Politically engaged homeowners actively generate value by purchasing undervalued properties, investing more in improvements, and selling at a premium, indicating individual-level differences rather than passive market exposure. An original survey shows that these homeowners also systematically differ in personality traits, pointing to deeper individual differences associated with both political engagement and housing-market performance.

title: When Resources Meet Relationships: The Returns to Personalized Supports for Low-Income Students
affiliations: Cornell University,  and Government of the United States of America - Bureau of the Census

detail.title: When Resources Meet Relationships: The Returns to Personalized Supports for Low-Income Students
detail.abstract:
Children from low-income families face barriers outside the classroom that impede learning and limit opportunities for economic mobility. We study Communities In Schools (CIS), a program that places coordinators in high-poverty schools to connect struggling students with personalized support. Coordinators match students to resources that address academic, behavioral, and basic needs—such as tutoring, mental health counseling, and housing stabilization. CIS is the largest program of its kind in the U.S., reaching 2 million students annually. Using the staggered rollout of CIS, we find that the program boosts test scores for struggling students. These gains persist, raising high school completion and adult earnings. Improvements in test scores explain only about half of CIS's impact on high school graduation; the remainder reflects progress on non-cognitive outcomes such as attendance and behavior. Consistent with CIS's emphasis on personalization, coordinators tailor services to distinct student needs, yet students with different needs experience comparable long-run gains. Placing a trusted adult in schools, backed by a network of programs and services, may offer a scalable way to improve economic mobility.

title: Disappearing Dollar Convenience?
affiliations: Stanford Graduate School of Business and

detail.title: Disappearing Dollar Convenience?
detail.abstract:
We measure the convenience yield on dollar safe assets over the last 5 years to answer this question. We find that within the set of U.S. dollar assets, safe asset convenience yields are about the same in 2025 as they were in 2019, and these levels are expected to persist for the next decade. Across the globe, the richness of U.S. dollar safe assets, particularly Treasurys, compared to the safe assets of other currencies have fallen considerably. There is also evidence that the U.S. dollar repo is currently the highest convenience dollar safe asset. In short, our answer is, no for domestic liquidity purposes, and yes for global liquidity purposes.

title: Immigration and Child Mortality during the Age of Mass Migration
affiliations: University of California, Davis, Western Kentucky University and Miami University

detail.title: Immigration and Child Mortality during the Age of Mass Migration
detail.abstract:
In the late nineteenth century, Americans feared that crowded immigrant neighborhoods were spreading disease through industrial cities. We study this claim using newly constructed town-level panel data from Massachusetts, 1860 to 1915, a setting uniquely suited to this exercise because its early vital registration system allows consistent measurement of mortality before national registration became widespread. Using a shift-share instrumental variable strategy based on historical settlement patterns, we estimate the effect of local exposure to immigration on mortality. The relevant question is not whether immigrant families themselves experienced higher mortality, but whether immigration altered the local disease environment more broadly. We find that increases in the foreign-born share significantly raised infant and child mortality, with the infant effect falling disproportionately on the post-neonatal period. Mechanical changes in the composition of births by parent nativity account for only a portion of the estimated effect, implying that the results are not driven primarily by higher mortality among immigrant births. Instead, the evidence is consistent with increased exposure to immigrants, communicable disease, and spillovers to children of native-born parents. These findings highlight immigration as one factor shaping the mortality transition in crowded high-mortality environments.

title: The Measurement Revolution? Credible Measurement and Inference in the Age of AI
affiliations: Harvard University - Department of Economics and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

detail.title: The Measurement Revolution? Credible Measurement and Inference in the Age of AI
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming measurement in economics. AI models convert unstructured data, such as text and images, into structured variables at low cost, making previously prohibitive measurement feasible at scale. This shifts the bottleneck from finding any scalable measure of a phenomenon to choosing among many plausible ones, which may support different empirical conclusions. This review provides guidance for navigating that shift. We describe three stages at which AI enters the measurement pipeline—discovery, construct definition, and observation—and what each demands of researchers. We argue that credible inference with AI-generated variables requires appropriately designed validation: anchoring measurement to explicit criteria, rather than informal claims that a proxy is reasonable. We then examine how validation samples support valid inference even when AI predictions are arbitrarily biased, and what can be done when a random validation sample is unavailable.

title: Diamond-Mirrlees meets Sims: Optimal Taxation with Rational Inattention
affiliations: Northwestern University and University of Zurich

detail.title: Diamond-Mirrlees meets Sims: Optimal Taxation with Rational Inattention
detail.abstract:
We study optimal commodity taxation when consumers are rationally inattentive and the planner internalizes their attention costs. In our setting, consumers may underreact to taxes, may allocate attention unevenly across goods, and may display sparse behavior or mental accounting. Our main result is that this need not change tax design: in a benchmark, optimal taxes satisfy the same sufficient-statistics formulas as in classical public finance, regardless of the extent and endogeneity of inattention. Away from this benchmark, we offer a dual rationale for state-dependent taxes and a new lens on tax salience; but we still find no room for the adjustments emphasized in recent work on behavioral public finance.

title: Social Capital and Innovation: Evidence from Facebook Friendship Networks
affiliations: Binghamton University, University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business - Finance and Business Economics Department and Baylor University

detail.title: Social Capital and Innovation: Evidence from Facebook Friendship Networks
detail.abstract:
Using Facebook friendship data, we study how three aspects of social capital shape innovative activity. We find that the most important aspect of social capital in explaining innovation is Economic Connectedness (EC)--the share of high-income friendships. One standard deviation greater EC is associated with 97% more patents per capita among patenting ZIP Codes and 45% more breakthrough patents per capita among ZIP Codes with breakthrough patents. Reverse-causality tests, a within-inventor relocation design, and a quasi-experiment using fracking-driven economic shocks to non-local friends support a causal interpretation. Mechanism tests provide evidence consistent with a financing channel.

title: Automation and Optimal Taxation: A Task-Based Theory
affiliations: Princeton University - Princeton School of Public and International Affairs and Princeton University

detail.title: Automation and Optimal Taxation: A Task-Based Theory
detail.abstract:
We characterize optimal labor and capital income taxation in a task-based model of automation. Workers and machines are perfect substitutes in automatable tasks, which run from the bottom of the skill distribution up to a threshold. Workers supply labor on the extensive margin. Capitalists supply machines at a finite elasticity. In this general-equilibrium automation economy, optimal tax formulas take canonical partial-equilibrium forms. Yet automation substantially changes optimal tax rates because wages and capital returns are endogenous. We calibrate the model to the US wage distribution and automation exposure. In equilibrium, the middle class is the most automated, with machine intensity peaking around the 40th wage percentile. Relative to a no-automation benchmark, the optimal labor tax schedule is more progressive: a larger EITC subsidy at the bottom, lower taxes in the middle, and higher taxes at the top. The optimal capital tax is sizable but unaffected by automation.
