title: The Federal Lands: An Economic Property Rights Perspective
affiliations: University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB)

detail.title: The Federal Lands: An Economic Property Rights Perspective
detail.abstract:
The US federal government owns and administers 472,892,659 acres or 21% of the land area of the lower 48 states, the country’s largest landowner. The resource is held and managed as a collective resource, the Federal Lands, through political and bureaucratic interpretation of the Multiple Use principle and generally, the biological aim of maximum sustained-yield. By contrast, access, exchange, and investment for most other US natural resources are through private property rights and markets. Despite the magnitude of the resource, economists have devoted relatively limited attention to the economic and welfare impact. The objective is to suggest economic implications and to encourage additional economic analyses. The discussion summarizes federal lands privatization through 1891, when withholding of federal lands began. The literature reveals no demonstratable market failure or increased resource scarcity from private exploitation between 1870 and 1957 when most lands were withheld. Because land was nonmobile and observable private property rights could have been assigned and any externalities addressed via Pigouvian restrictions or Coasean exchange. Federal ownership was not obviously required. Progressive Era reformers, driven by concerns of impending resource depletion, called for scientific, sustained-yield management by government officials. The institutional change is economically important. As outlined by Dixit and others, private rights holders have high powered incentives for efficient resource use that are lacking in decision making by agency officials who do not hold exchangeable property rights and do not directly bear the economic costs and benefits of their actions. Consequential public goods delivery could be an offset, but these are not measured for tradeoff calculations. Following Krueger, a rent-seeking framework is presented for comparing outcomes with economic property rights and political management. The analysis suggests that a.) federal lands will have lower production value than comparable private, all else equal; (b). federal lands management will be less responsive to shifts in economic costs and benefits. Public goods may be provided for high amenity, recreation, and ecological areas, but the dominant Multiple Use management principle provides no objective criteria for allocation or for periodic outcome assessment and adjustment. A literature review and data for contemporary federal forests, range, and oil and gas lands are provided.

title: Does Information Influence the Choice between Social Security Disability and Early Retirement Benefits?
affiliations: George Mason University, George Mason University and George Mason University - School of Policy, Government, and International Affairs

detail.title: Does Information Influence the Choice between Social Security Disability and Early Retirement Benefits?
detail.abstract:
We examine how information affects the choice between Social Security Disability Insurance (DI) and Old-Age Insurance (OAI) benefits for people between 62 and full retirement age. We find that receiving an initial Social Security statement, which provides recipients with personalized estimated benefit amounts available from DI and OAI, increases the probability of applying for both programs among those with a work-limiting health condition or a low work ability index, and this response is concentrated among people who are further from full retirement age. The increase in DI applications is split between applications for DI only and applications for both programs.

title: Heritability and Social Interaction in Labor Market Outcomes: Evidence from the Population of Twins in the United States
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Department of Economics, University of California, Berkeley, The Richard & Rhoda Goldman School of Public Policy and U.S. Census Bureau

detail.title: Heritability and Social Interaction in Labor Market Outcomes: Evidence from the Population of Twins in the United States
detail.abstract:
We use data on 44,000 twin pairs observed as adolescents in the 2000 Census, linked to their earnings 20 years later, to study the heritability of labor market outcomes. We extend the Classical Twins Design (CTD), which identifies heritability from contrasts between monozygotic and dizygotic twins, to settings where an analyst does not observe zygosity but can measure outcomes for same-sex and opposite-sex twins. We also allow for the presence of a family- and sex-specific component affecting same-sex siblings but only partly shared by opposite-sex siblings. Our extended model identifies heritability from the difference-in-differences of same-sex vs. opposite-sex twins vs. siblings. The estimates indicate strong heritability (h2 approximately 0.36) of log earnings. Using an AKM (Abowd et al., 1999) decomposition that separates the person-specific component of earnings from employer-specific pay premiums, we find that both components are heritable. The heritability of employer pay premiums, however, is mainly driven by same-sex twins who work at the same firm, suggesting that social interactions may lead to an over-estimate of the genetic component in earnings. Excluding siblings who work together leads to estimates of the heritability of log earnings that are 15% lower. Similar biases may be present in CTD-based estimates of heritability for other social outcomes like education.

title: Informed Choices: Gender Gaps in Career Advice
affiliations: University of Chicago and University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Anderson School of Management

detail.title: Informed Choices: Gender Gaps in Career Advice
detail.abstract:
This paper provides the first causal evidence that gender affects the information an individual receives about careers. We conduct a large-scale field experiment in which real college students seek career information from 10,000 working professionals. We randomize whether a professional receives a message from a male or a female student. When students ask broadly for information about a career, female students receive substantially more information on work/life balance than male students. This gender difference persists when students specifically ask about work/life balance. A survey of professionals suggests non-altruistic motives for discussing work/life balance with women. Combining findings from the field experiment and results from an information intervention, we conclude that gender gaps in information received about work/life balance are consequential for gender gaps in career intentions.

title: Asset Privatization as Intergenerational Redistribution
affiliations: Emory University - Department of Economics, University of Pennsylvania - Department of Economics and Nanyang Technological University (NTU)

detail.title: Asset Privatization as Intergenerational Redistribution
detail.abstract:
Rapid economic growth creates large differences in lifetime incomes across generations. This paper examines the intergenerational redistribution generated by subsidized access to appreciating public assets in rapidly growing economies. We show that providing incumbent generations with subsidized access to these assets before future growth is fully capitalized into market values gives them an early claim on subsequent economic growth, thereby redistributing resources from future to incumbent generations. In the context of housing privatization, subsequent capital gains on privatized housing enable homeowners to trade up, further amplifying housing demand, house prices, and intergenerational redistribution. We evaluate the early ownership and capital gains channels of asset-based redistribution in a quantitative equilibrium model calibrated to China's housing privatization. Relative to more standard pension-based redistribution, we show that asset-based redistribution delivers higher welfare for future cohorts while substantially reducing long-run fiscal burdens once economic growth unexpectedly slows.

title: We've Got You Covered: Establishment-Level Evidence on California's Fast-Food Minimum Wage
affiliations: Archbridge Institute, University of California, Irvine - Department of Economics, Knee Regulatory Research Center and University of Louisiana at Lafayette

detail.title: We've Got You Covered: Establishment-Level Evidence on California's Fast-Food Minimum Wage
detail.abstract:
We study the employment effects of California’s $20 fast-food minimum wage. Evaluating this policy poses two challenges in commonly used aggregate datasets: coverage is based on 60-establishment chain-size threshold that cannot be identified; and there is measurement error in the industry codes used to identify fast-food restaurants. We address these challenges using establishment-level data. We find evidence of negative employment effects, but they are concentrated among small chains, among which the policy also slowed entry and increased exit. Thus, the primary effect of the fast-food minimum wage was to disadvantage small chains, albeit with modest overall employment effects thus far.

title: Did the Affordable Care Act Save Lives?
affiliations: Loyola University of Chicago - Department of Economics, Georgia Southern University and University of Chicago - Harris School of Public Policy, National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER)

detail.title: Did the Affordable Care Act Save Lives?
detail.abstract:
While recent research has provided evidence that the Medicaid expansions of the Affordable Care Act (ACA) reduced mortality, there is no evidence on the effect of the Affordable Care Act (ACA) net of the Medicaid expansions on mortality. This is an important gap in knowledge because the ACA significantly increased health insurance coverage in non-expansion states. In this article, we exploit the large increase in health insurance coverage brought forth by the ACA to examine the effect of the ACA and Medicaid expansions on mortality. Unlike prior studies that relied solely on geographic variation in Medicaid expansions to estimate the net effect of the expansion, we use a novel empirical approach that allows us to investigate the effect of the ACA net of Medicaid expansion on mortality, the incremental effect of the Medicaid expansion, and the overall effect of the ACA including Medicaid expansion. We use longitudinal data from the NHIS Linked Mortality Files (LMF) and a nationally representative sample of 40 to 58-year-olds combined with a difference-in-differences and a difference-in-differences-in-differences research design to obtain estimates of the effect of the ACA on mortality. We find no evidence that the Medicaid expansions had a beneficial effect on mortality but do find that the ACA net of Medicaid expansion reduced mortality.

title: Did COVID Change the Black Neighborhood Startup Deficit? Evidence from the Startup Cartography Project
affiliations: Boston University, Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management and

detail.title: Did COVID Change the Black Neighborhood Startup Deficit? Evidence from the Startup Cartography Project
detail.abstract:
Motivated by William Julius Wilson’s account of concentrated disadvantage, we examine a local poverty-trap interpretation of low entrepreneurship in Black neighborhoods. Using registration data from 38 states, we document a long-standing Black neighborhood startup deficit. Amid shocks that raised expectations of greater economic activity, the deficit reverses sharply in 2020, particularly where pre-existing deficits were larger. While the overall surplus attenuates, relative entrepreneurship remains elevated in high-deficit Black neighborhoods, and neighborhood-oriented entrepreneurship also remains elevated through 2024. Together, these patterns are consistent with a partially sustained shift toward a higher-activity equilibrium.

title: The Macroeconomic Returns to School Finance Reforms: Micro-Calibrated Predictions Meet Causal Evidence
affiliations: Northwestern University

detail.title: The Macroeconomic Returns to School Finance Reforms: Micro-Calibrated Predictions Meet Causal Evidence
detail.abstract:
A large literature posits a central role for human capital in determining macroeconomic output, while another documents substantial private returns to educational investment. However, whether private gains translate into aggregate gains remains uncertain, as signaling, displacement, or general-equilibrium adjustment may drive a wedge between private and aggregate returns. This paper bridges these literatures with causal evidence that state-level school finance reforms (SFRs) increase macroeconomic output. First, I combine design-based micro estimates of SFR effects on private earnings with a cohort replacement framework to simulate state-level earnings per worker. The simulation predicts little change for 10 to 15 years, then gradual gains as treated cohorts enter the labor force, reaching 7.8 percent after 60 years. Next, I test this prediction using the staggered implementation of SFRs across U.S. states. In an event-study framework, state-level earnings per worker track the predicted path, remaining flat through about 15 years before rising roughly 4.7 percent above counterfactual levels after 30 years — consistent with private earnings gains aggregating to the broader economy. Finally, I show that these effects extend to broader economic output, with GDP per capita declining modestly initially before rising to more than 5 percent above its counterfactual path after 30 years.

detail.abstract: Over the past 15 years, inflation in Switzerland has, on average, been almost 2 percentage points lower than in the euro area. This note shows that two-thirds of the Swiss inflation gap with the euro area was driven by goods, in particular food and energy, while the remaining third was driven by services. The note also shows that inflation was lower in Switzerland than in the euro area primarily because of smaller price increases rather than different consumption habits.

title: Do Female Directors Face Larger Career Consequences After Financial Distress?
affiliations: Oklahoma State University - Stillwater - Department of Finance, Miami University and State University of New York, SUNY at Stony Brook University, College of Business

detail.title: Do Female Directors Face Larger Career Consequences After Financial Distress?
detail.abstract: High-visibility labor markets predict larger career penalties for women after negative performance shocks. We test this among bank directors using the 2007-2009 financial crisis and post-crisis failures from 2012-2019, comparing female and male co-directors of the same distressed bank. Difference-in-differences and triple-difference estimates find no gender-asymmetric decline in appointments, appointment quality, committee assignments, or exits; Bayes factors and equivalence tests confirm the null. Failed banks recruit their first female director 1.5 years faster than non-failed peers. One exception is that female directors from poorly performing banks are less likely to gain seats on boards with multiple incumbent women.

title: Do Social Norms Substitute for Enforcement? Evidence from Public Officials’ Home Purchases in Singapore
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Finance, Stanford University, The University of Hong Kong and Stanford University

detail.title: Do Social Norms Substitute for Enforcement? Evidence from Public Officials’ Home Purchases in Singapore
detail.abstract:
We study whether pro-integrity social norms can substitute for formal enforcement in deterring misconduct by public officials. Singapore, widely regarded as one of the world’s least corrupt countries, provides a sharp setting to examine whether decades of successful anti-corruption enforcement can produce self-sustaining norms. Using universe-level housing transactions, we identify informed home purchases by civil servants around expansions of the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) system. Relative to a matched uninformed control, civil servants disproportionately purchase homes near planned—but not yet publicly announced—stations, with the effect concentrated one to two years before public announcements. The behavior is concentrated among mid-level officials and agencies connected to rail planning, generates meaningful private gains, and also appears among relatives, consistent with information leakage. Stronger formal enforcement substantially reduces both direct and indirect misconduct. We combine the transaction evidence with independent survey measures of perceived corruption, public trust, and pro-integrity norms and develop a dynamic model in which norms are persistent but fragile, enforcement both directly deters misconduct and indirectly sustains norms, and policymakers learn about the persistence of norms from noisy integrity signals. Observed pre-tightening misconduct, deterioration in survey-based integrity measures, and the subsequent decline in misconduct following stronger enforcement are more consistent with policymakers learning that norms have limited persistence than with a response to transitory noise. The findings suggest that even in high-integrity societies, social norms may not be sufficiently self-sustaining to maintain a low-corruption equilibrium without continued formal enforcement.

detail.abstract: This work presents novel structure-preserving formulations for stable model order reduction in the context of time-domain room acoustics simulations. A solution to address the instability in conventional model order reduction formulations based on the Linearized Euler Equations is derived and validated through numerical experiments. For the scenarios presented, the proposed formulation demonstrates 3.5 times speedup in calculating the full-order model compared to the unstable formulation. A critical stability analysis is performed to identify the eigenvalues of the reduced operator matrices falling on the right half of complex plane along with their out of phase eigen angles as the source of instabilities in the reduced system. The performance of the proposed MOR formulation is tested for perfectly rigid, frequency-independent, and locally reacting frequency-dependent boundary conditions in two-dimensional cases. The study shows that MOR using the stable formulation results in a 100-fold speedup. The proposed formulation is further evaluated to assess its impact on accuracy, computational speedup, and overall reduction potential of the system. 1 | Introduction Room acoustics simulations are widely used for various applications in various industries, for example, architectural design [1, 2], sound system design [3], healthcare [4], hearing health research [5], entertainment [6], industrial facilities [7], hospitality [8, 9], transportation [10], virtual acoustics [11], and in the building industry [12]. These simulations are predominantly performed by geometrical acoustics (GA) methods [13, 14], such as ray tracing [15]. title: Buying a Station or Relaxing a Constraint? Spectrum Repacking and Dirac's Conjecture
affiliations: Harvard University

detail.title: Buying a Station or Relaxing a Constraint? Spectrum Repacking and Dirac's Conjecture
detail.abstract:
Spectrum repacking auctions can restore feasibility along two margins: retiring a station via buyout or relaxing a pairwise engineering restriction. I represent stations as vertices in a network and interference restrictions as edges between them, and so station buyouts delete vertices and engineering waivers relax edges. This paper shows that buying out any one station can reduce the number of channels needed, even though relaxing any single interference restriction cannot. The smallest feasible number of channels is k . For every k≥4, I show that there is a network in which removing any station saves one channel, while relaxing any single pairwise restriction does not. This main result follows directly from Dirac’s half-century-old conjecture on vertex-critical graphs, whose chromatic number falls after any vertex is removed. By constructing the missing counterexample at k=4 and combining it with earlier results for k≥5, I show that at every k≥4, some k-vertex-critical graph has no critical edge, resolving Dirac's conjecture. Market designers auditing feasibility link-by-link systematically can mistake combinatorial complementarity for remedy failure, overlooking station buyouts that unlock the clearing target.

title: Global Union Federations and Human Rights DueDiligence: Strategic Repertoires in a Shifting Legal Terrain
affiliations: Monash University, Monash University,  and Tel Aviv University - Buchmann Faculty of Law

detail.title: Global Union Federations and Human Rights DueDiligence: Strategic Repertoires in a Shifting Legal Terrain

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the strategic engagement of global union federations (GUFs) with emerging human rights due diligence (HRDD) legislation as a mechanism of transnational labour governance. Drawing on a multimethod qualitative design—including legal and document analysis and interviews with union officials—the study identifies six distinct repertoires of action evident in the empirical material: consultation and dialogue, regulatory advocacy, capacity-building, campaigning in the shadow of the law, regulatory innovation and litigation. These repertoires suggest an ongoing process of strategic recalibration of institutional, associational and societal (ideational and coalitional) power resources across scales. Although HRDD laws offer potential procedural leverage, their use is shaped by legal design, sectoral context and disparities in union capacity. The findings highlight both strategic innovation and ambivalence, with GUFs navigating tensions between legal formalism and grassroots mobilisation. The paper contributes to scholarship on transnational labour regulation by theorising HRDD laws as evolving legal opportunity structures and mapping the differentiated pathways through which GUFs seek to assert and embed worker voice in global supply chains.

detail.abstract:
This research reflects on a journey along Yunnan’s Ancient Tea Road, exploring how ecological systems, cultural practices, and networks of exchange have co-evolved over centuries across one of Asia’s most significant mountain corridors.

Drawing on conversations with members of the Naxi and Bai communities, field observations, and historical research, the study examines how tea cultivation, mountain landscapes, customary knowledge, and long-distance trade shaped interconnected systems of livelihood, resource stewardship, and resilience. Rather than viewing ecology, culture, and commerce as separate domains, the paper considers how they developed through continuous interaction and mutual dependence.

The paper argues that the Ancient Tea Road offers valuable insights into contemporary questions of climate resilience and biodiversity, illustrating how the resilience of communities and local economies is shaped by relationships between people, ecosystems, and systems of exchange, and how these dependencies might be better recognised in financial decision-making.

By documenting local perspectives alongside the historical evolution of the Tea Road, the research seeks to broaden current sustainability debates, highlighting how community knowledge and mountain landscapes can inform more integrated approaches to socio-ecological resilience, natural capital, and long-term value creation.

title: The Impact of the Circular Economy on Carbon Emissions

detail.title: The Impact of the Circular Economy on Carbon Emissions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Governments worldwide have committed to ambitious net-zero emission targets by 2050, and the circular economy has gained momentum as a structural response that targets the material basis of economic activity. Using an unbalanced panel of 22 European countries over 2000-2024, this study constructs a multidimensional Circular Economy Index (CEI) that combines principal component analysis for indicator screening with Shannon entropy weighting, based on the municipal-waste recycling rate, resource productivity, and municipal waste generation per capita. The impact of the CEI on per-capita CO₂ emissions is estimated using two-way fixed-effects panel regressions, Lewbel heteroskedasticity-based instrumental variables that address endogeneity, and dynamic panel methods. The results reveal pronounced crosscountry heterogeneity in circular economy development, with the Netherlands, Luxembourg, and Belgium at the top of the ranking. The strong negative bivariate correlation between the CEI and CO₂ emissions is driven largely by time-invariant structural differences across countries: once country and year effects are absorbed, the within-country CEIemissions link is statistically weak, while energy consumption per capita and the renewable-energy share emerge as the dominant within-country determinants of emissions. The findings imply that circular economy policies deliver climate benefits mainly through long-run structural transformation and should complement, rather than substitute for, energy-based decarbonisation policy.

title: Here Be Dragons: A Carbon Reward for Stabilizing the Carbon Cycle

detail.title: Here Be Dragons: A Carbon Reward for Stabilizing the Carbon Cycle

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author, Delton B. Chen, originated and advocates the carbon reward policy described in this manuscript. This work was conducted under the auspices of Global Carbon Reward/Inquiring Systems, Inc., Santa Rosa, USA, where the author serves as a policy researcher. The author declares no financial interest whose value depends on the policy's adoption. The author has no other personal or financial relationships with other people or organizations that may have or could be perceived to have influenced this study.
declarations.funderStatement: Anonymous private donors part-funded this work and had no role in the analysis, manuscript preparation, or publication decision. Most of the work was contributed pro bono by the author with the assistance of pro-bono volunteers.

detail.abstract:
Climate mitigation is falling short of the Paris Agreement, with warming projected to reach approximately 2.8°C by 2100, carbon pricing covering less than one-third of global emissions at roughly one-tenth of the social cost of carbon, and climate finance meeting only a quarter of the annual requirement. Carbon taxes and cap-and-trade—market ‘sticks’ rooted in neoclassical welfare economics—are frequently delayed by political opposition. The resulting climate change is then amplified by non-linear Earth system feedbacks, creating a systemic risk to the Holocene-like stability of the carbon cycle: a metaphorical dragon that threatens global public safety.


I frame this unpriced systemic risk as a systemic externality and quantify it with the risk cost of carbon, defined as the marginal cost of the precautionary rate of CO2 removal needed for a relatively safe carbon budget (distinct from the social cost of carbon). A carbon reward instrument, denoted XCR, is recommended to internalize the risk cost of carbon by financing comprehensive decarbonization. XCR is a sovereign-backed, tradeable asset—a ‘carrot’—with a price floor anchored to the risk cost of carbon and guaranteed by central banks through a purchase programme. It can mobilize multiple trillions of dollars annually without taxes, fiscal spending, or debt, diffusing the cost thinly across the global financial system to avoid political opposition. This framework renames the whole problem a market-and-system failure, resolvable by pairing sticks for market efficiency with carrots for public safety: metaphorically mapping the dragon and steering a safer course of economic development.

title: A CRITICAL ANALYSIS OF THE INTERSECTION BETWEEN INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY LAW AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
affiliations: Osun State University, College of Law, Ifetedo

detail.title: A CRITICAL ANALYSIS OF THE INTERSECTION BETWEEN INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY LAW AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: Personal

detail.abstract: The rapid advancement of AI technologies within the contemporary digital era has significantly altered the traditional landscape of IP law. Consequently, the increasing capability of artificial intelligence systems to generate literary works, artistic expressions, inventions, trademarks and commercially valuable information has generated complex legal and regulatory concerns particularly in relation to ownership, authorship, inventorship, liability and protection under traditional intellectual property frameworks. This development has further raised questions as to the adequacy and adaptability of existing intellectual property laws in effectively regulating AI-generated works. This study therefore seeks to critically examine the intersection between AI and IP law with particular focus on copyright, patents, trademarks and trade secrets. In doing so, the study examined the concepts of AI and IP law alongside the applicability of existing intellectual property frameworks to AI-generated and AI-assisted works and inventions. Furthermore, comparative analyses of various jurisdictions were undertaken in order to evaluate the legal and institutional responses towards the challenges resulting from artificial intelligence technologies. This study consequently revealed that contemporary IP frameworks both within Nigeria and across several jurisdictions remain largely inadequate in comprehensively addressing the legal and technological complexities introduced by artificial intelligence systems. Finally, recommendations were made towards proactive legislative reforms, harmonization of international legal standards and adaptive regulatory frameworks capable of fostering a balanced coexistence between artificial intelligence innovation and intellectual property protection within the contemporary digital era.

title: Lawyer as Treatise Writer
affiliations: National Law School of India University

detail.title: Lawyer as Treatise Writer

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: There is no funding received for this work.

detail.abstract: Of all the endeavours professionals take up, treatise writing by practicing lawyers stands apart in its scope and ambition. A lawyer who commits to write a treatise is wedded to a particular branch of law: he undertakes to update the book that bears his name with every change in the law and is likely to keeping working on it for a long time. We may ask this question: is there another professional endeavor-one that a person's work and livelihood do not demand-that a person would commit to and continue the way a practicing lawyer revises and updates the treatise he writes? We may never fully know what drives some lawyers to take up such monumental tasks. Those who write, and continue to write, do so because the writing is tied to their name-they have developed the identity of a treatise writer. This article, part analytical and part biographical, draws on the human stories of three first books, written by their authors at the launch their careers: Palkhivala's The Law and Practice of Income Tax (1950), Datar's Guide to Central Excise (1988) and the author's own The Law of Patents (2007). It looks at how a treatise writer makes a field choice and makes it his own. A treatise is defined as the systematic exposition (structure) of an entire field of law (scope), kept current with the law's changes (currency), carried beyond its editions and its author's lifetime (continuity), under a name that becomes synonymous to the work (identity). This article makes a case for the lawyer as treatise writer: an identity honed over decades, tested in courts, cited by the name and in an age of AI, it is the only thing that cannot be artificially generated. It also counts the human cost in its creation and ends with an invitation to write one.

title: Text-Based Network Industries and Endogenous Product Differentiation
affiliations: Dartmouth College - Tuck School of Business and University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business - Finance and Business Economics Department

detail.title: Text-Based Network Industries and Endogenous Product Differentiation
detail.abstract: We study how firms differ from their competitors using new time-varying measures of product differentiation based on text-based analysis of product descriptions from 50,673 firm 10-K statements filed yearly with the Securities and Exchange Commission. This year-by-year set of product differentiation measures allows us to generate a new set of industries and corresponding new measures of industry competition where firms can have their own distinct set of competitors. Our new sets of industry competitors better explain specific discussion of high competition by management, rivals identified by managers as peer firms and firm characteristics such as profitability and leverage than do existing classifications. We also find evidence that firm R&D and advertising are associated with subsequent differentiation from competitors, consistent with theories of endogenous product differentiation.

title: When Local Governments Go on Camera: Economic Narrative and Municipal Bond Market
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) - Sustainable & Green Finance Institute (SGFIN), Zhejiang University and Zhejiang University

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none

detail.abstract: Political power reaches markets not only through policy but also through official economic narratives. Using 6,327 videos of Chinese local officials from 2015 to 2025, we apply machine-learning methods to extract narrative themes and sentiment from words, voice, and facial expressions. The extracted themes track national initiatives and changing local priorities, supporting the measures' validity and documenting shifts in China's local political-economic landscape. Further, we find that more positive sentiment is associated with lower LGFV bond spreads at the first secondary-market trade, but not at issuance. Both vocal and visual sentiment drive this relation. The initial spread compression later reverses, and land prices show a similar riseand-reversal pattern. These findings suggest that official economic narratives temporarily shift market beliefs, providing a channel through which political power enters asset prices.

title: Does Board Gender Diversity Temper Regulatory Enforcement?

detail.title: Does Board Gender Diversity Temper Regulatory Enforcement?

detail.abstract: The SEC is less likely to investigate companies with more female directors: firms with at least 35% women directors are 26% less likely to be investigated. To establish causality, we exploit exogenous variation in board gender diversity induced by the Big Three campaign and show that firms with more women directors were significantly less likely to be targeted by the SEC. Companies targeted by an SEC investigation respond by appointing more women to their boards, indicating that firms also view female directors as being beneficial in times of crisis and scrutiny.

title: Weight, Quality, and Market Segment: An Empirical Assessment of the Alwadhi Power-Law of Gemstone Pricing Against D2C Market Data

detail.title: Weight, Quality, and Market Segment: An Empirical Assessment of the Alwadhi Power-Law of Gemstone Pricing Against D2C Market Data

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares an interest as Chairman of The Mint AS (issuer of the GNRC token) and as a principal of GEMNYX. The empirical assessment in this paper is conducted by GEMNYX as an entity independent of The Mint AS.
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Private funding

detail.abstract: Al-Wadhi (2026) proposes a universal power-law framework for gemstone pricing, deriving the functional form P = B•W^α from first principles and reporting category-specific exponents across ten stone types. This paper provides the first independent empirical assessment of that framework, testing it against a preliminary subset of the GEMNYX database-41,207 direct-to-consumer (D2C) retail listings across eight coloured gemstone categories drawn from a broader dataset combining 83,304 verified D2C retail listings, 78,841 verified wholesale transactions, and inventory data covering more than 500,000 stones. We find that the power-law functional form is empirically confirmed for blue sapphires (R² = 0.81, fitted α = 1.818 vs. Alwadhi's 1.620), but breaks down for rubies in pooled D2C data (R² = 0.27, fitted α ≈ 1.0), where quality heterogeneity overwhelms the weight signal. Results for spinel and tanzanite are inconclusive pending quality stratification. Across all categories tested, Alwadhi's published base price coefficients (B values) systematically overestimate D2C retail prices by approximately 3×, consistent with calibration against wholesale and auction reference prices rather than retail markets. We conclude that: (i) the Alwadhi axiomatic framework is mathematically sound and the functional form is a credible structural description of gemstone price scaling; (ii) the framework's empirical coefficients require market-segment calibration before applied use; and (iii) quality stratification is a prerequisite for valid application to ruby and other categories with extreme quality-driven price dispersion. These findings are consistent with and extend the three-tier NAV methodology for gemstone-backed asset-referenced tokens developed in Eide (2026) under the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA). We identify three workstreams where a joint empirical programme could materially strengthen the Alwadhi framework and propose a collaboration accordingly.

title: Correlation Neglect in Asset Prices
affiliations: and University of Pennsylvania - Finance Department

detail.title: Correlation Neglect in Asset Prices
detail.abstract: We document a strong negative serial correlation between stock market returns in i) the second month of a quarter and ii) the first month of the subsequent quarter. This pattern arises as investors fail to fully recognize the predictably repetitive aggregate earnings “news” conveyed by the late earnings announcements in the second month of a quarter. The neglected correlation leads to overreaction, which is in turn corrected when earnings of a new quarter are announced. Consistent with this hypothesis, returns in the second month of a quarter positively correlate with those of the preceding month, and the return pattern amplifies when earnings announced in these two months are more similar. Survey data and industry-level returns lend further support to this mechanism. These results provide evidence of correlation neglect even among sophisticated, financially incentivized decision-makers, underscoring its importance as a behavioral phenomenon.

title: The Dynamics of Household Financial Fragility: Natural Disasters and Asymmetric Regime Transitions
affiliations: Washington and Lee University - Department of Economics and Florida International University

detail.title: The Dynamics of Household Financial Fragility: Natural Disasters and Asymmetric Regime Transitions
detail.abstract: We develop a dynamic approach to household financial fragility, conceptualized as an unobserved latent state spanning objective precautionary liquidity and subjective appraisals of solvency and borrowing capacity. Using five waves (2021-2025) of the Federal Reserve's SHED and estimating a latent Markov model, we identify three fragility regimes — Secure, Coping, and Fragile—and trace transitions following natural disaster exposure. Disaster exposure exhibits an asymmetric relationship with financial deterioration: higher odds of downward transitions — Secure to Coping and Coping to Fragile — but no statistically detectable association with upward transitions. We find no evidence that race or gender moderates these dynamics, but age does. Relative to prime-age adults, younger adults show a bifurcated response: disaster exposure is linked to higher odds of both climbing to Secure and falling to Fragile from Coping. Older adults, by contrast, have elevated odds of falling from Coping to Fragile, without evidence of an offsetting recovery. Our framework highlights state-dependent, asymmetric transition dynamics and persistent financial scarring that remain invisible to conventional analyses.

title: Against Expressivism in Judicial Tort-Making
affiliations: University of Oxford, Faculty of Law, Students  and University of Ottawa - Common Law Section

detail.title: Against Expressivism in Judicial Tort-Making

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the Harry Arthurs Award for Research Excellence.

detail.abstract: In recent years, there has been a resurgence of interest in tort law's expressive dimension. Prior to the Supreme Court of Canada’s judgment in Ahluwalia v. Ahluwalia, 2026 SCC 16, commentators argued that the judicial creation of new torts is justified on the ground of expressing or symbolically vindicating public values. This article defends the orthodox view that the expression of public condemnation or social disapproval is not an aim of the Anglo-Canadian law of torts, such that it does not suffice on its own to motivate doctrinal developments such as the judicial creation of new causes of action. Descriptively, it argues that the extant doctrine in tort law does not principally embrace the expression of public values as a basis of common law development. Normatively, it contends that expressivism is inapt in the context of private wrongs, as these wrongs do not characteristically attract condemnation on the part of the whole community. By instrumentalizing tort law to express public values, these approaches undermine the distinctive public value of tort law itself, namely, to instantiate a practice of relational accountability between equal persons.

title: Ahluwalia v Ahluwalia 2026 SCC 16: a new tort of intimate partner violence
affiliations: University of Oxford, Faculty of Law, Students

detail.title: Ahluwalia v Ahluwalia 2026 SCC 16: a new tort of intimate partner violence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by a SSHRC Doctoral Fellowship.

detail.abstract: In Ahluwalia v Ahluwalia, the Supreme Court of Canada took the unprecedented step of inaugurating a novel ‘tort of intimate partner violence’ targeting coercive control. In giving benediction to this new nominate tort, the judgment charts a creative path for the law of torts in Canada, which will be of interest to Anglo-Commonwealth scholars and jurists more broadly. This comment highlights the principal innovative aspects of the Court’s decision, while identifying some analytical issues in its reasoning and cautioning against its uncritical adoption.

title: Income, Wealth, and Redistribution in a Tax Haven: Distributional National Accounts for Switzerland
affiliations: ETH Zürich, ETH Zürich, ETH Zürich and ETH Zürich

detail.title: Income, Wealth, and Redistribution in a Tax Haven: Distributional National Accounts for Switzerland
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the composition and distribution of national income, private wealth, and the extent of redistribution in Switzerland from 2003 to 2022, combining micro tax, survey, and national accounts data. Constructing Distributional National Accounts (DINA) requires addressing two features of the Swiss setting. Switzerland is a tax haven, so we correct for cross-border profit shifting by multinationals. It is also fiscally decentralized. Lacking nationally representative tax microdata, we reweight cantonal micro tax records to match national distributions. We find that pre-tax income inequality is substantially higher than suggested by tax statistics: the top 1% income share increases by 50% once retained earnings and privileged dividends are included. Compared to previous estimates, wealth inequality is somewhat higher but shows no upward trend. The overall Swiss tax-and-transfer system is close to flat across most of the distribution, at around 45% of pre-tax income, declining to below 30% for the top 0.01%.

title: Risk Perceptions as a Multivariate System: Crowding Out, Affect Generalization, and Heterogeneous Belief Updating
affiliations: Berlin School of Economics and Law, Berlin School of Economics and Law and Berlin Centre for Empirical Economics (BCEE)

detail.title: Risk Perceptions as a Multivariate System: Crowding Out, Affect Generalization, and Heterogeneous Belief Updating
detail.abstract: Crises rarely arrive alone: pandemics overlap with wars, financial shocks with climate risks, personal hardship with collective upheaval. When one risk becomes salient, does worry about the others recede or spread? We provide a multi-domain, multi-shock field test using the German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP), which elicits worries across eight domains from 1999 to 2022, and exploit quasi-random survey timing around major societal crises and within-person variation around idiosyncratic personal life events. Risk perceptions are not separable: a shock in one domain moves worries in others, even when the underlying risks are unrelated. The direction depends on the shock's proximity to the individual. Distant societal crises crowd out competing worries (Finite Pool of Worry); proximal personal events amplify worry across domains (Affect Generalization). Combining imputation-based difference-in-differences with latent profile analysis, we find the population splits into qualitatively distinct types: 27% generalize worry, 62% reallocate it, 11% suppress it. Profile membership is organized above all by neuroticism, revealing that personality shapes not only the level of worry, but the structure of belief updating itself. Interdependent worries imply that crises generate externalities in the mental economy of risk perception: displacing concern from persistent risks for some individuals, diffusing pessimism for others.

title: Consistent Non-Utilitarian Welfare Weights
affiliations: Tulane University and Tulane University

detail.title: Consistent Non-Utilitarian Welfare Weights
detail.abstract: Saez and Stantcheva (2016) proposed evaluating tax reforms using generalized welfare weights, which encode the social value of giving a dollar to each person, to incorporate non-utilitarian values without specifying a social welfare function. However, Sher (2024) showed that generalized welfare weights cannot both incorporate non-utilitarian values and evaluate tax reforms consistently (in the sense that they do not generate preference cycles). We show that by relaxing a restriction imposed by both Saez and Stantcheva (2016) and Sher (2024) on how weights vary with the tax schedule, the generalized welfare weight approach can achieve both of these objectives. We characterize when weights are consistent: a policymaker with consistent generalized welfare weights necessarily behaves as if they were determining desirability of tax reforms via a well-defined global objective function, even if they never wrote one down; we show consistency can be checked via a symmetry condition. We also show that consistency does not require the policymaker to specify the underlying objective: any set of mechanical weights (society's valuation of a dollar transferred to each person, holding behavior fixed), utilitarian or not, can be completed into consistent generalized welfare weights by adding a term that captures the implicit value of behavioral responses. Our results are robust to multidimensional tax schedules and heterogeneity, behavioral agents, general equilibrium effects, and non-smooth behavioral responses such as bunching.

title: Regulatory Delay, Uncertainty, and the Cost of Foreign Investment Screening
affiliations: University of Melbourne and University of Melbourne

detail.title: Regulatory Delay, Uncertainty, and the Cost of Foreign Investment Screening
detail.abstract: Many countries screen foreign direct investment through discretionary approval regimes that operate primarily through delay rather than outright prohibition. Because few transactions are blocked, governments describe screening as "light touch." We show that this characterization is misleading. When approval is costly to reverse and information arrives over time, screening functions as a real option: regulatory delay creates uncertainty that is capitalized into asset prices during review. Using Australian data, we estimate a 2.9% approval-event abnormal return for target firms, equivalent to around 20% of expected target-shareholder surplus. This measures the market value of resolving screening uncertainty for announced transactions. Aggregated across transactions, the implied valuation exposure is large relative to estimates of goods-trade barriers and rises further once deterred deals are considered. Screening also generates spillovers to rival firms and persistent valuation effects through repeated review of subsequent acquisitions by foreign-owned firms, with international spillovers particularly for Chinese investors.

title: Racial Animus, Employment Risk, and Analyst Forecasts during the COVID-19 Pandemic
affiliations: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey - Rutgers Business School at Newark & New Brunswick, , Tulane University and Rutgers University - Rutgers School of Business-Camden

detail.title: Racial Animus, Employment Risk, and Analyst Forecasts during the COVID-19 Pandemic

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Leveraging the exogenous surge in anti-Asian racial animus during the COVID-19 pandemic, we examine its effects on analysts' forecasting behavior. We find that Asian financial analysts become less bold in their forecasts, particularly among those most sensitive to career concerns. Consistent with the evidence that heightened anti-Asian sentiment adversely affects mental health and psychological well-being, their forecasts become more pessimistic as well. Moreover, the market responds less strongly to revisions issued by Asian financial analysts, particularly for upward revisions. These findings suggest that racial animus influences not only analysts' forecasting decisions but also the extent to which their information is incorporated into stock prices, with potential implications for market efficiency.

title: Aspirations as Reference Points *
affiliations: Aix-Marseille University - Aix-Marseille School of Economics and University of Strathclyde

detail.title: Aspirations as Reference Points *

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No personal or financial relationship
declarations.funderStatement: Fongoni acknowledges financial support from the French government under the “France 2030” investment plan managed by the French National Research Agency Grant ANR-17-EURE-0020, and by the Excellence Initiative of Aix-Marseille University - A*MIDEX.

detail.abstract: We develop a model of individual effort choice towards the achievement of an outcome, where realised outcomes are compared to an aspiration reference point. We provide sufficient conditions for the dual role of aspirations: moderate aspirations can motivate, but high aspirations can discourage; and for the possibility that aspirations are exactly fulfilled. We then study how this relationship between aspirations and effort interact in a dynamic environment when aspirations are endogenous to one's realised outcomes in the past. We show how traits such as aversion to failure, grit, and ambition can crucially affect the fulfilment of aspirations in the long run, providing a more nuanced and novel perspective on the dual role of aspirations: holding ambitious aspirations can be frustrating, but can also lead to generating strictly better outcomes when individuals particularly dislike failure and have grit in the pursuit of their goals. Finally, we use our framework to explore the welfare implications of aspirations.

title: Cognitive Liberty as Constitutional Autonomy: Mental Privacy, Neural Integrity and the Juridical Protection of the Inner Self

detail.title: Cognitive Liberty as Constitutional Autonomy: Mental Privacy, Neural Integrity and the Juridical Protection of the Inner Self

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. During the preparation of this manuscript, the author used AI-based language and research-assistance tools for drafting support, research organization, literature discovery, analytical structuring, and language refinement; the author critically reviewed, edited, verified, and assumed responsibility for all legal analysis, argumentation, sources, interpretations, data, and conclusions contained in the final manuscript.
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no specific financial support or funding for this research.

detail.abstract: Constitutional and data-protection systems increasingly recognize a right to cognitive liberty, activating heightened protection whenever a technology measures or modulates brain activity. This article argues that the trigger these systems actually use-technological contact with the brain-is doctrinally mismatched to the interest they claim to protect, because it is indifferent to whether the measured signal validly discloses mental content at all. Electroencephalographic and related neural signals vary enormously in inferential specificity, from crude arousal correlates to, in narrow laboratory conditions, reconstructable semantic content; existing frameworks treat all of it as presumptively revelatory once it originates in the skull. Drawing on Chile's constitutional neurorights reform and the Supreme Court's 2023 decision in Girardi v. Emotiv, Spain's 2021 Digital Rights Charter and subsequent data-protection guidance on neurodata, France's 2011/2021 bioethics-law provisions on cerebral-activity intervention and the joint 2026 opinion of the CCNE and CCNEN on brain-computer interfaces, the European Union's data-protection and AI-Act architecture, and the OECD's 2019 Recommendation on Responsible Innovation in Neurotechnology, the article identifies a recurring "inference validity gap": legal instruments name mental privacy as their object but operationalize protection through a technology-contact proxy rather than a measure of decoding validity. This produces simultaneous over-and under-inclusion-trivial arousal metrics receive the same categorical protection as genuine semantic decoding, while non-neural behavioral-inference technologies achieving comparable predictive power over mental states escape scrutiny entirely. The article proposes the Neural Inference Validity Standard (NIVS), a graduated evidentiary framework that calibrates legal consequence to the demonstrated specificity, reliability, and semantic content of a given inference, embedded within-not substituting for-existing constitutional-autonomy and data-protection doctrine. The analysis is doctrinal and comparative; it does not report an empirical study of decoding accuracy but draws on the published record of neurotechnological capability to assess the fit between technological reality and current legal design.

title: Fiscal policy and sectoral spillovers in open-economy HANK
affiliations: Research Department and

detail.title: Fiscal policy and sectoral spillovers in open-economy HANK
detail.abstract: Government spending falls disproportionately on non-tradable services. We show empirically that government spending shocks stimulate private consumption along with sizable spillovers to the goods sector and a relative decline in goods prices. We rationalize these findings with a two-sector open-economy HANK model. Uninsurable income risk and precautionary savings lead to a persistent income-driven expansion in private consumption. In the tradable sector, import intensity and limited labor reallocation dampen wage pass-through to prices, matching observed co-movements. The resulting expenditure switching produces a positive tradable output response despite deteriorating net exports. Household heterogeneity and trade openness jointly shape sectoral fiscal multipliers.

title: Judged in Advance: Legal Outcome Prediction and the Temporal Structure of Adjudication

detail.title: Judged in Advance: Legal Outcome Prediction and the Temporal Structure of Adjudication

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author reports no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

publicationDetails.detailsText: Law, Innovation, and Technology, Volume 19, No 2 (2027)

detail.abstract: What happens when law learns to predict its own future? Systems forecasting judicial outcomes are typically assessed for accuracy and bias. This article argues the challenge is more fundamental: prediction reconfigures adjudication's temporal structure, collapsing the distinction between anticipation and judgment on which law's authority depends. Reconstructing that structure through Hart, Fuller, and Dworkin, it shows each presupposes a diachronic ordering in which conduct precedes judgment and legal meaning is fixed retrospectively through public reasons. Legal outcome prediction inverts that order. Once forecasts circulate as actionable probabilities embedded in case selection, settlement, and strategy, they become operationally prior to judgment, and reason-giving gives way to expectation management. Recent scholarship embracing algorithmic adjudication as textualism's endpoint confirms the trajectory rather than refuting it. The stakes are constitutive, not regulatory: the erosion of temporal openness is an erosion of legal freedom-the space in which one acts first and is judged later.

title: Retail Trading and the Varying Predictive Power of Aggregate Short Interest
affiliations: Binghamton University, , Simon School, University of Rochester and SUNY at Binghamton - School of Management

detail.title: Retail Trading and the Varying Predictive Power of Aggregate Short Interest

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: The authors gratefully acknowledge financial support from Binghamton University, SUNY, and the Simon School at the University of Rochester.

detail.abstract: Prior research identifies aggregate short interest as one of the strongest predictors of aggregate stock market returns. Yet, the informativeness of aggregate short interest ultimately depends on the composition of market participants whose trading activity it reflects, a population that has changed significantly over the past decade. We hypothesize and find that the predictive ability of aggregate short interest has declined significantly over time and that this decline is negatively associated with the concurrent rise in retail investor participation. Additional analyses suggest that retail investor participation affects predictability through two mechanisms: a growing share of retail short selling activity and a greater risk of short squeeze activity. Collectively, our findings highlight the importance of investor composition in shaping the information content of short selling activity and its ability to predict aggregate stock market returns.

detail.abstract: Price subsidies are widely proposed to promote lower-carbon diets, yet real-world evidence on their effects remains scarce, and whether any effect persists once the subsidy is withdrawn is largely untested. Using two natural experiments in university cafeterias, we study the introduction and withdrawal of price subsidies on vegetarian meals, distinguishing temporary price responses from durable behavioural change in a high-frequency, repeated choice setting. One cafeteria introduced a 5% subsidy on vegetarian meals, while another removed a pre-existing 14% subsidy. Analysing over 110,000 meal choices, we find that introducing the subsidy raises vegetarian uptake by 3 percentage points, while removing one reduces it by a comparable amount. In both experiments, responses are concentrated among consumers with more vegetarian baseline diets. Event-study estimates show that behaviour adjusts immediately at each policy change, and we find no evidence of persistence once the subsidy is removed. These findings are more consistent with heterogeneous price responsiveness than with habit formation. Back-of-the-envelope calculations imply an abatement cost of roughly £1,180 per tonne of CO2e, an order of magnitude above standard social cost of carbon estimates and well above comparable non-price interventions such as carbon labelling. Food subsidies thus lower the carbon footprint of diets while incentives are in place, but do not appear to produce lasting behavioural change.

detail.abstract:
This paper gives the formal framework behind Health 4.0: a closed-loop architecture for observing, modeling, and intervening on the health trajectory of each person in a population. Trajectory Engineering (TE) is the set of methods, infrastructures, and governance arrangements required to observe, model, and intervene on the propagation of health and disease through time; its unit of analysis is the individual, its scale the population, and its domains biological, environmental, and cultural. The paper states TE's primitives, assumptions, and operator form as a closed-loop, domain-coupled specification architecture; gives a well-posedness/specification theorem under explicit regularity assumptions; develops an uncertainty-quantification framework with epistemic/aleatory decomposition; and states a corrected K-truncation trajectory-error bound (Proposition 4.1).

The medical application is developed through the MBSAQIP accreditation program in metabolic and bariatric surgery, shown as a worked example of a learning health system that closes the observation-inference-intervention loop, and through the COVID-19 pandemic response. Three further structured case studies (the 2008 financial crisis, coupled climate forecasting, and geopolitical conflict trajectories) show that the same architectural pattern is already standard in adjacent disciplines. The principal analytical claim is that the closed-loop intervention architecture available in those disciplines is also available in medicine, and that the reform program implied by closing the temporal loop, modeling cross-domain coupling rather than zeroing it, and admitting governance as an endogenous variable constitutes the formal substance of Health 4.0: the person-governed system of care, the Health Trajectory Benefit that finances it, and the learning health system that improves it.

This is No. II in The Trajectory Engineering Papers. Papers I, III, and IV are on SSRN (abstracts 6612840, 6784098, 6827879). This version (v1.3, 15 May 2026) is deposited on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20218602; the series roster and persistent identifiers are maintained in the Series Roster Note (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22726698).

detail.abstract: Twenty-five Fields medalists have declared artificial intelligence and mathematics misaligned. I observe that the wait between a mathematical result and its use was in large part transmission: a result reached a use only when someone along the way knew both the problem and the theorem, and a language model can now be that person at every use. In a minimal model of reach, adoption cost, and lag, the value of a marginal result rises by a multiple and the wedge between social and private returns widens. Before language models could match and implement, elementary economics already said underinvestment was likely. If language models remove a substantial part of a delay measured in decades, it becomes very hard to argue that the present level could be optimal, and the observed allocation is moving the other way.

title: The Geoeconomic Role of Sovereign Wealth Funds: Effects on Global Trade
affiliations: UCLA Anderson School of Management and

detail.title: The Geoeconomic Role of Sovereign Wealth Funds: Effects on Global Trade
detail.abstract: Sovereign wealth funds (SWFs) have emerged as potent instruments of geoeconomic strategy. Using comprehensive data on 3,051 private-market deals by 51 SWFs, we show that an initial SWF investment increases its home-country's exports by 9.4%, generating roughly $0.14 in additional annual exports per dollar invested. These gains concentrate in flows from developing to advanced economies, inverting a conventional trade hierarchy.  We establish causality by exploiting the 2018 U.S. Foreign Investment Risk Review Modernization Act, which exogenously diverted SWF capital to non-U.S. destinations, triggering a significant surge in exports.  Crucially, we find no crowding out of other exporters, indicating net trade creation.  Mechanism tests show that SWF stakes act as “credibility bridges” that substitute for weak institutions in the origin country and function most effectively within physically proximate and politically stable trade corridors.

detail.abstract:
The ongoing advancement and adoption of artificial intelligence continues to raise concerns about widespread job losses. Over the past three years, our regional business surveys have asked firms about their AI adoption and its effects on their workforces. This year, we found that AI use among regional businesses has continued to rise sharply, with more than 60 percent of service firms and about half of manufacturers now using AI—a notable increase from 40 percent and 26 percent, respectively, reported in 2025. Despite this rapid adoption, regional firms’ investments in AI are generally modest, usage tends to be concentrated among a small share of workers within firms, and layoffs have remained uncommon. And, while some firms have scaled back hiring due to AI, others have added workers to help them use it. Retraining employees in response to AI remains the primary way firms are adjusting their workforces.

detail.abstract: India's attainment of below-replacement fertility marks a major demographic milestone, yet it presents a paradox when viewed against international experience. In most countries that successfully harnessed a demographic dividend-particularly in East Asia and parts of Europe-fertility decline emerged alongside broad improvements in education, health, women's agency, labour-market opportunities, and structural economic transformation. In contrast, India's fertility transition was unusually rapid, compressed into a few decades, and was driven to a significant extent by state-led family-planning interventions, especially female sterilisation, rather than by comparable advances in human development. This divergence weakened the conventional linkage between fertility decline and socioeconomic transformation.

title: The Carbon Pricing Dilemma: Strategic Change or Strategic Persistence?
affiliations: Satya Wacana Christian University, Curtin University, Curtin University and Curtin University

detail.title: The Carbon Pricing Dilemma: Strategic Change or Strategic Persistence?
detail.abstract: The growing adoption of carbon pricing creates regulatory and financial pressures on firms, yet its implications for the extent of corporate strategic adaptations remain unclear. Drawing on dynamic capabilities and threat-rigidity theories, this study investigates whether carbon pricing induces firms to undertake strategic change or instead reinforces strategic persistence. We exploit the staggered introduction of carbon pricing across 17 Asia-Pacific countries between 2003 and 2023 as a quasi-natural experiment. Our analyses show that carbon pricing is associated with greater strategic change. This effect is concentrated among analyzer firms and those with more versatile resource portfolios. We further identify heightened financial pressure as an important channel through which carbon pricing induces strategic change. Finally, our outcome analysis finds that firms undertaking less strategic change experience a subsequent deterioration in financial performance. Overall, the findings suggest that carbon pricing prompts strategic reconfiguration as a coping response, even under conditions that could otherwise encourage rigidity and persistence.

title: Trader position changes and risk of jet fuel exposure
affiliations: Pusan National University and Sungkyunkwan University

detail.title: Trader position changes and risk of jet fuel exposure
detail.abstract: We examine whether weekly trader position changes in New York Harbor ultra-low-sulfur diesel futures are informative about subsequent realized risk in U.S. Gulf Coast jet fuel. Jet fuel has no liquid futures market and no Commitments of Traders report; ULSD futures serve as the cross-hedge instrument. Across the four trader categories and their reported field sets, we construct nondirectional measures of weekly gross changes in reported positions. After we control for trailing volatility, fuel market conditions, and macrofinancial conditions, the evidence is strongest for the managed money measure based on reported long and short positions. An increase in the measure is followed by higher jet fuel variance and fixed-ratio hedged-residual variance. Both associations remain statistically significant when the outcomes are recomputed after excluding March-May 2020 price changes. Out of sample, the managed money measure lowers mean squared forecast error for jet fuel variance against a persistence model. Hedge ratios conditioned on trader position changes do not significantly reduce mean squared hedged price changes relative to a naive one-for-one benchmark.​

title: Scope 2 Emissions and Financial Performance: Do Location- and Market-based Differences Matter?
affiliations: University of Hamburg - Faculty of Business, Economics, and Social Sciences, University of Edinburgh - Business School and University of Hamburg - Faculty of Business, Economics, and Social Sciences

detail.title: Scope 2 Emissions and Financial Performance: Do Location- and Market-based Differences Matter?
detail.abstract: International carbon accounting standards require firms to report their scope 2 location-based emissions (S2Loc) and/or market-based emissions (S2Mar). However, whether the S2Loc and S2Mar methods accurately reflect firms’ emission profiles and transition risks from purchased energy is contested. We investigate the relationship between firms’ energy-related scope 2 emissions and their operating performance using detailed information on scope 2 emission reporting methods and contractual instruments for a global sample of 1,888 firms between 2018 and 2025.First, we find a significant negative association between S2Loc and operating performance, irrespective of firms’ direct emissions and electricity intensities. Second, changes in S2Mar do not explain systematic differences in operating performance. Third, power purchase agreements (PPAs) can moderate the negative association between S2Loc and operating performance, while standalone renewable energy certificates (RECs) and green energy tariffs cannot. In further analysis, we find that regulatory carbon pricing coverage moderates the association between S2Loc and operating performance for European firms. As an open empirical anomaly, we find that the association between S2Loc and firm valuation measures is significantly positive. Our findings are robust to alternative methodological specifications.Bridging a gap between conceptual and empirical research, our study provides the first comprehensive analysis of the financial relevance of scope 2 emissions. The findings suggest that scope 2 market-based standards mislead rather than help investors to evaluate firms’ energy-related transition risks. Investor-focused standard-setters should therefore treat market-based emissions as optional rather than required.

detail.abstract: Contested cultural practices create identity benefits while imposing external costs. Using respondent-level data from nine waves of the Northern Ireland Life and Times Survey (2016-2024; N = 11,308), this paper distinguishes the cultural legitimacy of July and August bonfires from organiser accountability. Legitimacy is observed in 2016-2024; accountability and joint attitudes in 2016-2022. Only 32-42 per cent regard bonfires as legitimate, whereas 83-93 per cent support accountability; 49-59 per cent support accountability without endorsing legitimacy. Religious and political identity strongly divide legitimacy but much less accountability. The findings show that broad support for organiser accountability can coexist with substantial disagreement over cultural legitimacy, identifying a potential basis for agreement on responsibility for harm.

detail.abstract: This essay looks at the transformation of Vietnam’s steel industry from an import-dependent, construction-led market toward a more integrated domestic production structure. title: Combining Inverse Optimization and Modeling-to-Generate-Alternatives to Reveal Epistemic Uncertainty in Merit-Order Recovery: A Proof of Concept for the Iberian Electricity Market
affiliations: and Delft University of Technology

detail.title: Combining Inverse Optimization and Modeling-to-Generate-Alternatives to Reveal Epistemic Uncertainty in Merit-Order Recovery: A Proof of Concept for the Iberian Electricity Market
detail.abstract: Understanding how electricity prices are formed is important for both market analysis and forward-looking decision-making, especially when the underlying bids and offers cannot be directly observed. This paper develops a three-layer framework that combines market-data clustering, inverse optimization (IO), and modeling to generate alternatives (MGA), enabling the recovery of merit orders from observed market outcomes and the generation of plausible alternatives that capture parametric and structural uncertainties in the recovered market model. The framework addresses four methodological needs: (i) transforming heterogeneous market disclosures into model-ready inputs through two clustering algorithms suited to different data-availability settings; (ii) incorporating electricity-gas price coupling directly into the recovery process to better represent gas-fired bidding behavior; (iii) explicitly modeling multi-zone market clearing so that recovered merit orders capture zonal price formation and interzonal interactions; and (iv) extending the conventional single-solution IO setting with an MGA layer that generates alternative merit orders. As a proof of concept, the framework is demonstrated using 2024 data from the Iberian electricity market, covering Spain and Portugal. Results show that preserving generation-technology information during clustering improves the accuracy of zonal price reproduction by up to 26.97% relative to price-only clustering, while electricity-gas price coupling further improves the accuracy of zonal price reproduction by up to 5.15%. The MGA layer is used to generate alternative merit orders that reveal the uncertainty on the bids of gas-fired generators. These alternative merit orders are subsequently tested under out-of-sample high-gas-price conditions. Overall, the proposed framework extends merit-order recovery beyond static estimation into a more flexible tool for analyzing electricity price formation and exploring the epistemic uncertainty in forward-looking analyses.

title: Industrial Natural Gas Demand in MENA Countries: Bringing CCE-MG into Autometrics
affiliations: King Abdullah Petroleum Studies and Research Center (KAPSARC) and King Abdullah Petroleum Studies and Research Center (KAPSARC)

detail.title: Industrial Natural Gas Demand in MENA Countries: Bringing CCE-MG into Autometrics
detail.abstract: This study examines what drives industrial natural gas demand over the period 1990–2022 in eight gas-producing MENA countries, namely Algeria, Bahrain, Egypt, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (KSA), Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, and United Arab Amirates (UAE). Departing from standard approaches, it employs the Common Correlated Effects Mean Group (CCE-MG) estimator within the Autometrics framework with super saturation. This methodology accounts for cross-country heterogeneity, unobserved common factors, and both temporary and permanent structural breaks, thereby ensuring robust estimation of long- and short-run relationships. The results suggest that the Autometrics-based CCE-MG estimates are more credible than those obtained from standard implementations, both statistically and theoretically.Empirical findings for the panel of these countries indicate that income is the main long-run driver of industrial natural gas demand, with an elasticity slightly above unity, 1.1, implying that demand increases with industrial activity more than proportionally. Own-price effects are statistically significant, although demand remains relatively price-inelastic at –0.30.Country-specific estimations reveal that there is also evidence of substitution between natural gas and electricity and/or diesel in Algeria, Egypt, Oman, and UAE. In addition, common global and regional factors play an important role in the formation of demand for natural gas in the industry sector in Algeria, KSA, Kuwait, and Oman, reflecting shared economic and energy market dynamics among the countries. Error-correction estimates confirm stable long-run relationships between natural gas demand and its determinants and adjustment from market disequilibrium, caused by policy and other shocks, toward equilibrium in all countries.From a policy perspective, continued industrial expansion is likely to exert upward pressure on natural gas demand. Gradual and credible energy price reforms may help contain demand growth. Given the influence of common factors, greater regional coordination in energy policies could also be beneficial. Any policy intervention to the natural gas demand, through prices or other channels, would adjust relatively fast back to the equilibrium level determined by the drivers in KSA, Kuwait, Oman, and UAE. Whereas restoration from such an intervention would take longer time in Algeria, Egypt, Bahrain, and Qatar.
