detail.abstract: With over 63.3 million units employing around 110 million workmen (MSME Ministry, Government of India, 2025) and contributing 45% of the nation’s industrial production (Statista, 2025; SME Chamber of Commerce, 2025), micro, small & medium Enterprises (MSMEs) constitute the bedrock of Indian economy. However, MSMEs face major challenges, especially during the start-up phase with almost 70% mortality within the first ten years of operation (Jamil, 2023; Garcia, 2022). Although several factors contribute to the failure of MSMEs, Governmental policies and regulations are observed to exert significant influence on their functioning. This study aims to study the impact of the key elements of the statutory framework on MSMEs in India. Based on extensive literature review and informal discussions with industry experts, four key elements of the government policy with the most significant impact on MSMEs have been identified as regulatory framework, availability of funds, labor laws and infrastructure. The impact of each of these major elements on the   success or failure of start-up MSMEs have been analyzed based on credible inputs obtained from a carefully selected sample of respondents with relevant experience in the MSME segment. The research is India-centric and across industry segments. While there is considerable study on the impact of statutory policies on large enterprises, the MSME sector and specifically start-ups are largely overlooked. The study aims at addressing this gap. Primary data has been collected using a judicious mix of intensive one-to-one interviews, focus groups discussions and a survey questionnaire for added credibility. A convergent parallel mixed methods approach was adopted to facilitate a comprehensive study of this complex social phenomenon. It leverages the depth of human experience with the statistical breadth of numbers. The data collected was carefully analyzed, major themes and patterns identified and logical conclusions arrived at. The conclusions, apart from generating deep insights, highlight a significant impact of all the four elements studied. It enables us to recommend realistic strategies to decrease mortality and stimulate healthy growth of MSMEs.

detail.abstract:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as an important technological force influencing production, employment, productivity and economic growth. The increasing adoption of AI is changing the way firms produce goods and services, organise work and develop human capital. For a developing economy such as India, AI provides opportunities for productivity enhancement, innovation and new employment, but it may also create challenges through automation, occupational restructuring and skill gaps. 

The present study examines the role of Artificial Intelligence in employment transformation and economic growth in India through a descriptive, conceptual and analytical approach based on published secondary sources. The study draws upon reports and publications of the International Labour Organization, International Monetary Fund, World Bank, OECD, NITI Aayog and Government of India institutions. The analysis focuses on AI adoption, productivity, employment transformation, human capital, digital development, sectoral opportunities and economic challenges. No primary survey data are used, and no numerical observations are invented or simulated.

 The study indicates that AI has considerable potential to improve productivity, support innovation and contribute to economic growth. At the same time, its employment effects are likely to differ across occupations, sectors and skill groups. The economic benefits of AI therefore depend strongly on human capital, digital infrastructure, reskilling, institutional preparedness and equitable access to technology. The study argues that India's AI strategy should focus not only on technological adoption but also on inclusive employment transformation, productivity enhancement and human-capital development.

title: The Context-Dependent Organizational Persona: Why the Same Organization Displays Different Behavioral Faces Across Domains, Threats, and Key Persons

detail.abstract:
Organizations are often described through relatively stable characterizations such as trustworthy, bureaucratic, defensive, or employee-oriented. Yet the same organization may behave differently across customer relations, personnel management, internal criticism, crisis response, and other domains. This paper develops the concept of the Context-Dependent Organizational Persona (CDOP) to explain why different behavioral faces of the same organization become salient under different conditions.

CDOP conceptualizes organizational persona not as a single fixed attribute but as a repertoire of historically and institutionally formed behavioral tendencies. Which tendency becomes dominant depends on the configuration of domain, threat appraisal, key-person involvement, symbolic capital, relational networks, institutional history, and latent interests. The framework integrates research on within-person variability and trait activation, multiple and adaptive organizational identities, threat-rigidity, organizational defensive routines, resource dependence, upper echelons, organizational imprinting, and the behavioral theory of the firm.

The model further proposes that a coherent organizational persona can emerge without unified intent. Different actors may seek to protect different objects, such as self-image, operational continuity, procedural consistency, prior decisions, or institutional legitimacy. When these locally rational defensive actions converge in the same direction, they may collectively generate an observable organizational pattern of dialogue, formalization, avoidance, sanction, or defensive distancing. Once expressed, such patterns may be incorporated into organizational memory and precedent, thereby altering the conditions under which similar personas are activated in the future.

The central argument is that organizational persona should be understood not only by asking what an organization is, but also under what conditions it becomes what it becomes. CDOP therefore shifts analysis from static organizational labels toward the conditions that activate particular organizational behavioral expressions.

detail.abstract: This study replicates Merkoulova and Veld (2022) in a cross-border regional context by examining whether stock return ignorance (SRI)-the inability to make return predictions, to answer questions about the distribution of expected returns or to reveal unlikely beliefs about distributions-is associated with stock market participation and investment intensity in Tyrol (Austria) and South Tyrol (Italy). Further, this study investigates whether these two regions differ in stock return ignorance and investment behaviour, and whether any regional differences in investment behaviour can be explained by stock return ignorance, financial literacy, and sociodemographic characteristics. Using quantitative data from 151 adults, the results show that SRI is highly prevalent but not a robust predictor of stock market participation or investment intensity. By contrast, financial literacy was positively associated with stock market participation; specifically, each additional correct answer was associated with roughly 30% higher odds of owning stocks.

detail.abstract: When the Bundeskartellamt was handed the world's first bespoke competition toolkit against the largest digital platforms in January 2021, it was billed as a genuine breakthrough. Section 19a of the Act against Restraints of Competition (GWB) allows the authority to designate a company as being "of paramount significance for competition across markets" and then, without first having to prove market dominance or actual harm in the traditional sense, prohibit specific conduct-such as self-preferencing or data leveraging-before the damage is done. To speed up things, the legislator even replaced the normal two-tier system of judicial review with a single-instance appeal. Five years, a single prohibition decision and a fresh legislative reform later, it is worth asking how far that promise has been realised.

title:
Testing Fama-French Factors in a Thin Market:

Evidence from NGX-Listed Banks

detail.title:
Testing Fama-French Factors in a Thin Market:

Evidence from NGX-Listed Banks

detail.abstract:
We test whether standard asset-pricing factors, including market risk, company size, value, and a Nigeria-specific liquidity measure, explain the returns of Nigerian Exchange (NGX)-listed banks and related financial firms. Using a 17-firm sample over 46 months (2022–2026), we examine these effects through two approaches: portfolio strategies and regression loadings.

The regression results indicate that bank returns move closely with the broader market and, to a lesser extent, with company size. A liquidity effect is present but only marginally significant, and we find no evidence of a value effect. However, when we test the same relationships as tradeable strategies, buying illiquid, small, or high-book-to-market stocks while shorting the opposites, none of the resulting spreads earns a statistically meaningful return. A further robustness check using an alternative liquidity measure, the Amihud illiquidity ratio, weakens rather than strengthens the liquidity result.

Our central finding is that factor loadings and factor premia can diverge in this market. A factor may exhibit significant covariation with stock returns without generating a positive return when implemented as a trading strategy. We treat this divergence as our primary result.

title: Modular Execution, Sticky Accountability: Firm Scope and Value Capture under Agentic AI
affiliations: and The Mirandola Institute

detail.title: Modular Execution, Sticky Accountability: Firm Scope and Value Capture under Agentic AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract:
Agentic artificial intelligence changes firm boundaries by increasing productive modularity faster than accountability modularity. Execution can be decomposed and externalized, while responsibility for consequential work may remain attached to the focal firm. This paper develops a strategy theory of that lag. The central mechanism is boundary decoupling: execution moves outward while accountability remains sticky. The central hazard is institutional verification failure, which arises when a firm remains answerable for AI-mediated work it cannot reconstruct, explain, correct, or credibly defend.

The paper introduces accountable-scale capability: the capability to increase AI-mediated execution volume in high-accountability workflows without proportional increases in governance cost or residual risk. It is constituted by evidence architecture, accountable judgment routines, and remediation-and-standing capacity. The theory predicts that firms using similar AI technologies will differ in scope, failure-adjusted workflow scale, vendor bargaining power, strategic-group position, and value capture.

The paper’s distinctive claim is dynamic. Accountability-based advantage depends on how long productive modularity outruns accountability modularity in a sector. As assurance markets, certification regimes, statutory duties, and provider obligations mature, accountability does not disappear; it re-anchors in actors with portable assurance capacity, formal duty, or institutional standing. Evidence-architecture rents should erode faster than judgment and standing rents, and accountable firms may gain bargaining power over AI vendors when standing is the scarce access good. Under agentic AI, scalable execution may become generic; scalable accountability does not.

title: Analyzing the Impact of Real-World Propagation Environments on Beamspace Channel Estimation for 5G mmWave Communications
affiliations: and

detail.title: Analyzing the Impact of Real-World Propagation Environments on Beamspace Channel Estimation for 5G mmWave Communications

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests relevant to this work.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific external funding and was supported solely by the author's institutional resources.

detail.abstract: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) communications, a cornerstone of fifth-generation (5G) New Radio and beyond, rely heavily on accurate channel state information to realize the promised gains of massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) beamforming and spatial multiplexing. Beamspace channel estimation, enabled by metallic lens antenna arrays, has emerged as an energy-efficient solution that exploits the inherent sparsity of mmWave propagation to reduce the dimensionality of the channel estimation problem. While extensive research has demonstrated the theoretical effectiveness of beamspace estimation algorithms under idealized channel models-typically assuming single-cluster line-of-sight or simplified clustered delay-line configurations-the impact of real-world propagation environments on estimation performance remains critically underexplored. Real-world mmWave channels are characterized by complex phenomena including dynamic human blockage, vehicular mobilityinduced Doppler shifts, atmospheric attenuation, rainfall fading, foliage scattering, and multipath richness that violates the conventional sparsity assumptions. These environmental factors introduce time-varying sparsity patterns, beam misalignment, beam squint effects across wide bandwidths, and non-stationary channel statistics that fundamentally alter the performance landscape of beamspace estimation techniques. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the impact of real-world propagation environments on beamspace channel estimation performance for 5G mmWave communications. We develop a realistic simulation framework that integrates statistical channel modeling with empirical ray-tracing data from urban microcellular, urban macrocellular, and indoor hotspot deployment scenarios, incorporating dynamic environmental effects including pedestrian blockage, vehicular traffic, and meteorological conditions. Using this framework, we systematically evaluate the performance degradation of both conventional compressed sensing-based algorithms (orthogonal matching pursuit, iterative shrinkage-thresholding algorithm) and state-of-the-art deep learning-based estimation approaches across diverse environmental conditions. Our results reveal that environmental complexity causes severe performance degradation, with normalized mean-square error increasing by up to 8.5 dB in dense urban environments compared to idealized line-of-sight scenarios. Human blockage events trigger sudden drops in estimation accuracy of up to 70%, with recovery times lagging behind channel coherence by 15-30 ms. Rain attenuation at intensities above 25 mm/hour degrades estimation performance by over 4 dB. We further demonstrate that the sparsity levels assumed in conventional beamspace designs (typically 3-5 dominant paths) are frequently violated in rich scattering environments where 12-15 paths carry significant energy, invalidating the compressed sensing foundation. The analysis identifies that beam squint effects across 100 MHz bandwidth cause additional estimation errors of 2-3 dB that are unaccounted for in narrowband channel models. Deep learning-based approaches exhibit greater robustness to environmental variations than compressed sensing algorithms but suffer from catastrophic performance degradation when tested on channels with propagation characteristics unseen during training. We quantify the generalization gap of neural network-based estimators as a function of environmental diversity in the training dataset. Based on these findings, we propose environmental-aware adaptation strategies including dynamic sparsity estimation, adaptive measurement matrix design, and transfer learning frameworks for rapid adaptation to changing propagation conditions. Our analysis provides critical insights for the practical deployment of beamspace channel estimation in real-world 5G networks, challenging the prevailing assumption that sparse estimation algorithms designed under idealized conditions will maintain efficacy in operational environments. The findings underscore the necessity of environmentally robust channel estimation frameworks and establish the performance bounds that practical systems must address to achieve reliable mmWave communication in dynamic urban environments.

title: The Long Term Effects of School Prayer
affiliations: University of Cambridge,  and University of Cambridge

detail.title: The Long Term Effects of School Prayer
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether school prayer and Bible reading affect adult beliefs and behavior. We exploit the U.S. Supreme Court’s early-1960s school-prayer decisions, which removed these practices only from states where they were still legal. Linking this state-by-cohort variation to adult outcomes in the General Social Survey, we estimate the long-run effects of removing school prayer on religiosity, family formation, labor market outcomes, gender attitudes, and social views. The abolition of school prayer lowers adult religiosity; reduces marriage and fertility; increases employment; and shifts gender and selected social attitudes in a less traditional direction. The employment effect is driven by women, and may operate partly through decreased full-time homemaking and less traditional gender roles. A decomposition indicates that school prayer bans explain more than half the decline in American religious attendance, and roughly one quarter of the decline in fertility and rise in female labor force participation. The findings show that even brief daily devotional practices in childhood can shape adult beliefs, family life, and economic behavior.

title: AI’s Role in Gender Diversity: A New Era for Corporate Leadership

detail.abstract:
Gender diversity in corporate boardrooms remains a persistent challenge despite decades of regulation, from European quotas to the United Kingdom’s comply or explain model. Traditional appointment processes, shaped by opaque networks and entrenched bias, reproduce homogeneity and limit women’s access to leadership. This paper examines Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a data-driven, merit-focused mechanism for identifying and evaluating candidates. Through doctrinal and thematic analysis, it argues AI can mitigate bias and broaden candidate pools, though its value depends on enforceable oversight against automating existing inequalities. The paper does not argue that AI should be mandated. It argues that where a company elects to

use AI to identify, assess, or shortlist candidates, that use should trigger mandatory safeguards, namely disclosure in the annual

report, an annual fairness assessment incorporating a data protection impact assessment, a right to a reasoned explanation

of adverse decisions, and independent algorithmic review under an AI Review Clause. Beyond these safeguards, it supports

disclosure obligations that encourage responsible adoption without compelling it. Locating these duties in the UK Corporate

Governance Code, Companies Act 2006, Equality Act 2010, and UK GDPR, the paper concludes that AI, so governed, can credibly advance gender diversity while preserving board independence and accountability.

detail.abstract: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) in its Fifth Assessment Report from 2014[1] highlighted the disproportionate impact of climate change on low-income and marginalised groups. It outlined how climate vulnerability is exacerbated by entrenched socioeconomic, political, and cultural structures, besides the obvious escalating environmental shocks and stresses. This article evokes the Rawlsian principles of justice and critically analyses procedural and distributive justice within public-sector and multilateral mechanisms that prevent the scaling up of climate finance. Both procedural and distributive justice emphasise equitable distribution. While the former calls for equitable power in making decisions, the latter advocates for equitable distribution of benefits and costs, thus facilitating the participation of marginalised groups[4]. This article highlights the systemic inefficiencies or challenges within public-sector climate finance highlighting the processes that undermine procedural fairness, and distributive justice.

detail.abstract: Digital gold products promise to combine the monetary and investment characteristics of physical gold with the accessibility, divisibility, and transferability of digital platforms. Yet the credibility of these products cannot be established solely through blockchain records, price tracking, or reserve disclosures. A more demanding test is whether a holder can convert a digital claim into the underlying physical asset under clearly defined, operationally feasible, and legally enforceable conditions. This article develops a conceptual framework for understanding physical redemption as a critical credibility signal in digital gold markets. Drawing on the literature on stablecoin runs, commodity-backed digital assets, allocated and unallocated precious-metal accounts, tokenized real-world assets, and market microstructure, it argues that redemption performs four distinct functions. First, it anchors the digital claim to an external non-digital reference asset. Second, it disciplines issuer behavior by exposing discrepancies between token supply and physical inventory. Third, it supports secondary-market price formation through arbitrage. Fourth, it transforms an abstract promise of backing into a testable ownership claim. However, the existence of a nominal redemption clause is insufficient. Credibility depends on the entire redemption architecture: legal title, allocation of bars, custody, auditability, minimum redemption size, fees, geographic restrictions, settlement time, operational capacity, and the issuer’s ability to perform during stress. The article distinguishes between formal redeemability and economically meaningful redeemability and proposes a Redemption Credibility Index based on six dimensions. It concludes that physical delivery should be treated not as a supplementary product feature but as a core market-infrastructure mechanism. Digital gold platforms seeking durable trust should therefore design redemption as a measurable, continuously monitored, and independently verifiable process.

detail.abstract: The price of 18-karat gold in Iran is frequently interpreted as a direct reflection of the international gold price. This interpretation is incomplete. Domestic 18-karat gold prices are jointly determined by the international gold benchmark, the exchange rate between the US dollar and the Iranian rial, domestic inflation, market liquidity, expectations, transaction costs, and institutional conditions. The interaction between these variables creates a pricing structure in which exchange-rate dynamics may dominate global gold movements, particularly during periods of currency depreciation and elevated uncertainty. This article develops an analytical framework for understanding the price formation of 18-karat gold in Iran. It first derives the theoretical relationship between the international gold price, exchange rate, and domestic purity-adjusted gold price. It then examines the role of inflation, real interest rates, oil prices, monetary conditions, sanctions-related uncertainty, market segmentation, and behavioral expectations. The article also distinguishes between the theoretical bullion value of 18-karat gold and the retail price of jewelry, which includes manufacturing charges, dealer margins, taxes, and other market-specific components. The central argument is that the domestic price of 18-karat gold should be modeled as a multidimensional price system rather than as a simple translation of the global gold price. For research and practical valuation, changes in the exchange rate, international gold returns, domestic inflation, and market spreads should be analyzed jointly. The framework proposed here can support more transparent pricing, improved risk management, and more disciplined interpretation of gold-market signals.

detail.abstract: Canada has spent three decades constructing a dense architecture of innovation and productivity programs, yet its business sector productivity gap with the United States has widened substantially. This article asks, "why policy-supported capital, knowledge, and commercially viable firms do not reliably propagate into aggregate productivity?" Organizing Canadian and comparative evidence around an interdependent pipeline, it identifies three necessary economic conversion gates: productive investment to effective technology adoption, technical discovery to recurring commercial revenue, and commercial viability to economic scale and resource reallocation. The central argument of the article is that the aggregate impact of a policy intervention is constrained by these conversion points which hold back otherwise promising developments. For policy applications, the article proposes a five-question intervention diagnostic screen that any intervention should satisfy, a three-layer architecture for the specific intervention, and long-term evaluation designs that measure sustained productivity and market outcomes.

title: Comparative Analysis of AI-based and Compressive Sensing Techniques for Beamspace Channel Estimation in 5G mmWave Systems

detail.title: Comparative Analysis of AI-based and Compressive Sensing Techniques for Beamspace Channel Estimation in 5G mmWave Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests relevant to this work.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific external funding and was supported solely by the author's institutional resources.

detail.abstract: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) technology forms the bedrock of fifth-generation (5G) wireless networks, delivering exceptional data throughput through large-scale antenna arrays and abundant high-frequency spectrum. Beamspace channel estimation has emerged as a pivotal technique to mitigate the prohibitive pilot overhead and computational burden associated with conventional channel estimation in massive MIMO configurations, leveraging the inherent sparsity of mmWave propagation channels. Traditional approaches to beamspace channel estimation have predominantly relied on compressive sensing (CS) algorithms, such as Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP) and its variants, which exploit channel sparsity to reconstruct the channel from a reduced set of measurements. In parallel, the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning methodologies has introduced new paradigms for channel estimation, offering the potential for enhanced accuracy, reduced computational complexity, and improved robustness to non-ideal channel conditions. This paper presents a comprehensive comparative analysis of AI-based and compressive sensing techniques for beamspace channel estimation in 5G mmWave massive MIMO systems. The investigation employs the 3D metallic plate lens antenna architecture as the beamspace transformation mechanism, with the statistical channel modeling framework capturing realistic mmWave propagation characteristics including multipath effects, power leakage, and varying sparsity conditions. Three CS algorithms-Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP), Generalized Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (gOMP), and Compressive Sampling Matching Pursuit (CoSaMP)-are systematically compared against a deep learning-based approach utilizing a fully connected neural network architecture trained to map received pilot signals to beamspace channel estimates. Performance evaluation considers multiple metrics including normalized mean square error (NMSE), spectral efficiency, computational complexity during both training and inference phases, and robustness to channel impairments such as power leakage and noise. Simulation results reveal that AI-based approaches achieve superior estimation accuracy under ideal training conditions, with NMSE improvements of 3-6 dB over CS-based methods at moderate SNR levels. However, the CSbased algorithms demonstrate significantly better generalization to unseen channel conditions and sparsity levels, maintaining consistent performance across a wide range of propagation environments. The AI-based approach exhibits notable performance degradation when tested on channels with sparsity characteristics or power leakage profiles that deviate from the training distribution, highlighting the critical challenge of generalization in data-driven methods. In terms of computational efficiency, CS algorithms offer superior performance during the inference phase with substantially lower latency, while AI-based approaches require significant offline training but enable rapid real-time estimation once trained. The findings also reveal that hybrid approaches, combining CS-based support detection with AI-based coefficient refinement, achieve a favorable balance between accuracy and robustness across diverse channel conditions. This investigation provides essential design guidelines for the selection of beamspace channel estimation techniques in 5G systems, demonstrating that while AI-based methods offer compelling performance benefits in controlled environments, CSbased approaches provide superior reliability and generalization in the complex, dynamic propagation scenarios encountered in practical mmWave deployments. The results underscore the importance of considering both accuracy and robustness when selecting channel estimation strategies, and suggest that future systems may benefit from adaptive architectures that leverage the complementary strengths of both paradigms.

title: A New AAA Supply Chain Model for Ultra-Fresh Fashion with Tariff Uncertainty
affiliations: Cornell University - Samuel Curtis Johnson Graduate School of Management, Stanford Graduate School of Business and Monash Business School, Monash University

detail.title: A New AAA Supply Chain Model for Ultra-Fresh Fashion with Tariff Uncertainty

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest. We have no financial or personal relationships with other people or organizations that could influence this study.

detail.abstract: Supply chain management has become increasingly challenging due to the turbulence of natural and manmade disruptions, as well as the geopolitical frictions of tariff wars and trade restrictions. The classic Triple-A Supply Chain concept (referred to as "AAA" henceforth, standing for Agility, Adaptability and Alignment) has been a cornerstone of effective supply chain management in the literature. With the turbulence of recent times, we reexamine an extended new AAA concept to see how companies should develop supply chain strategies that could be agile, adaptable and aligned. We use the ultra-fresh fashion sector as a case in point, since tariffs have been viewed as detrimental to ultra-fresh fashion companies. We capture the operational representation of the new AAA via three key model parameters. First, higher agility would mean a lower cost to design and make a variant of a product, enabling an agile process to have more product variety and more frequent launches of new products. Second, higher adaptability is modeled as a lower cost to operate a reconfigured supply chain for order fulfillment, making such reconfiguration more cost affordable. Third, more alignment is modeled as the firm giving more weight to reducing the environmental externality cost in the business objective that balances profit and sustainability. Our model analysis reveals managerial insights about how the AAA capabilities affect the firm's supply chain reconfiguration strategy, its resilience against tariff uncertainty, as well as the stakeholder impacts from the reconfiguration. Our findings suggest that companies must consider the interactive nature of AAA in seeking the right supply chain strategy, instead of pursuing the three A's independently. Moreover, the AAA capabilities can have differential stakeholder impacts in terms of economic, social, and environmental gains or losses.

title: Stocks as Time-Varying Investment States: Cross-Ticker Similarity, Dynamic Allocation, and the Limits of Predictive Transfer

detail.title: Stocks as Time-Varying Investment States: Cross-Ticker Similarity, Dynamic Allocation, and the Limits of Predictive Transfer

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: A stock is a persistent legal entity but not a persistent investment opportunity. This paper represents equities as time-varying stock-time states and asks whether similarity across companies supports predictive transfer and adaptive allocation. The analysis uses 4,597 stock-time observations for 30 U.S.-listed equities, 16 price-and market-state variables, and a 63-trading-day forward log-return target under walk-forward label maturity. In the raw historical pool, the nearest cross-ticker state is closer than the nearest same-ticker state in 93.3% of 2,562 comparable cases. That result is strongly affected by candidate availability: after matching the number of cross-ticker candidates to the available same-ticker history, the corresponding probability is 40.4% (95% moving-block interval 38.7-42.0%). Same-ticker observations also appear 1.60 times as often among the 30 nearest pooled states as their share of the eligible history would predict. Thus a large cross-sectional pool supplies many close analogues, while ticker identity retains measurable local structure. Predictive transfer is weaker. At k = 30, same-ticker kNN has MAE 14.14%, versus 14.60% for cross-ticker-only and 14.64% for pooled kNN; the paired sameminus-cross 95% interval is [-1.03, 0.09] percentage points. On the common 2,549-row sample, a pooled historical-mean forecast has lower MAE (13.71%) than any of the three kNN rules, and moving-block intervals for monthly cross-sectional rank correlations all include zero. A separate Bayesian-Thompson incremental-allocation demonstration produces a 39.58% time-weighted CAGR versus 39.63% for equal-weight dollar-cost averaging, with a modestly smaller maximum drawdown (-36.61% versus-39.38%). Because the 30-stock universe is ex-post selected and not survivorship-free, these portfolio returns are descriptive rather than evidence of alpha. The evidence supports a narrower methodological conclusion: state representation, local similarity, and return predictability are distinct objects. A more defensible next model is hierarchical partial pooling that learns how much information to share across state similarity and ticker identity.

detail.abstract: This paper asks whether the Italian stock market prices the acts of capital-goods incentive policy (Transizione 4.0, Transizione 5.0, Nuova Transizione 5.0) when they are issued, and whether a large language model (LLM) reading those acts can extract a signal that the market incorporates with a lag. A corpus of 37 legislative and administrative acts between April 2019 and June 2026 is coded manually and, independently and blind, by an LLM; concordance is near-complete on category and date, substantial on intensity and moderate on expected sign. A market-model event study on 30 directional events and a two-tier basket of eight Euronext Milan stocks (domestic users of incentivised assets and suppliers of eligible capital goods) finds no abnormal return after the event under any coding: signed CAAR of +0.09% on [+1, +5] and +0.39% on [0, +5] under the manual coding, both indistinguishable from zero; a publication-day estimate of +0.29% that does not survive multiple-testing correction, the Corrado rank test, the Kolari-Pynnönen cross-correlation adjustment, the clustering of overlapping acts or the LLM coding. The result holds at the political-announcement date, is robust to estimation windows, basket composition and a survivorship control, and has a minimum detectable effect of about 1.5%. A post hoc hypothesis that the direction of acts follows the sector cycle is rejected on machine-tool orders and on official Eurostat data: the direction of an act is explained by its administrative nature (industrial policy versus spending control). The contribution is a documented negative result on a source of unstructured open data not covered by the financial text-mining literature.

detail.abstract: The purpose of this paper is to systematically review and analyse the adoption of IFRS S1 and S2, which were introduced by the International Sustainability Standard Board in 2023. By examining the peer-reviewed academic research papers in the SCOPUS Q1 journals from 2023 to 2025, this paper aims to examine key themes, methodologies and theories used, including key findings and directions for further research. 96 articles were received from the initial search, and 30 articles met the inclusion criteria with the PRISMA guidelines. Keywords analysis identified the ten research clusters related to sustainability reporting, assurance, auditing perspectives, legitimacy, and adoption in emerging countries. The review identified that quantitative methodology was dominantly used, and legitimacy theory, institution theory, and voluntary disclosure theory were the most frequently used. Findings suggest that this standard becomes a global baseline; however, there are a few deficiencies in its adoption, such as in assurance mechanisms, integration into double materiality concepts, and adoption by SMEs and emerging countries. Future research is suggested in the areas of assurance mechanisms, expertise development requirements for standards adoption, and insights from context-based adoption in emerging countries. This review contributes to understanding the early adoption experiences of the first two sustainability standards, highlighting their integration into dynamic corporate reporting practices.

detail.abstract: Government-supported finance programmes are intended to expand credit access among enterprises underserved by conventional financial institutions, but whether such support reaches particular types of firms and translates into improved enterprise performance remains unclear. Evidence on these questions is particularly limited in Sierra Leone. This study examines programme access and subsequent enterprise outcomes using panel data on 378 small and mediumsized enterprises observed between 2021 and 2023 in the context of the Munafa Fund. Probit estimates show little systematic differentiation in programme access across observed firm and owner characteristics. Firm fixed-effects estimates find no significant association between Fund access and revenue, profit, employment, or business expansion. Propensity-score matching produces a similar pattern for revenue, profit, and employment. The relationship varies, however, by financial literacy. Fund access is more favourably associated with revenue, employment, and business expansion among financially literate firms, while the difference is not statistically significant for profit. The findings suggest that expanding access to government-supported finance alone may not generate broad-based enterprise gains when firms differ in their capacity to manage and deploy financial resources.

title: From Static Composition to Dynamic Make-Up: Industrial Adaptation of Ceramic–Steel Media in Secondary Grinding

detail.title: From Static Composition to Dynamic Make-Up: Industrial Adaptation of Ceramic–Steel Media in Secondary Grinding
detail.abstract: Steel and ceramic grinding media differ markedly in density and loss characteristics, so a laboratory-optimized charge composition may not translate directly into an industrial make-up strategy. Seven ceramic:steel mass ratios were screened in batch grinding tests, and 5:5 gave the highest technical grinding efficiency (87.91%). The result was then evaluated during an approximately two-month industrial trial. Daily 1:1 make-up (500 kg steel and 500 kg ceramic) did not provide sustained improvement, while retaining the 1:1 ratio with additions every other day also failed to restore grinding performance, with technical grinding efficiency decreasing to 47.66%. The strategy was subsequently changed to daily additions of 500 kg steel and 300 kg ceramic media. Grinding performance recovered and reached a maximum monitored efficiency of 70.90%. Under stabilized mixed-media operation, the −15 μm product fraction decreased from 33.85% to 27.33%, while the −74 μm fraction remained 87.17%. Average mill power was 1927.82 kW during the all-steel monitoring period and 1136.91 kW during stabilized mixed-media operation. These results show that charge composition, make-up ratio and addition frequency should be considered separately when mixed grinding media are transferred from laboratory tests to continuous industrial operation.

title: Seven Presumptions Associated with the Mistaken Equity-Efficiency Paradigm (MEEP)

detail.title: Seven Presumptions Associated with the Mistaken Equity-Efficiency Paradigm (MEEP)

detail.abstract: The equity-efficiency trade-off provides economists with a useful way to recognize that changes in distribution can affect incentives, saving, investment, labor supply, and productive performance. These mechanisms can generate genuine equity-efficiency trade-offs. The problem arises when contingent findings acquire broader presumptive force. I call the resulting orientation the Mistaken Equity-Efficiency Paradigm (MEEP). In its minimal form, MEEP combines two presumptions: greater equity ordinarily carries an efficiency cost, while substantial economic concentration performs important productive functions. Strong-form MEEP adds a third proposition: gains attributed to concentration diffuse sufficiently broadly to support a claim of wider economic benefit. I identify seven analytically distinct presumptions associated with MEEP and organize them into three Core Presumptions-Concentration, Equity-Cost, and Diffusion-and four Derived Presumptions-Growth-First, Necessity, Burden-of-Proof, and Concentration-Tolerance. The list is not intended to exhaust every presumption that may be associated with MEEP. Rather, each proposition warrants separate treatment because it makes a distinct claim, requires evidence not supplied automatically by the others, and can in principle succeed or fail independently. Productive contribution does not establish necessity; a particular equity cost does not establish a generalized negative relationship; growth does not establish diffusion; and diffusion does not establish that concentration caused the underlying gain or that the resulting distribution is comparatively preferable. The decomposition therefore converts a bundled orientation into separately testable propositions and supports an open-sign approach in which the relevant criterion, counterfactual, mechanism, and evidence determine the equity-efficiency relationship.

title: Strictness versus Caution: The Fair Share Condition as an Instrument in AI Competition Law

detail.title: Strictness versus Caution: The Fair Share Condition as an Instrument in AI Competition Law

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract:
Competition law's fair share condition, whether under Article 101(3) TFEU or section 9(1) of the Competition Act 1998, asks which benefits count toward an exemption. The debate over that question has run for two decades without terminating, because it has been conducted as an argument about what competition law is ultimately for, a register in which no criterion decides between rival premises. This article proposes a different register, adapted from a study of situs rules in the taxation of digital assets: treat a fair share rule not as a claim about the nature of a benefit but as an instrument, a function taking an agreement and returning the benefits that count. Recast that way, five candidate rules drawn from the Competition and Markets Authority, the European Commission, and the Netherlands Authority for Consumers and Markets become specifications of one instrument, comparable along three axes (whose benefit, what kind of benefit, and which quantity stands as the benefit) and four structural properties (exhaustiveness, determinacy, robustness, and registrability). A previously unexamined temporal sub-axis, whether the beneficiary class extends to persons not yet born, cuts across all five candidates and is confronted by none.

The instrument is tested against a case study in coordinated pre-deployment safety evaluation among frontier artificial intelligence developers, an arrangement whose asserted benefit, a reduced probability of catastrophic harm, accrues overwhelmingly outside the market and to future persons. The case separates the candidates cleanly and shows why markets in frontier capability development reliably generate inputs of this shape. Three propositions follow: that a rule's performance depends on what it returns rather than its doctrinal provenance; that robustness and registrability trade off in a way no candidate escapes; and that under-inclusion, not over-inclusion, is the fair share condition's more dangerous error, since an over-inclusive rule generates its own litigants and pressure for correction while an under-inclusive rule produces an agreement that is never made, and so no litigant at all. The inversion runs against the field's received instinct and, on the terms of its own error-cost framework, against Easterbrook's classical case for under-enforcement.

title: Tax-Rate Risk: Pricing and Hedging Legislative Uncertainty in After-Tax Portfolios

detail.title: Tax-Rate Risk: Pricing and Hedging Legislative Uncertainty in After-Tax Portfolios

detail.abstract:
Almost every tax-aware calculation in wealth management assumes today's capital-gains rate persists until the investor sells. Statute says otherwise: the top US long-term rate has moved between 15% and 28% five times since 1978, and the scheduled sunset of current law keeps the question live. Deferring a gain is therefore not a free option. It converts a tax liability known at today's rate into one owed at an unknown future rate. We show that holding an unrealized gain is economically a short position in the future tax rate, and we price it.

A two-date result gives the deferral advantage in closed form, Delta = g0*(tau0*e^{rho T} - tau_T), and a certainty-equivalent haircut for rate uncertainty equal to (gamma/2)*g0^2*Var[tau_T], quadratic in the embedded gain. We then embed the realization decision in a continuous-time regime-switching model and solve the resulting optimal-stopping problem via its Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman variational inequality. Under constant or mean-reverting rates the investor never voluntarily realizes a gain, recovering the Constantinides (1983, 1984) tax-timing policy. Under a risk-neutral rate drift above a computable threshold the free boundary opens and the optimal policy accelerates realizations, with the trigger given by a single inequality: realize when the risk-neutral expected future rate exceeds today's rate grossed up by compounding.

Calibrating the regimes loosely to the historical US rate path (illustrative, fixed seed), we find mean reversion barely dents the deferral benefit, while an upward drift erodes it and can reverse it for short-horizon or low-return positions. The largest, lowest-basis holdings carry the most rate risk, since both the benefit and the risk scale with the embedded gain, the risk faster. The practical hedge is realization timing itself, which the stopping policy delivers.

title: A Nazi, an HR Manager, a Compliance Officer and Hannah Arendt Walk Into a Bar | Legality as Alibi and the Limits of the Compliance Function

detail.abstract:
A man works nine years at the gate of a large organisation. He is employed by a contractor. Until the week the contract began, the organisation paid fifty thousand shillings a month for the same work done by its own employee; it now pays the contractor forty thousand, of which the man receives twenty. One evening he is told that his job is under review. He has not eaten since the morning. He walks the twelve kilometres home, as he does every day, and is killed on the road.
Nobody broke any rule. This article asks who killed him.

It puts the question to each of the ten people whose decisions bore on the death — the board, the consultants who recommended a leaner structure, the procurement officer who awarded on price, the lawyer who passed the standard clause without comment, the operations manager, the supervisor, the personnel officer, the compliance officer — and finds that every one is acquitted on ordinary principles of individual responsibility. That result is the article's starting point rather than its failure. The arrangement produced a death that no participant caused, using instruments each of which is lawful and has a good reason to exist.

The article's central claim concerns how this is survivable for the people who operate it. A compliance function holds wage orders, filing deadlines, licensing requirements and working-time limits. Every one of these marks the point at which conduct becomes an offence, and none of them says what is owed to anybody. An organisation in full compliance has therefore established only that it is not, on any tested measure, a criminal. What the function supplies its officers is not principally a rule to follow but a true sentence to say — he was not our employee; the obligation was contracted to a licensed provider; there was no material non-compliance — and the sentence arrives in the place where a judgement about the man would otherwise have had to be formed, which is why it never is.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a deterministic, non-prescriptive accountability architecture based on bounded multi-signal coherence assessment and multi-party verified outcomes. The framework formalizes a coherence function over structured signal sets within discrete temporal windows; a required-verifier-set primitive under which no outcome is established by a single source and the party the outcome belongs to is always a required verifier; and a deterministic translation of bounded conditions into governance states. It extends the same verification discipline to the cost of delivered outcomes (establishing what an outcome cost, with provenance and a declared corroboration tier) without introducing cost-effectiveness ranking. The architecture prohibits predictive scoring, comparative ranking, optimization objectives, and automated sanctioning; it preserves mandatory human oversight for escalations, version-controlled governance, arm's-length standards authorship, and structured remediation with notice and appeal. By separating coherence assessment and multi-party verification from causal inference and behavioral prescription, and by requiring that every result return to the party who produced it, the framework provides a structurally bounded, implementation-neutral alternative to scoring-based accountability that is forkable across domains under a single governing standard.

detail.abstract: We study how oil well transactions between public and private firms affect carbon emissions. Using precise geographic coordinates to link wells to gas flaring events detected in satellite imagery, we show that wells sold by public firms to private operators experience increased flaring intensity relative to geographically adjacent, non-transacted control wells. Further tests suggest that this increase is unlikely to reflect the selection of increasingly polluting wells, and is more consistent with private acquirers, who face weaker environmental scrutiny, raising flaring at the wells they purchase. Our findings suggest a novel channel through which environmental shareholder pressure can prove counterproductive: porous firm boundaries facilitate the transfer of polluting assets to operators willing to increase emissions.

title: Do Evaluators Reward Effort?
affiliations: , Monash University and

detail.title: Do Evaluators Reward Effort?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest to declare.

detail.abstract: Does evaluation reward only performance, or also the effort required to achieve it? This distinction is increasingly important as artificial intelligence allows people to produce more with less effort. We study whether evaluators reward effort independently of performance. In a preregistered randomized experiment, participating K-12 teachers regraded student work paired with an erroneous initial score. We randomized whether teachers received information about the student's classroom effort. When provided, the effort information was directionally consistent with the erroneous initial score, thereby providing a rationale consistent with it: Low effort accompanied an unduly harsh score, whereas high effort accompanied an unduly generous score. We also varied whether the initial score was attributed to a human colleague or an AI system. Because the quality of the work and its objective grade were known, we can determine whether effort information moves evaluations toward or away from actual performance. A high-effort signal led teachers to assign more generous grades, moving evaluations farther from the objective grade. In contrast, a low-effort signal had no detectable effect. These results were similar under human and AI attribution. The high-effort signal also improves teachers' perceptions of the initial grader's ability, comprehension, fairness, and responsibility. The findings indicate that high effort can serve as a source of deservingness in evaluation, selectively licensing generosity even when doing so moves judgments away from performance.

title: Why Europe should strategise on the U.S. DBCFT debate, and fast

detail.abstract: The United States is once again looking into a Destination-Based Cash Flow Tax (DBCFT) as a corporate tax reform initiative; a tax system based on cash flows that shifts the geographic allocation of corporate tax base from the investment jurisdiction to the market jurisdiction, combined with border adjustments. Adopting such a model would significantly advantage U.S. domestic production and investment, while disadvantaging foreign businesses, particularly those in countries that maintain a traditional corporate income tax model and Pillar Two minimum taxation. For European countries, this development constitutes both a strategic threat and a strategic opportunity. Remaining on the sidelines would mean falling behind the moment the United States makes the first move. The European Union and its Member States should therefore avoid a reactive posture and develop their own alternative. That alternative lies in a destination-based excess profits tax for multinational enterprises, equipped with a robust allowance for corporate equity and free of protectionist elements. Such an approach would allow Europe to lead the debate rather than follow it, strengthening both its competitiveness and its resilience in the area of corporate taxation. The time to wake up is now.

title: Quantity Constraints, Shadow Prices, and Linear Consumption Taxation

detail.title: Quantity Constraints, Shadow Prices, and Linear Consumption Taxation

detail.abstract: Essential services such as healthcare and education are often subject to institutional restrictions on the quantity or distribution of access. Such restrictions are commonly interpreted as departures from market allocation or as instruments motivated primarily by distributional considerations. This note studies the dual interpretation of such quantity constraints, relating the shadow-price representation of quantity restrictions to the broader distinction between quantity and price-based instruments. We show that when access to an essential service is subject to a distributional constraint on consumption dispersion, the associated shadow price generates an affine consumption-dependent wedge. In particular, a quadratic constraint on the variance of service consumption generates a wedge proportional to the deviation of individual consumption from its population mean. This wedge can be represented as a linear consumption tax combined with a uniform transfer: the tax is positive for above-average consumption and negative for below-average consumption, with zero aggregate fiscal incidence by construction. The note further shows how pointwise floor and ceiling constraints can be interpreted through individual shadow prices, while a variance constraint provides a distributional analogue in which the shadow price varies continuously across individuals. The analysis is formulated as a dual representation of quantity regulation rather than as an optimal tax model.

title: Beyond Rhetorical Reform: Structural Obstacles, Governance Architecture, and the Conditions for Durable Institutional Change in Caribbean Small Island Developing States

detail.title: Beyond Rhetorical Reform: Structural Obstacles, Governance Architecture, and the Conditions for Durable Institutional Change in Caribbean Small Island Developing States

declarations.funderStatement: I covered all the costs associated with this study.

detail.abstract: A newly appointed permanent secretary opens the shared drive her three predecessors left behind and finds four strategic plans, two accountability frameworks, and a digitisation strategy and no one left in the building who can explain why any of them stalled. Across the Caribbean region, governance reform has been a persistent and recurrent agenda item for over two decades, generating constitutional revisions, public service modernisation programmes, anti-corruption frameworks, and strategic planning exercises of considerable formal sophistication. Yet the empirical impact of these efforts on institutional performance has remained, by most assessments, weak and unsustained. This paper argues that the failure is not primarily attributable to resource deficits, implementation capacity shortfalls, or the technical inadequacy of reform designs, but to a more fundamental problem: the systematic neglect of governance architecture as the necessary precondition for sustainable institutional change. Drawing on public administration theory, new institutionalism, and the comparative literature on small state governance, the paper identifies three structural obstacles that recurrent reform programmes have consistently failed to address: the pervasive politicisation of institutional culture and its effects on organisational mandate orientation; the absence of performance measurement infrastructure as the foundational precondition for accountability; and the structural deficits in leadership formation that constrain the human capacity available to sustain reformed governance systems. Against these obstacles, the paper proposes four conditions for durable institutional reform: context-sensitive diagnostic approaches that eschew the transplantation of large-state templates; sequencing frameworks calibrated to institutional absorptive capacity; the integration of leadership development as a reform component rather than a precondition; and the systematic management of institutional memory as a governance asset. The paper concludes by examining the potential for a distinctively Caribbean school of governance that draws on regional intellectual and institutional capital rather than externally imported frameworks, and argues that regional integration mechanisms provide realistic foundations for such an endeavour.

title: How Exposed are Workers in MENA to AI? Evidence on Occupational Risks, Complementarity and the Digital Divide

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly reshaping labor markets worldwide, yet its impact remains understudied in regions with weaker digital infrastructure and significant skill-supply constraints, such as the Middle East and North Africa (MENA). This study investigates how the diffusion of AI may transform employment in MENA, where structural vulnerabilities and heterogeneous digital infrastructure may mediate the transition from theoretical task exposure to actual productivity gains and heighten the risks of unequal technological penetration. Using detailed occupational microdata from Egyptian (2018, 2023), Jordanian (2016, 2025) and Tunisian (2014, 2022, 2023) nationally representative labor-market surveys, we classify workers by their AI exposure and complementarity using alternative task-based indices. Further, we evaluate the feasibility of AI-driven augmentation by cross-referencing these indices with realized worker access to computing and high-speed internet at work. The analysis documents substantial crosscountry and within-country heterogeneity. While highly educated and formal workers in high-skill occupations are theoretically positioned to benefit from performing AI-complementary tasks, their ability to realize these gains is severely constrained by an infrastructural bottleneck. Across all three economies, between 33% and 39% of workers are trapped in functional obsolescence-holding high-complementarity jobs without workplace digital access. Notably, while highly educated women are concentrated in AI-complementary roles, they face a disproportionate workplace digital divide that blocks their capacity to leverage these skills. Comparative results show that Jordan exhibits the highest exposure, Tunisia the lowest, and Egypt a prominent concentration of high-exposure, low-complementarity employment. By quantifying the gap between theoretical complementarity and infrastructural readiness, the study offers targeted recommendations for firm level digital connectivity, education systems, and social protection to facilitate an inclusive AI transformation.

detail.abstract: Every asset price is a ratio of something to a unit, and the unit is almost always a currency. This note proposes and tests a different unit — nominal GDP per hour worked, chained across 38–43 countries at GDP weights, referred to as the world hour (CC-WH) — and re-measures a half-century of asset prices in it, using only free public data. Against a currency basket, consumer prices, wages, money per person and gold, the world hour has similar volatility and a drift between prices and money; what distinguishes it is that it omits the labour–capital split and asset-market expectations. Dividing by GDP and by GDP per hour are shown to be different questions, separated by the growth of hours worked. In world hours, the S&P 500 with dividends rose 3.5× from 2014 to 2026 against 5.0× in dollars, and about 2.7× since 2000 against 7×. A global market portfolio held since 2020 is roughly flat; over 1972–2025 world equities and the GMP beat the world hour in every rolling twenty-year window. Robustness to weights, hours sources and seasonal adjustment is reported; panel composition, chiefly China, is the dominant sensitivity.

detail.abstract:
This paper proves the sufficiency direction under the L² functional regime switching model: if a regime switch exists, then the statistical structure can detect it. Three core results are established. Theorem 1 (L² Sufficiency Theorem): under the local continuity assumption A0′ and the conditional non-degeneracy assumption A0″, the L² version of the unified shape function h_{L²}(τ) = ||Δ̄f(τ)||²_{L²(P_X)} attains a global unique maximum at the true regime boundary τ*. Theorem 2 (Multi-Regime Sufficiency Theorem): the functional-space BIC attains a global minimum at the true boundary set B*, with complete proofs covering underfitting, overfitting, and mislocation, where the effective parameter dimension is d_n. Theorem 3 (Spectral Weighted Sufficiency Theorem): for any α ∈ [0,1], when the fractional power kernel K_α satisfies the multiplier algebra condition and Δf ∈ H_{K_α}, the spectral weighted unified shape function h_α(τ) = ∑_{k=1}^{∞} a_k(τ)²/λ_k^α attains a global maximum at τ*; strict uniqueness holds for α=0 under A0″, and for α ∈ (0,1] under the multiplier contraction condition. Lemma 2 provides a verifiable sufficient condition for the multiplier contraction condition under the Gaussian kernel, and Appendix A gives the complete rigorous proof. Lemma 1 (X-Dependent Convex Combination Lemma) is the core technical contribution of this paper: under A0′, A0″(a), and the overlap condition, the conditional mean function of the mixed subsample is an X-dependent convex combination. Corollary 1 (Detection Information Loss) defines the information loss quantity I(τ) = C - h_{L²}(τ), explicitly I(τ) = ∫_X (1 - w(τ,x)²)(Δf(x))² dP_X(x), and proves that I(τ) > 0 holds for any τ ≠ τ*. Theorem 4 (Uniform Convergence of ĥ_{L²}) gives the finite-sample uniform convergence rate of ĥ_{L²}(τ). Theorem 5 (Argmax Consistency) proves τ̂_n → τ* under the cusp separation condition. Theorem 6 (Convergence Rate) gives the O_p(r_n) convergence rate of τ̂_n. Theorem 7 (BIC Selection Consistency) proves that the boundary set selected by multi-regime BIC converges in probability to B*. Proposition (Density Sufficient Condition for A0″(a)) gives a verifiable sufficient condition for non-degeneracy of the conditional Gram matrix. Proposition (Detection Resolution–Information Lower Bound Duality) quantitatively connects detection geometry with the estimation information limit for the first time. Proposition (Positive Semi-Definiteness of the Information Loss Matrix) further enriches the geometric structure of information loss. This paper explicitly states that A0 (T ⊥ X) has been replaced by A0′.

title: How Choice Overload Can Change Market Competition: Higher Prices and Lower Profits
affiliations: Harvard University

detail.title: How Choice Overload Can Change Market Competition: Higher Prices and Lower Profits
detail.abstract: Choice overload—the reduction in consumers' satisfaction associated with excessively large assortments—has been widely studied for its psychological consequences, while its implications for market competition remain comparatively underexplored. We develop a stylized model of price competition in which some consumers respond to excessive choice by comparing only a subset of the available alternatives. We show that reduced consumer comparison weakens competitive pressure, allowing sellers to charge higher prices. Choice overload therefore affects consumer welfare not only through its psychological consequences but also through higher prices.The analysis reveals a less obvious consequence on the supply side. Although weaker competition permits higher markups, competitive sellers earn lower expected profits because the increase in markup is more than offset by the lower probability of making a sale. We further show how these profit losses—and the additional profits foregone when sellers fail to recognize market overload—can be inferred from purchasing behavior and market prices. While illustrated using experimental evidence from the choice overload literature, the framework applies more generally whenever suitable purchasing and price data are available. Our findings reveal a market paradox: excessive product variety may ultimately leave both consumers and competitive sellers worse off.

title: Self-admitted technical debt in modular open-source Ruby on Rails ecosystems: a multi-project empirical study
affiliations: Moscow State University

detail.title: Self-admitted technical debt in modular open-source Ruby on Rails ecosystems: a multi-project empirical study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Background: Self-Admitted Technical Debt (SATD)-intentional shortcuts documented by developers in source code comments-has been extensively studied in Java and Python, but the Ruby on Rails ecosystem remains unexamined despite its scale in civic tech, e-commerce, and social networking. Aim: This study investigates the prevalence, distribution, and types of SATD in five prominent Ruby on Rails open-source projects, focusing on how modular architectures based on Rails engines shape SATD distribution. Method: We mined 1.55 million lines of Ruby across Decidim, Discourse, Solidus, Spree, and Mastodon, extracted 907 SATD comments using keyword-based heuristics, analyzed density and module-level correlations, and manually classified a stratified sample of 400 comments. Results: We report SATD under two scenarios: inclusive (treating rubocop:disable as formalised SATD) and classical (excluding it). The mean density is 0.50 SATD/KLOC in the inclusive scenario and 0.26 SATD/KLOC in the classical scenario-substantially below Java figures under either view. Formalised SATDpredominantly inline linter-suppression markers and dependency workaroundsaccounts for 55.1% of validated instances, a category absent from Java-focused taxonomies. Module size predicts SATD count (ρ = 0.684, p < 0.001) but not density. Manual validation reveals a 9.8% overall false-positive rate, concentrated in the REVIEW and TEMPORARY keywords. Conclusion: Ruby on Rails projects exhibit a distinct SATD profile in which debt is often expressed through RuboCop interaction rather than free-text comments. SATD taxonomies and detection tools should be extended with a formalised subclass to accommodate dynamically-typed ecosystems with strong linting cultures.

title: Waste Pricing, Recycling, and Household Adjustment: Evidence from Massachusetts
affiliations: University of Rhode Island, University of Rhode Island and University of Rhode Island - Department of Environmental and Natural Resource Economics

detail.title: Waste Pricing, Recycling, and Household Adjustment: Evidence from Massachusetts
detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the environmental effectiveness and distributional consequences of Pay-As-You-Throw (PAYT) in Massachusetts. We find that PAYT reduces municipal solid waste disposal by approximately 31 percent while increasing recycling by about 13 percent. Responses differ by income: lower-income municipalities respond primarily through reducing trash disposal, while higher-income municipalities rely more on recycling. Household scanner data provide complementary evidence: lower-income households exhibit larger declines in packaged-goods expenditure following PAYT adoption. These findings demonstrate that waste pricing can substantially reduce disposal while generating heterogeneous adjustment margins across income groups, with important implications for the distributional effects of environmental waste pricing policies.

title: Property Value Effects of Voluntary and Mandatory Flood Buyouts
affiliations: Purdue University and Purdue University - College of Agriculture

detail.title: Property Value Effects of Voluntary and Mandatory Flood Buyouts
detail.abstract: Flood buyout programs are widely used to reduce long-term exposure to flood risk, yet their effects on surrounding property values remain uncertain. This paper estimates the capitalization of flood buyout activity into residential property values using a hedonic pricing model and transaction-level data from Harris County, Texas, covering 2000–2024. We distinguish between voluntary and mandatory buyouts and examine how their effects on property values vary with spatial proximity and the intensity of nearby buyout activity. Using propensity score matching to improve comparability between treated and control properties, we estimate hedonic models across multiple distance bands and buyout counts. We find limited evidence of negative effects associated with voluntary buyouts, with the estimated decline in property values remaining small even at higher levels of exposure. In contrast, greater exposure to mandatory buyouts is associated with larger increases in property values. At the mean level of exposure, voluntary buyouts are associated with an approximately 0.4% decline in property values, compared with increases of 5–7% for mandatory buyouts, depending on distance. To our knowledge, this study provides the first empirical evidence on the property-value effects of mandatory flood buyouts while extending the literature on voluntary buyouts. Overall, the results suggest that the capitalization of buyout activity varies with buyout type and the scale and spatial concentration of acquisitions.

title: Locally Weighted Unified Shape Function and the One-to-One Correspondence with Regime Boundaries: Multi-Regime Local Peak Correspondence, Population Limit Geometry, and the Pseudo-Peak Phenomenon of Global Splitting

detail.title: Locally Weighted Unified Shape Function and the One-to-One Correspondence with Regime Boundaries: Multi-Regime Local Peak Correspondence, Population Limit Geometry, and the Pseudo-Peak Phenomenon of Global Splitting

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract:
In multi-regime structural break detection, the global unified shape function produces “convex-combination pseudo-peaks” because the two groups on the left and right each mix multiple regimes, causing the local peaks to lose the one-to-one correspondence with the true boundaries. This paper proposes the one-sided kernel locally weighted unified shape function: within the left and right windows of a candidate threshold τ, locally weighted least squares are performed separately, and the squared Mahalanobis norm of the coefficient difference is taken. Under the k-regime linear switching model (A0–A13), three core results are established. Theorem 1 (Two-Regime Bijection): a regime switch exists if and only if the population unified shape function attains a global unique maximum at the true boundary. Theorem 2 (Local Bijection Theorem, the core result of this paper): under the bandwidth condition b_n → 0 with n b_n / log n → ∞, the set of local maxima of h_{b_n} corresponds pointwise to the set of true boundaries in probability, with error O_p(b_n). Proposition (Pseudo-Peak Phenomenon of Global Splitting): there exists an explicit three-regime counterexample in which the global unified shape function produces a pseudo-peak in the inter-boundary region that is strictly greater than the peak of the weakest true boundary, whereas the locally weighted version is identically o_p(1) in the same region. This counterexample establishes the necessity of localization. In addition, Theorem 3 proves that under the null hypothesis sup_τ h_{b_n} = O_p(log n / (n b_n)) and the permutation test exactly controls the false positive rate; Lemma (population shape) gives a deterministic geometric characterization of the population limit shape (single peak plus zero band); Lemma (uniform convergence) proves the uniform convergence of the sample function to the population limit. Corollaries 1 and 2 generalize the results to the L² function space and give the consistency of the permutation test. Numerical verification includes a multi-regime counterexample (global pseudo-peak h(0.5) = 46.23 > h(τ₁*) = 30.71, local two-boundary correct rate 100%) and a bandwidth plateau.

title: No-False-Peak Theorem and Extreme Value Limit under the Null Hypothesis of Regime Switching: Necessity Direction, Exact Control of Permutation Tests, and Function-Space Generalization

detail.title: No-False-Peak Theorem and Extreme Value Limit under the Null Hypothesis of Regime Switching: Necessity Direction, Exact Control of Permutation Tests, and Function-Space Generalization

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract:
This paper proves the necessity direction of structural break detection: if a regime switch does not exist, then the statistical structure produces no false signal. Under the null hypothesis of the k-regime linear switching model (the required assumptions for each theorem are specified in the main text), three core results are established. Theorem 1 (No-False-Peak Theorem): the sample unified shape function ĥ(τ) tends to zero in probability at every candidate threshold τ,

sup_{τ ∈ [π, 1-π]} ĥ(τ) = O_p(n^{-1} log n).

No “false peak” exists—the statistical structure carries no spurious regime-structure information when no switch is present. Theorem 2 (Finite-Sample False-Peak Control): under the null hypothesis and A0 (T ⊥ X), the permutation test exactly controls the false positive rate at any significance level α,

P(permutation test rejects H_0 | H_0 holds) ≤ α,

and this control is non-asymptotic—it holds strictly for any finite sample size n. Theorem 3 (Extreme Value Limit Theorem): define the standardized statistic

M_n = max_{τ ∈ [π,1-π]} [n ĥ(τ) F̂_n(τ)(1 - F̂_n(τ))] / σ̂²,

then under the null hypothesis M_n converges to a non-degenerate limit distribution G,

M_n →_d G,

where G = sup_{u ∈ [π,1-π]} ||B̃(u)||²/[u(1-u)], B̃(·) is a p-dimensional standard Brownian bridge, and the limit distribution is completely identical to that of the sup-Wald statistic of Andrews (1993); the permutation version M_n* converges to the same G in the permutation-probability sense. Proposition (non-asymptotic bound) gives a non-asymptotic upper bound on sup_τ ĥ(τ). Proposition (power) proves that the permutation test has power tending to 1 under a fixed alternative. Proposition (local power) gives the non-degenerate power limit under a local alternative as the supremum of a drifted Brownian bridge (which degenerates to a noncentral χ²_p if the boundary is known), where the drift function is the product of the contraction weight w(τ) and the local parameter μ, and w(τ) is continuous at τ* with w(τ*)=1. Proposition (residual permutation) establishes the asymptotic false-positive control framework of the residual permutation test under the conditional independence assumption A0′ (which allows T and X to be correlated). Corollary (L²) generalizes Theorems 1–3 to the null hypothesis of the L² functional regime switching model (f_1 = ⋯ = f_k), where the no-false-peak property and the exact control of the permutation test hold only under A0, while under A0′ only the residual permutation test is asymptotically valid; for B-spline bases and Fourier bases, the Donsker-class condition of the extreme value limit is explicitly verified, and when d_n is fixed and the series basis consists of linear regressors, the limit distribution degenerates to G. The proofs of this paper directly cite the regime mixing lemma of Tang (2026af), the L² sufficiency framework of Tang (2026aq), and empirical process theory. Together with the sufficiency direction of Tang (2026aq), this paper constitutes the complete mathematical formalization of the correspondence level of structural break detection.
