title: Anthropomorphization of an Abstract Sign as a Source of Emotional Capital and Heavy-Tailed Market Concentration From Point Zero to the Upper Tail

detail.title: Anthropomorphization of an Abstract Sign as a Source of Emotional Capital and Heavy-Tailed Market Concentration From Point Zero to the Upper Tail

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests and no personal or institutional relationships that could have influenced this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study because it did not involve human participants, patients, animals, clinical intervention, or identifiable personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes testing whether latent anthropomorphization of an abstract sign constitutes the content of initial heterogeneity that is subsequently amplified by known mechanisms of cumulative advantage and manifests as heavy-tailed market concentration. The central distinction is between point zero, when the sign already exists but its market history is not yet known, and the subsequent trajectory, where repeated choice, social proof, accumulated size, copying, and path dependence operate. At point zero, abstract signs are examined without names, real logos, or information about the producer. The hypothesis states that some signs can unconsciously activate human representations and acquire ratings of trustworthiness, attractiveness, agency, character, status, and social closeness. The aggregate of these transferred properties forms initial emotional capital, treated as a candidate substantive component of the fitness parameter. The directionality of the relation "sign → human representation" is separated from the reverse relation and proposed for testing with asymmetric distributional measures, including Kullback-Leibler divergence. At the population level, the paper does not derive a heavy tail from anthropomorphism from scratch: existing models already explain the amplification of differences. The new claim concerns the missing level of seeding-the systematic measurement of the sign itself before history accumulates. Hypotheses are formulated concerning latent anthropomorphization, transfer of human properties, initial emotional capital, enrichment of the upper tail, cumulative amplification, condensation of feature space, and control for survivorship bias. The paper contains no empirical results.

title: Respondent Covariates Can Lie: Evidence From Hierarchical Choice Models – an Empirical Stress Test of Model Flexibility, New-Person Generalization, Fitted Heterogeneity, and Decision Consequences
affiliations: Red Analytics

detail.title: Respondent Covariates Can Lie: Evidence From Hierarchical Choice Models – an Empirical Stress Test of Model Flexibility, New-Person Generalization, Fitted Heterogeneity, and Decision Consequences

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this secondary analysis of de-identified market-research data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
A natural expectation when adding respondent covariates to hierarchical choice models is that useful information will matter while unhelpful information will mostly get out of the way. That expectation can fail. 

We deliberately broke the respondent-level relationship between a binary characteristic and preference, then entered twenty shuffled versions of that characteristic as upper-level covariates. The ordinary specification looked extraordinarily successful in sample, receiving large rewards from both likelihood and the NR-LMD approximation. 

On respondents held entirely outside estimation, the result reversed: prediction deteriorated sharply, while covariate-level regularization returned performance essentially to the no-covariate benchmark. Applied covariate cases produced smaller prediction differences. In a targeted case, better new-person prediction under regularization was not achieved by simply eliminating the differentiation the respondent information was added to capture. 

The resulting modeling problem is one of attribution: how much systematic preference heterogeneity should a model assign to respondent information, and what evidence should be required to support it? The results establish a failure mode, not its prevalence, and evaluate one regularization response rather than a uniquely correct solution. 
Model fit is treated as the beginning of the evidence chain, not the end. We follow the fitted structure through new-person transfer, heterogeneity attribution, and into quantities used for decisions.

title:
From Efficiency Inflation to Judgment Density: A Measurement Framework for AI-Augmented

Knowledge Work

detail.title:
From Efficiency Inflation to Judgment Density: A Measurement Framework for AI-Augmented

Knowledge Work

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this conceptual and methodological paper, as it does not report research involving human participants, personal data, or identifiable individual-level data. The empirical studies described in the paper constitute a proposed validation agenda and have not yet been conducted.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or external funding from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Generative and agentic AI have sharply reduced the marginal cost of producing professional outputs, making baseline reports, presentations, code, summaries, and plans faster and more abundant. Prior work introduced efficiency inflation as a value-dilution mechanism and judgment density as the human contribution that preserves value when ordinary output becomes abundant. The present paper narrows that theory-building argument to a measurement problem: how can judgment density be observed, scored, calibrated, and eventually validated in AI-augmented knowledge work? The paper provisionally models judgment density as a formative measurement framework rather than a reflective psychological scale. It specifies five observable dimensions: J1 Problem Definition, J2 Context and Evidence, J3 Choice and Tradeoffs, J4 Risk and Boundaries, and J5 Responsibility and Defensibility. Ratings are anchored in observable judgment events-such as explicit assumptions, evidence trails, rejected alternatives, escalation conditions, and accountable decision ownership-rather than surface polish, verbosity, or whether AI was used. A three-phase validation agenda is proposed: (1) content-domain review and rater calibration, including inter-rater reliability assessment; (2) a blinded 2 x 2 construct-discrimination experiment that independently manipulates surface quality and judgment quality; and (3) an eight-week organizational field test linking J1-J5 profiles to structural rework, first-pass acceptance, material-error incidence, decision adoption, and decision time. The paper does not claim that judgment density is already a validated scale. Its contribution is a falsifiable measurement architecture that moves the Efficiency Inflation research program from conceptual explanation toward empirical testing and organizational application.

title: Social Perceptions of Conversational AI Media: The Protective Role of Warmth in Personalized Advertising

detail.title: Social Perceptions of Conversational AI Media: The Protective Role of Warmth in Personalized Advertising

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author reports there are no competing interests to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study received approval from the Ethics Committee on Human and Animal Research of Meiji University: School of Commerce (approval number: 26-C-1). All participants provided digital informed consent prior to their participation.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by JSPS KAKENHI Grant Number 23K12564.

detail.abstract:
Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in everyday life and perceived not merely as a tool but as a social actor. Notably, conversational AI platforms have started to incorporate advertising. Although recent studies have begun to explore personalized advertising in this emerging medium, little is known about social perceptions of conversational AI in such advertising. Based on the stereotype content model, this research aims to examine how perceived warmth and competence shape consumer responses to personalized advertising on conversational AI platforms. Building on the key benefits and costs identified in personalized advertising research, this study explores whether warmth and competence strengthen the positive effect of perceived relevance and weaken the negative effect of privacy concerns on continuance use intention. The results showed that only warmth had a significant moderating effect, a protective role, in attenuating the negative effect of privacy concerns. This research broadens the conceptualization of personalized advertising media by highlighting consumer perceptions of conversational AI as a social actor characterized by warmth and competence. These findings offer practical guidance for conversational AI service providers and advertisers.

title: The Skills Absurdity and Wage Polarization
affiliations: ALTAX

detail.title: The Skills Absurdity and Wage Polarization

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships that could have influenced or be perceived as influencing this research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding

detail.abstract:
his study analyzes the structural transformations of the labor market in Albania during the period 2018–2026, focusing on the paradox between the historical growth of employment and the deepening of the skills gap. Based on quantitative, qualitative and comparative analysis of data from INSTAT, ILO, ETF, CEDEFOP, RCC and other international institutions, the study highlights that the Albanian economy has moved from a model constrained by unemployment to one constrained by the lack of qualified human capital.

In parallel, wage growth is not uniform, but is accompanied by significant polarization between professions with high demand and traditional sectors with low productivity. The analysis also examines the impact of labor migration, weaknesses of the vocational education system, comparison with Western Balkan countries, and develops three scenarios until 2035.

This edition also presents an original synthetic index, the ALTAX Skills Readiness Index, and a policy impact matrix.

title: So Far Away? Hiring Discrimination Against Female Commuters
affiliations: Monash University - Department of Economics, ,  and Johannes Kepler University Linz

detail.title: So Far Away? Hiring Discrimination Against Female Commuters
detail.abstract: We study gender differences in employers' responses to commuting distance using data from a large-scale correspondence test in Germany, Switzerland, and Austria. A 10 km increase in driving distance reduces women’s probability of receiving an interview invitation by 1.8 percentage points, around 9 percent of the mean female invitation rate, while commuting distance has no corresponding effect for men. The gender difference is statistically significant and robust to alternative distance measures and thresholds, firms’ rural or urban location, and local labor-market tightness. The female distance penalty does not vary detectably with applicants' reported marital status or the presence of children, providing no support for screening based on these observed indicators of household responsibilities.
